## 1. Real Numbers ## (CONCEPT MAP) ## Euclid's Division Algorithm Euclid's division algorithm is a technique to compute the Highest Common Factor of two given positive integers. To get H.C.F. of two positive integers c and d,c>d following steps are to be followed. (i) Apply Euclid's division lemma (iii) Continue the process till the ## Note: to c and d to get whole numbers q and r such that c=dq+r,0≤r<d. (ii) If r=0, then d is H.C.F. of c and d. If r≠0, apply division lemma to d and r. remainder is zero. The divisor at this stage will be the required H.C.F. (i) Euclid's division lemma and algorithm are closely interlinked but lemma is a proven statement used to prove the division algorithm. (ii) Euclid's division algorithm is stated for only + ve integers but it can be extended for all integers except zero. ## DIFFERENT TYPES OF REAL NUMBERS ## SYMBOLS OF SOME SETS OF SPECIFIC TYPE NUMBERS

Note: (a) Identity element of addition of a given real number is a real number which when added to the given number, the sum will be the given number itself. Therefore, 0 is the identity element of addition for any real number ' a ' because a+0=0+a=a, for all real number a. (b) Identity element of multiplication of a given real number is a real number which when multiply to the given number, the product will be the given number itself. Therefore, 1 is the identity element of multiplication for any real number ' a ', because 1. a=a.1=a, for all real number a. (c) Additive inverse of a given real number is a real number which when added to the given number, the sum will be 0 (zero). Therefore, −a is called the additive inverse of any real number a, because a+(−a)=(−a)+a=0, for all real number a. (d) Multiplicative inverse of a given real number is a real number which when multiply to the given number, the product will become 1 . Therefore, 1a is the multiplicative inverse of any non-zero real number a, because a×1a=1, for all real number a. ## TEST FOR DIVISIBILITY (i) A number is divisible by 2 when its units digit is even or zero e.g., 350,7916 , etc. 0 is an even number. (ii) A number is divisible by 3 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 3 e.g., 342, 13791, etc. (iii) A number is divisible by 4 when the number formed by last two right hand digits is divisible by 4 or if the last two digits are zero. e.g., 1264, 1500, etc. (iv) A number is divisible by 5 when its unit's digit is either 5 or 0 e.g., 50 , 245, etc. (v) A number is divisible by 6 when it is divisible by 2 and 3 both e.g., 354 . (vi) A number is divisible by 8 when the number formed by the last three right hand digits is divisible by 8 or when the last three digits are zero e.g., 1000,87895432 , etc. (vii) A number is divisible by 9 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 9 e.g., 39537. (viii) A number is divisible by 10 when its unit's digit is 0 e.g., 510,1350 , etc. (ix) A number is divisible by 11 when the difference between the sum of the digits in the odd and even places is either zero or a multiple of 11 . (x) A number is divisible by 12 when it is divisible by 3 and 4 both e.g., 624 , etc. (xi) A number is divisible by 25 when either last two digits are zero or the number formed by last two right hand digits is divisible by 25 e.g., 123475, etc. (xii) A number is divisible by 125 when the number formed by last three right hand digits is divisible by 125 e.g., 743625 , etc. ## EUCLID'S DIVISION LEMMA Euclid's Division Lemma states that for given positive integer a and b, there exist unique positive integers q and r satisfying a=bq+r;0≤r<b. ## TO FIND THE H.C.F. OF TWO POSITIVE INTEGERS USING EUCLID'S DIVISION ALGORITHM To obtain the H.C.F. of two positive integers, say a and b, with a>b, follow the step below : Step (i) : Apply Euclid's division lemma, to a and b. So, we find whole numbers, q and r such that a=bq+r,0≤r<b Step (ii) : If r=0,b is the H.C.F. of a and b. If r≠0, apply the division lemma to b and r. Step (iii) : Continue the process till the remainder become zero. The divisor at this stage will be the required H.C.F. ## Let us find the H.C.F. of 60 and 108 using the Euclid's Division Algorithm. ## SOLUTION : Step (i) : Since, 108 > 60 applying Euclid's Lemma to 60 and 108, we have 108=60×1+48 where 0≤48<60 Step (ii) : Since, remainder 48≠0 So, again applying the division lemma to 60 and 48, we have 60=48×1+12 where 0≤12<48. Step (iii) : Again remainder 12≠0 so applying division lemma to 48 and 12, we get 48=12×4+0, Here remainder is zero. Therefore, 12 is the required H.C.F. ## SOLUTION : Since 140 > 90, applying Euclid's Lemma 140=90×1+50 Since, remainder 50≠0 So, again applying Euclid's Lemma to 90 and 50, we have &90=50×1+40&50=40×1+10&40=10×4+0 Here, remainder is zero. Therefore, H.C.F. of 140 and 90 is 10 Now, find the H.C.F. of 10 and the third number 54. Since, 54>10, then by Euclid's Lemma &54=10×5+4&10=4×2+2&4=2×2+0 Here, remainder is zero. Therefore, 2 is H.C.F. of 10 and 54. Hence, required H.C.F. (140,90,54)=2. ## FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ARITHMETIC Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes and this factorisation is unique, except the order in which the prime factors occur. ## TO FIND THE H.C.F. AND L.C.M. BY PRIME FACTORISATION METHOD ## Algorithm (i) Factorize and express integers as a product of primes with powers. (ii) To find H.C.F. find the product of each common prime factor(s) with smallest power involved in the numbers. (iii) To find L.C.M. find the product of each prime factors with greatest power involved in the numbers. (iv) For any two positive numbers a and b, H.C.F. (a,b)× L.C.M. (a,b)=a×b Let ab,pq and ℓm be some fractions, then (a) LCM of ab,pq and ℓm=LCM(a,p,ℓ)HCF(b,q,m) (b) HCF of ab,pq and ℓm=HCF(a,p,ℓ)LCM(b,q,m) ## SOLUTION : First we write the prime factorisation of each of the given numbers. 8=2×2×2=23,9=3×3=32,25=5×5=52 ∴ L.C.M. =23×32×52=8×9×25=1800 and H.C.F. =1 Remark : The product of two positive integers is equal to the product of their H.C.F. and L.C.M., but the same is not true for three or more positive integers. Did You Know! The symbol π is called pi and this is a famous irrational number. The symbol π was introduced by an Anglo-Welsh philogist William Jones in 1706. ## CONSEQUENCE OF FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM Let p be a prime number and ' a ' be a positive integer. If p divides a2, then p divides ' a '. ## PROVING IRRATIONALITY OF NUMBERS In proving a number is an irrational number or not, we will use the 'consequence of fundamental theorem of Arithmetic'. ## SOLUTION : Let us assume, to the contrary, that 2 is rational. So, we can find integers r and s(≠0) such that 2=rs. Suppose r and s have a common factor other than 1 . Then, we divide by the common factor to get 2=ab, where a and b are co-prime i.e. they have no common. Factor other than 1 . So, b2=a Squaring on both sides and rearranging, we get 2b2=a2. Here we see that, 2 divides a2. Since 2 is a prime number and divides square of a positive number ' a ', therefore according to consequence of fundamental theorem 2 divides a also. So, we can write a=2c for some integer c. Substituting for a, we get 2b2=4c2, that is, b2=2c2. This means that 2 divides b2, and so 2 divides b (again using consequence of fundamental theorem) Therefore, a and b have at least 2 as a common factor. But this contradicts the fact that a and b have no common factors other than 1 . This contradiction, has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that 2 is rational. So, we conclude that 2 is irrational. Some properties of Rational and Irrational numbers. (a) Sum or difference of two or more irrational number is either zero or an irrational number (i) 7+(−7)=0 (ii) 3−3=0 (iii) 25−5=5 (irrational) (iv) 2−82=−72 (irrational) (v) 3+5−3=5 (irrational) (b) Product of two or more irrational numbers can be rational or irrational (i) 3×3=3 (rational) (ii) 513·513·513=513+13+13=533=5 (rational) (iii) 2·2·2=22 (irrational) (iv) 8·7=56=214 (irrational) (c) Division of one irrational number by another irrational number can be rational or irrational. (i) 277=2 (rational) (ii) 532=532 (irrational) ## DECIMAL EXPANSION OF RATIONAL NUMBERS (i) If a number in the form pq is such that p and q are co-prime (i.e. p and q have no common factor other than 1 ) and prime factorisation of q is of the form 2n5m, where n and m are non-negative integers then decimal expansion of pq terminates i.e. when we divide p by q, then we get an integer or a number upto a certain decimal place. i.e. when we divide p by q, then we get an integer or a number upto a certain decimal place. (ii) Let x be a rational number whose decimal expansion terminates. Then, x can be expressed in the form pq where p and q are co-prime, and the prime factorisation of q is of the form 2n5m; where n,m are non-negative integers. (iii) Let x=pq be a rational number, such that the prime factorisation of q is not of the form 2n5m; where n,m are non-negative integers. Then, x has a decimal expansion which is non-terminating repeating (recurring) i.e. decimal expansion of x has infinite digits after decimal point but no part of digits after decimal point repeat continuously. ## ILLUSTRATIOM : 7 Without performing the long division, find the decimal expansion of the following expressions. (i) 38 (ii) 13125 (iii) 780 (iv) 14588625 ## SOLUTION : (i) 38=323=3×5323×53=375103=0.375 (ii) 13125=1353=13×2323×53=104103=0.104 (iii) 780=724×5=7×5324×54=875104=0.0875 (iv) 14588625=22×7×52154=26×7×52124×54=233408104=23.3408 ## SOLUTION : 6.235=62351000=1247200, which is in the form of pq. Also q=200=23×52, which is in the form 2n×5m. Note: We can also convert a rational number which is non-terminating reccuring (i.e., repeating) in the form of pq, where p and q are co-prime (but q≠0 ). ## SOLUTION : Let x=23.426―⇒x=23.426426426….. Multiply equation (i) by 1000 , so that in the right hand side of the equation (i), the point (.) comes just after the first repeating part (426). ∴1000x=23426.426426…. Subtracting equation (i) from (ii), we get 999x=23403 ∴x=23403999=7801333∴23.426―=7801333, which is in the required form of pq. ## - Show that there is no positive integer n for which n−1+n+1 is rational. ## CONNECTING TOPIC ## H.C.F. of polynomials To find H.C.F. of two or more given polynomials follow the following steps : Step (i) : Express each polynomial as a product of irreducible factors (simple factors) with power. Numerical factors, if any, are expressed as product of primes with power. Step (ii) : If there is no common factor, then the H.C.F. is 1 . If there are common simple factors find the smallest powers of these irreducible factors in the factorised form of the polynomials. Step (iii) : Raise the irreducible factors to the smallest power found in step (ii) and multiply them to get the H.C.F. ## L.C.M. of polynomials To find L.C.M. of polynomial follow the following steps : Step (i) : Express each polynomial as a product of irreducible factors with power. Express numerical factors, if any, as product of primes with power. Step (ii) : Consider all the irreducible factors occurring in the given polynomials once only. Find the greatest power of each of these irreducible factors in the factorised form of the given polynomials. Step (iii) : Raise each irreducible factor to the greatest power found in step (ii), and multiply them to get the L.C.M. ## Positive integer in different form. a=bq+r form is nothing but a division algorithm, where ' a ' is divided by ' b ', then quotient ' q ' and remainder ' r ' is obtained. If a number a in the form bq+r i.e. a=bq+r,0≤r<b represent all positive integer for different value of b and q. - In practical application questions of L.C.M. and H.C.F., students face difficulty whether they take L.C.M. or H.C.F. in a given problem. If minimum word is used in the problem, then use L.C.M. and if maximum word is used in the problem, then use H.C.F. Let us understand the above concepts in a better way in different cases through illustrative examples. ## CASE-I : Positive integer in different form. Illustration: Show that any positive integer is of the form 3q or, 3q+1 or, 3q+2 for some integer q. Sol. Let a be any positive integer and b=3. Applying division Lemma with a and b=3, we have a=3q+r, where 0≤r<3 and q is some integer ⇒a=3q+0 or, a=3q+1 or, a=3q+2 ⇒a=3q or, a=3q+1 or, a=3q+2 for some integer q. ## CASE-II : Use of L.C.M. Illustration: On a morning walk, three persons step off together and their steps measure 40 cm,42 cm and 45 cm, respectively. What is the minimum distance each should walk so that each can cover the same distance in complete steps? Sol. Step measures of three persons are 40 cm,42 cm and 45 cm . The minimum distance each should walk so that each can cover the same distance in complete steps is the L.C.M. of 40 cm,42 cm and 45 cm . Prime factorisation of 40,42 and 45 gives 40=23×5,42=2×3×7,45=32×5 L.C.M. (40,42,45)= Product of the greatest power of each prime factor involved in the numbers =23×32×5×7=8×9×35=72×35=2520 cm. ## Think Out of the Box again change simultaneously. [Hint: Find L.C.M. of 60, 75 and 90. Ans. 9 : 45 A.M.] Q. 2. The floor of room has dimensions 12 m and 10 m can be covered completely by square tiles. Find least number of square tiles. [Hint: No. of tiles = Area of floor / Area of tile Ans. 30] Q. 3. A number when divided by 187 leaves remainder 35 , what will be the remainder when the same number is divided by 17 ? [Hint: Divide 187 and 35 by 17 and add remainder Ans. 1] ## CASE-III : Use of H.C.F. Illustration: The areas of three fields are 165 m2, 195m2 and 285m2 respectively. From these, flowers beds of equal size are to be made. If the breadth of each bed be 3 metres, what will be the maximum length of each bed? Sol. The areas of three fields are 165 m2, 195 m2 and 285 m2. Maximum area of a flower bed = H.C.F. of 165 and 195 and 285. We first find the H.C.F. of 165 and 195. Using Euclid's Algorithm, we have the following equations: 195=165×1+30 165=30×5+15 30=15×2+0 Now, the remainder is zero. Since the divisor at this stage is 15 . ∴ H.C.F. (165,195)=15. Now we find the H.C.F. of 15 and 285. Using Euclid's Algorithm, we have the following equation: 285=15×17+0 Now, the remainder is zero. Since the divisor at this stage is 15 . ∴ H.C.F. (15,285)=15. So H.C.F of 165, 195 and 285=15 ∴ Length of a flower bed =153=5 m. Q. 1. The traffic lights at three different road crossing change after 60sec,75sec and 90 sec respectively. If they all change simultaneously at 9:30 A.M., when will they ## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES 1. If d is the H.C.F. of 56 and 72, find Integral values of x,y satisfying d=56x+72y. Sol. Applying Euclid's division lemma to 56 and 72, we get 72=56×1+16 [∵5672(15616] Since the remainder 16≠0, so, we consider the divisor 56 as dividend and the remainder 16 as divisor. Now, on applying division lemma, we get 56=16×3+8 [∵16\longdiv56(3488] Since the remainder 8≠0, so, we consider the divisor 16 as dividend and the remainder 8 as divisor. Now, on applying division algorithm, we get 16=8×2+0 [∵8\longdiv16(2160] We observe that the remainder at this stage is zero. Therefore, last divisor 8 is the H.C.F. of 56 and 72 . From (ii), we get, 8=56−16×3⇒8=56−(72−56×1)×3[∵16=72−56×1 (from (i))] ⇒8=56−3×72+56×3⇒8=56×4+(−3)×72∴∴=4 and y=−3. 2. Show that any positive odd integer is of the form 8q+1,8q+3,8q+5,8q+7, where q is some integer. Sol. Let a and (b=8) be two positive integers where a is odd. Applying division lemma a=8q+r where 0≤r<8. So, r can take any of the values 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 Therefore, a=8q,8q+1,8q+2,8q+3,8q+4,8q+5,8q+6,8q+7,8q+8 Since, a is odd. Therefore, a cannot take values 8q,8q+2,8q+4,8q+8, since they can expressed as multiples of 2 . So, a will take values 8q+1,8q+3,8q+5 and 8q+7. 3. Write the decimal expansion of the following using prime factorisation : (i) 3516 (ii) 178 (iii) 327500 (i) 3516=35×5424×54=35×625(10)4=2187510000=2.1875 (ii) 178=17×5323×53=17×125(10)3=21251000=2.125 (iii) 327500=3275×5×5×2×2=32753×22=327×253×23=654(10)3=0.654 4. Prove that if x and y are odd positive integers, then x2+y2 is even but not divisible by 4 . Sol. We know that any odd positive integer is of the form 2q+1 for some integer q. So, let x=2m+1 and y=2n+1 for some integers m and n. ∴x2+y2=(2m+1)2+(2n+1)2⇒x2+y2=4(m2+n2)+4(m+n)+2 ⇒x2+y2=4q+2, where q=(m2+n2)+(m+n)⇒x2+y2 is even and leaves remainder 2 when divided by 4 ⇒x2+y2 is even but not divisible by 4 5. Two bills of ₹ 6075 and ₹8505 respectively are to be paid separately by cheques of same amount. Find the largest possible amount of each cheque. Sol. Largest possible amount of cheque will be the H.C.F. of 6075 and 8505 . Applying Euclid's division lemma to 8505 and 6075, we have, 8505=6075×1+2430 Since, remainder 2430≠0, therefore again apply division lemma to 6075 and 2430 6075=2430×2+1215. Again remainder 1215≠0 So, again apply division lemma to 2430 and 1215 2430=1215×2+0. Here the remainder is zero. So, H.C.F. =1215 Therefore, the largest possible amount of each cheque will be 1215 . 6. Three wheels can complete respectively 60,36,24 revolutions per minute. There is a red spot on each wheel that touches the ground at time zero. After how much time, all these spots will simultaneously touch the ground again? Sol. 1st  wheel makes 1 revolutions per sec; 2nd  wheel makes 610 revolutions per sec. 3rd  wheel makes 410 revolutions per sec In other words 1st ,2nd  and 3rd  wheel take 1,53 and 52 seconds respectively to complete one revolution. L.C.M. of 1,53 and 52= L.C.M. of 1,5,5 H.C.F  of 1,3,2=5 Hence, after every 5 seconds the red spots on all the three wheels touch the ground. 7. Find the largest number that will divide 398, 436 and 542 leaving remainders 7 , 11 and 15 respectively. Sol. Clearly, the required number is the H.C.F. of the numbers 398−7=391,436−11=425 and 542−15=527. First we find the H.C.F. of 391 and 425 by Euclid's algorithm as given below : 425=391×1+34;391=34×11+17;34=17×2+0 Clearly, H.C.F. of 391 and 425 is 17. Let us now find the H.C.F. of 17 and the third number 527 by Euclid's algorithm: 527=17×31+0 The H.C.F. of 17 and 527 is 17. Hence, H.C.F. of 391, 425 and 527 is 17 . Hence, the required number is 17. ## SOLVED EXAMPLES BASED ON CONNECTING TOPIC 8. A number is divisible by 8 if the number formed by the last three digits is divisible by 8 . i.e., 58N is divisible by 8 . Clearly, N=4 Again, a number is divisible by 11 if the difference between the sum of digits at even places and sum of digits at the odd places is either 0 or is divisible by 11 . i.e., (M+9+4+4+8)−(3+0+8+5+N)=M+25−(16+N)=M−N+9, must be zero or it must be divisible by 11 . i.e. M−N=11−9⇒M=2+4=6. Hence, M=6,N=4 10. Find the L.C.M of the polynomials 12(x4−x3) and 8(x4−3x3+2x2) Sol.Let the given polynomials be denoted as p(x) and q(x) respectively We have p(x)=22×3×x3×(x−1);q(x)=23×x2×(x−1)×(x−2) Irreducible factors are 2,3,x,x−1 and x−2. The respective highest exponents are 3,1,3,1 and 1 . ∴ L.C.M. =23×3×x3×(x−1)×(x−2)=24x3(x−1)(x−2). 11. If a number 774958A96B is to be divisible by 8 and 9, then find the values of A and B. Sol. According to the question, the number 774958A96B is divisible by 8 and 9 . For the number to be divisible by 8 , its last three digits have to be divisible by 8 . Then 960― and 968― can be the possibilities. Therefore, B should be either 0 or 8 . For the number to be divisible by 9 , the sum of the digits of the number should be divisible by 9 . If B=0, then the sum of the digits of 774958 A96 B=A+55. Now, 774958A96B to be divisible by 9, ( A+55 ) should be divisible by 9. It is possible only when A=8. If B=8, then the sum of the digits of 774958A96B=A+63. Now, 774958A968 to be divisible by 9 , ( A+63 ) should be divisible by 9 . It is possible only when A=9. A number is divisible by 4 when the number formed by last two right hand digits is divisible by 4 or if the last two digits are zero. e.g., 1264, 1500, etc.
A number is divisible by 5 when its unit's digit is either 5 or 0 e.g., 50 , 245, etc.
A number is divisible by 6 when it is divisible by 2 and 3 both e.g., 354 .
A number is divisible by 8 when the number formed by the last three right hand digits is divisible by 8 or when the last three digits are zero e.g., 1000,87895432 , etc.
A number is divisible by 9 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 9 e.g., 39537.
A number is divisible by 10 when its unit's digit is 0 e.g., 510,1350 , etc.
A number is divisible by 11 when the difference between the sum of the digits in the odd and even places is either zero or a multiple of 11 .
A number is divisible by 12 when it is divisible by 3 and 4 both e.g., 624 , etc.
A number is divisible by 25 when either last two digits are zero or the number formed by last two right hand digits is divisible by 25 e.g., 123475, etc.
A number is divisible by 125 when the number formed by last three right hand digits is divisible by 125 e.g., 743625 , etc.

(xii) A number is divisible by 125 when the number formed by last three right hand digits is divisible by 125 e.g., 743625 , etc.

## EUCLID'S DIVISION LEMMA
Euclid's Division Lemma states that for given positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, there exist unique positive integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> satisfying <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>;</mi><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.

theory_sections.topics: TO FIND THE H.C.F. OF TWO POSITIVE INTEGERS USING EUCLID'S DIVISION ALGORITHM
theory_sections.markdown:
## TO FIND THE H.C.F. OF TWO POSITIVE INTEGERS USING EUCLID'S DIVISION ALGORITHM
To obtain the H.C.F. of two positive integers, say <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>></mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, follow the step below :
Step (i) : Apply Euclid's division lemma, to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
So, we find whole numbers, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>
Step (ii) : If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is the H.C.F. of a and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, apply the division lemma to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>.
Step (iii) : Continue the process till the remainder become zero.
The divisor at this stage will be the required H.C.F.

theory_sections.markdown: ## Let us find the H.C.F. of 60 and 108 using the Euclid's Division Algorithm.

## FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ARITHMETIC
Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes and this factorisation is unique, except the order in which the prime factors occur.

theory_sections.topics: TO FIND THE H.C.F. AND L.C.M. BY PRIME FACTORISATION METHOD
theory_sections.markdown: ## TO FIND THE H.C.F. AND L.C.M. BY PRIME FACTORISATION METHOD

## Algorithm
(i) Factorize and express integers as a product of primes with powers.
(ii) To find H.C.F. find the product of each common prime factor(s) with smallest power involved in the numbers.
(iii) To find L.C.M. find the product of each prime factors with greatest power involved in the numbers.
(iv) For any two positive numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and b, H.C.F. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo></mrow></math> L.C.M. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> be some fractions, then
(a) LCM of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>LCM</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>HCF</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(b) HCF of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>HCF</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>LCM</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

## CONSEQUENCE OF FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> be a prime number and ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ' be a positive integer. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> divides ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> '.

## PROVING IRRATIONALITY OF NUMBERS
In proving a number is an irrational number or not, we will use the 'consequence of fundamental theorem of Arithmetic'.

## DECIMAL EXPANSION OF RATIONAL NUMBERS
(i) If a number in the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> are co-prime (i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> have no common factor other than 1 ) and prime factorisation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> is of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> are non-negative integers then decimal expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> terminates
i.e. when we divide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>, then we get an integer or a number upto a certain decimal place. i.e. when we divide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>, then we get an integer or a number upto a certain decimal place.
(ii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> be a rational number whose decimal expansion terminates. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> can be expressed in the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> are co-prime, and the prime factorisation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> is of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>; where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> are non-negative integers.
(iii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> be a rational number, such that the prime factorisation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> is not of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>; where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> are non-negative integers. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> has a decimal expansion which is non-terminating repeating (recurring) i.e. decimal expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> has infinite digits after decimal point but no part of digits after decimal point repeat continuously.

## ILLUSTRATIOM : 7

## CONNECTING TOPIC

## H.C.F. of polynomials
To find H.C.F. of two or more given polynomials follow the following steps :
Step (i) : Express each polynomial as a product of irreducible factors (simple factors) with power. Numerical factors, if any, are expressed as product of primes with power.
Step (ii) : If there is no common factor, then the H.C.F. is 1 . If there are common simple factors find the smallest powers of these irreducible factors in the factorised form of the polynomials.
Step (iii) : Raise the irreducible factors to the smallest power found in step (ii) and multiply them to get the H.C.F.

## L.C.M. of polynomials
To find L.C.M. of polynomial follow the following steps :
Step (i) : Express each polynomial as a product of irreducible factors with power. Express numerical factors, if any, as product of primes with power.
Step (ii) : Consider all the irreducible factors occurring in the given polynomials once only. Find the greatest power of each of these irreducible factors in the factorised form of the given polynomials.
Step (iii) : Raise each irreducible factor to the greatest power found in step (ii), and multiply them to get the L.C.M.

## Positive integer in different form.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> form is nothing but a division algorithm, where ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ' is divided by ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ', then quotient ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> ' and remainder ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ' is obtained.
If a number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> in the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> represent all positive integer for different value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>.
- In practical application questions of L.C.M. and H.C.F., students face difficulty whether they take L.C.M. or H.C.F. in a given problem.
If minimum word is used in the problem, then use L.C.M. and if maximum word is used in the problem, then use H.C.F.
Let us understand the above concepts in a better way in different cases through illustrative examples.

theory_sections.topics: CASE-I : Positive integer in different form.
theory_sections.markdown:
## CASE-I : Positive integer in different form.
Illustration: Show that any positive integer is of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> or, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> or, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> for some integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>.
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> be any positive integer and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>. Applying division Lemma with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> is some integer
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> or, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> or, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> or, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> or, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> for some integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>.

## CASE-II : Use of L.C.M.
Illustration: On a morning walk, three persons step off together and their steps measure <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>40</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>42</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and 45 cm, respectively. What is the minimum distance each should walk so that each can cover the same distance in complete steps?
Sol. Step measures of three persons are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>40</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>42</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and 45 cm .
The minimum distance each should walk so that each can cover the same distance in complete steps is the L.C.M. of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>40</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>42</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and 45 cm .
Prime factorisation of 40,42 and 45 gives
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>40</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>42</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
L.C.M. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>42</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>45</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Product of the greatest power of each prime factor involved in the numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>72</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2520</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

## CASE-III : Use of H.C.F.
Illustration: The areas of three fields are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>165</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>195</mn><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>285</mn><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> respectively. From these, flowers beds of equal size are to be made. If the breadth of each bed be 3 metres, what will be the maximum length of each bed?
Sol. The areas of three fields are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>165</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>195</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>285</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
Maximum area of a flower bed = H.C.F. of 165 and 195 and 285.
We first find the H.C.F. of 165 and 195.
Using Euclid's Algorithm, we have the following equations:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>195</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>165</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>165</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Now, the remainder is zero. Since the divisor at this stage is 15 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> H.C.F. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>165</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>195</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math>. Now we find the H.C.F. of 15 and 285.
Using Euclid's Algorithm, we have the following equation:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>285</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Now, the remainder is zero. Since the divisor at this stage is 15 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> H.C.F. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>285</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math>. So H.C.F of 165, 195 and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>285</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Length of a flower bed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES
1. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is the H.C.F. of 56 and 72, find Integral values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> satisfying <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>56</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>72</mn><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.
Sol. Applying Euclid's division lemma to 56 and 72, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>72</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>56</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>∵</mo><mn>56</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>72</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" /><mtd columnalign="center"><mfrac><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Since the remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, so, we consider the divisor 56 as dividend and the remainder 16 as divisor. Now, on applying division lemma, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>56</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>∵</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn><mi>\longdiv</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn><mn>6</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" /><mtd columnalign="center"><mfrac><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Since the remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, so, we consider the divisor 16 as dividend and the remainder 8 as divisor. Now, on applying division algorithm, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>∵</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>8</mn><mi>\longdiv</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center" /><mtd columnalign="center"><mfrac><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
We observe that the remainder at this stage is zero. Therefore, last divisor 8 is the H.C.F. of 56 and 72 .
From (ii), we get, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>56</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>56</mn><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>72</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>56</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo>∵</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>72</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>56</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> (from (i))]
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>56</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>72</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>56</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>56</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mn>72</mn><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.
2. Show that any positive odd integer is of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> is some integer.
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be two positive integers where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is odd.
Applying division lemma <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>. So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> can take any of the values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>
Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>
Since, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is odd. Therefore, a cannot take values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>, since they can expressed as multiples of 2 .
So, a will take values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>.

5. Two bills of ₹ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>₹</mi><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">8</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn></mrow></mrow></math> respectively are to be paid separately by cheques of same amount. Find the largest possible amount of each cheque.
Sol. Largest possible amount of cheque will be the H.C.F. of 6075 and 8505 .
Applying Euclid's division lemma to 8505 and 6075, we have, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8505</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6075</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2430</mn></mrow></math>
Since, remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2430</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, therefore again apply division lemma to 6075 and 2430
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6075</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2430</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1215</mn></mrow></math>. Again remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1215</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
So, again apply division lemma to 2430 and 1215
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2430</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1215</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Here the remainder is zero. So, H.C.F. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1215</mn></mrow></math>
Therefore, the largest possible amount of each cheque will be 1215 .
6. Three wheels can complete respectively <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>36</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow></math> revolutions per minute. There is a red spot on each wheel that touches the ground at time zero. After how much time, all these spots will simultaneously touch the ground again?
Sol. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mtext>st </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> wheel makes 1 revolutions per sec; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext>nd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> wheel makes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> revolutions per sec. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> wheel makes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> revolutions per sec In other words <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mtext>st </mtext></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext>nd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> wheel take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> seconds respectively to complete one revolution.
L.C.M. of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> L.C.M. of </mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mtext> H.C.F </mtext><mtext> of </mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
Hence, after every 5 seconds the red spots on all the three wheels touch the ground.
7. Find the largest number that will divide 398, 436 and 542 leaving remainders 7 , 11 and 15 respectively.
Sol. Clearly, the required number is the H.C.F. of the numbers
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>398</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>391</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>436</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>425</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>542</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>527</mn></mrow></math>.
First we find the H.C.F. of 391 and 425 by Euclid's algorithm as given below :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>425</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>391</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>34</mn><mi>;</mi><mn>391</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>34</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>17</mn><mi>;</mi><mn>34</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Clearly, H.C.F. of 391 and 425 is 17.
Let us now find the H.C.F. of 17 and the third number 527 by Euclid's algorithm:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>527</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>31</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
The H.C.F. of 17 and 527 is 17. Hence, H.C.F. of 391, 425 and 527 is 17 . Hence, the required number is 17.

## SOLVED EXAMPLES BASED ON CONNECTING TOPIC 8. If p is a prime number greater than 3 , then find the number by which (p2−1) is always divisible : Sol.Let p=5,7,11,13,…..

____ Clearly, all the above numbers 24, 48, 120 and 168 are divisible by 24 . 9. What is the value of M and N if M 39048458 N is divisible by 8 and 11 , where M and N are single digit integers? Sol. A number is divisible by 8 if the number formed by the last three digits is divisible by 8 . i.e., 58N is divisible by 8 . Clearly, N=4 Again, a number is divisible by 11 if the difference between the sum of digits at even places and sum of digits at the odd places is either 0 or is divisible by 11 . i.e., (M+9+4+4+8)−(3+0+8+5+N)=M+25−(16+N)=M−N+9, must be zero or it must be divisible by 11 . i.e. M−N=11−9⇒M=2+4=6. Hence, M=6,N=4 10. Find the L.C.M of the polynomials 12(x4−x3) and 8(x4−3x3+2x2) Sol.Let the given polynomials be denoted as p(x) and q(x) respectively We have p(x)=22×3×x3×(x−1);q(x)=23×x2×(x−1)×(x−2) Irreducible factors are 2,3,x,x−1 and x−2. The respective highest exponents are 3,1,3,1 and 1 . ∴ L.C.M. =23×3×x3×(x−1)×(x−2)=24x3(x−1)(x−2). 11. If a number 774958A96B is to be divisible by 8 and 9, then find the values of A and B. Sol. According to the question, the number 774958A96B is divisible by 8 and 9 . For the number to be divisible by 8 , its last three digits have to be divisible by 8 . Then 960― and 968― can be the possibilities. Therefore, B should be either 0 or 8 . For the number to be divisible by 9 , the sum of the digits of the number should be divisible by 9 . If B=0, then the sum of the digits of 774958 A96 B=A+55. Now, 774958A96B to be divisible by 9, ( A+55 ) should be divisible by 9. It is possible only when A=8. If B=8, then the sum of the digits of 774958A96B=A+63. Now, 774958A968 to be divisible by 9 , ( A+63 ) should be divisible by 9 . It is possible only when A=9. Hence, possible value of A and B are (8,0) or (9,8). 12. Find the H.C.F. of the polynomials. 150(6x2+x−1)(x−3)3 and 84(x−3)2(8x2+14x+5) Sol.Let f(x)=150(6x2+x−1)(x−3)3 and g(x)=84(x−3)2(8x2+14x+5) Now, f(x)=150(6x2+x−1)(x−3)3=150(6x2+3x−2x−1)(x−3)3=150[(6x2+3x)−1(2x+1)](x−3)3 &=150[3x(2x+1)−1(2x+1)](x−3)3=150(2x+1)(3x−1)(x−3)3=2×3×52(2x+1)(3x−1)(x−3)3&g(x)=84(x−3)2(8x2+14x+5)=84(x−3)2(8x2+10x+4x+5)&=84(x−3)2[2x(4x+5)+1(4x+5)]=84(x−3)2(4x+5)(2x+1)=22×3×7(x−3)2(2x+1)(4x+5) Hence, required H.C.F. =21.31(2x+1)1.(x−3)2=6(2x+1)(x−3)2

## STANDARD FORM OF A POLYNOMIAL
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are standard form of the same polynomial in variable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, in which power of the variable are either increasing or decreasing.
- A symbol like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> in the above polynomial, which takes various numerical values is known as a variable.
- In a polynomial, powers of the variable are non-negative integer.
- Terms having same variable with same indices are called like terms.
- Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are real numbers. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are all integers then the above polynomial is said to be a polynomial over integers.
- If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then degree of the above polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.

(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> is a polynomial of degree 7 .
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is an expression but not a polynomial, since it contains a term in which power of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, which is not a non-negative integer.
(iii) In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math> is the coefficient of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>;</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is the variable and 2 is the power or index of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.

## DIFFERENT TYPES OF POLYNOMIALS
There are some important types of polynomial based on the numebr of terms in it. These are listed below:
(i) Monomial : A polynomial having one term is called a monomial. Example : 3, 5x, 6a etc.
(ii) Binomial : A polynomial having two terms is called a binomial. Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> etc.
(iii) Trinomial : A polynomial having three terms is called a trinomial. Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>30</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> etc.
There are some important types of polynomials based on degrees. These are listed below :
(i) Linear polynomials : A polynomial of degree one is called a linear polynomial. The general form of the linear polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are any real constant and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a linear polynomial.
(ii) Quadratic polynomials : A polynomial of degree two is called a quadratic polynomial. The general form of the quadratic polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is a quadratic polynomial.
(iii) Cubic polynomials : A polynomial of degree three is called a cubic polynomial. The general form of a cubic polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is a cubic polynomial.
(iv) Biquadratic polynomials : A polynomial of degree four is called biquadratic polynomial. The general form of biquadratic polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
## SOLUTION :
Both are polynomials.
## VALUE OF A POLYNOMIAL
A polynomial of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> can be represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, etc. The value of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> is obtained by substituting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> in the given polynomial and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Consider the polynomial : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
If we replace <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> by 1 everywhere in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
So, we say that the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is 4 .
## ZERO(ES) / ROOT(S) OF POLYNOMIALS
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> be a root or zero of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
In other words, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is a root or zero of a polynomial if it is a solution to the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
The process of finding the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is actually solving the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Let's first find the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math>. To find the zeroes, we simply solve the following equation.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
So, this second degree polynomial has two zeroes or roots -5 and 3 .

## GEOMETRICAL MEANING OF THE ZERO(ES) OF A POLYNOMIAL
Zero(es) of a polynomial is/are the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate of the point(s) where the graph of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> intersects the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
## GRAPHS OF POLYNOMIALS
Graph of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a smooth free hand curve passing through points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi></mrow></math>. etc., where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>. are the values of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi></mrow></math>. respectively.
