## GRAPH OF A LINEAR POLYNOMIAL
Consider a linear polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. In class IX we have studied that the graph of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is a straight line that has exactly one zero. That is why <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is called a linear polynomial. Since two points determine a straight line, so only two points needed to plot or draw the line <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>. The line represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> crosses the x -axis at exactly one point, namely <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
## GRAPH OF A QUADRATIC POLYNOMIAL
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> be real numbers and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is known as quadratic polynomial in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and it has either no zero or two zeroes.
## Example :
1. There are no zeroes of quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and thus the graph of the polynomial doesn't intersect <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
2. There are two zeroes of quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> i.e., 2,2 ; which means both zeroes are same and thus the graph of this polynomial intersects <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-axis only once at 2 .
3. There are two zeroes of quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math> that is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, thus the graph of this polynomial intersect <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-axis at two places, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>&</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
Note : (i) The two zeroes of quadratic polynomial can be either both rational or both irrational.
(ii) Graph of a quadratic polynomial is always a parabola.
The graph shown in the illustration 5 and 6 are the parabola.
Some parabola are upward open as in illustration 5 and others are downward open as in illustration 6.
If the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> in the quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is positive, then the parabola is upward open. If the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> in the quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is negative, then the parabola is downward open.

## DIVISION OF POLYNOMIALS
On dividing a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> by a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, let the quotient be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and the remainder be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> or deg. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo><</mo><mo>deg</mo><mo>.</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Here, Dividend <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, Divisor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, Quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and Remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Division algorithm of a polynomial by a polynomial :
Step 1: Arrange the terms of the dividend and the divisor in descending order of their degrees.
Step 2 : Divide the first term of the dividend by the first term of the divisor to obtain the first term of the quotient.
Step 3 : Multiply all the terms of the divisor by the first term of the quotient and subtract the result from the dividend.
Step 4 : Consider the remainder as new dividend and proceed as before.
Step 5 : Repeat this process till we obtain a remainder which is either 0 or a polynomial of degree less than that of the divisor.

- Factor Theorem

## SOLUTION :
Two zeroes are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, is a factor of the given polynomial.
Now, we divide the given polynomial by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mi>&</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mi>&</mi><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> (First term of quotient is </mtext><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mtext> ) </mtext></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>−</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>+</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable><mtext> (Third term of quotient is </mtext><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext> ) </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
Now, by splitting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, we factorise <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
So, the remaining two zero(es) are given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. Therefore, the zero(es) of the given polynomial are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and 1 .

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>

CASE-II : To find the quotient and remainder using division algorithm
Illustration: Apply the division algorithm to find the quotient and remainder on dividing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>, by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
Sol. We have,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
We find that degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> and degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. Therefore, quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is of degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and the remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is of degree zero.
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>.
By using division algorithm, we obtain

Illustration: Obtain all the zeroes of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>, if two of its zeroes are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>.
Sol. It is given that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> are two zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a factor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext> On equating the constant terms </mtext><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>
Solving these equations, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext> and </mtext><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
∴ Quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and, Remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Since, remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

[Hint: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>.</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Ans. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> ]

[Hint: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>94</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>388</mn></mrow></math>.
Ans. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>94</mn></mrow></math>, remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>388</mn></mrow></math> ]
## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES
1. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>. Find the roots of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and sketch the graph of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Sol. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Therefore, the roots are -1 and 3 .
The graph intersects the X -axis at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and 3 .
2. How many real roots, i.e., roots that are real numbers, has the parabola of each graph ?
Sol. Graph (a) has two real roots. It has two x -intercepts (i.e., the graph intersects the X -axis at two different points)
Graph (b) has no real roots. It has no x-intercepts. Both roots are complex.
Graph (c) has two real roots which are equal.
3. Inspect the following graph to solve this equation : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Sol. The quadratic polynomial will have the value 0 at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and 5 .
4. Find the zero(es) of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold">−</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></math> and verify the relationship between the zero(es) and the coefficients.
Sol. Recall the identity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Using it, we can write:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
So, the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> is zero when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Therefore, the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Now, Sum of zeroes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Product of zeroes </mtext><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Constant term </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
5. Show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></math> is a root of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> is a root of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
6. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is a root of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>, then find the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></math> and if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is root of polynomial, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>27</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>128</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>176</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mn>12</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>128</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>356</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>228</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></math>
7. | Consider the standard form of linear equations in two variables. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>;</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> While solving the above system of equation by this method following three cases arise. (i) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>; system is called consistent, having one or unique solution and pair of straight lines representing the above equations intersect at one point only. (ii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>; system is called dependent and have infinitely many solution. Pair of lines representing the equations coincide. (iii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>; system is called inconsistent and has no solution. Pair of lines representing the equations are parallel or do not intersect at any point. |
## Equations Reducible to a Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
By using the suitable substitution or simplification first we convert the given system into the system of a pair of linear equations in two variables. Then after using any algebraic or graphical method we solve the system.

key_points.text: A symbol like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> in the above polynomial, which takes various numerical values is known as a variable.
In a polynomial, powers of the variable are non-negative integer.
Terms having same variable with same indices are called like terms.

Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are real numbers. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are all integers then the above polynomial is said to be a polynomial over integers.

If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then degree of the above polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> is a polynomial of degree 7 .

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is an expression but not a polynomial, since it contains a term in which power of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, which is not a non-negative integer.

In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math> is the coefficient of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>;</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is the variable and 2 is the power or index of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> are like terms.
Monomial : A polynomial having one term is called a monomial. Example : 3, 5x, 6a etc.

Binomial : A polynomial having two terms is called a binomial. Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> etc.

Trinomial : A polynomial having three terms is called a trinomial. Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>30</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> etc.

Linear polynomials : A polynomial of degree one is called a linear polynomial. The general form of the linear polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are any real constant and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.

Quadratic polynomials : A polynomial of degree two is called a quadratic polynomial. The general form of the quadratic polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.

Cubic polynomials : A polynomial of degree three is called a cubic polynomial. The general form of a cubic polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.

Biquadratic polynomials : A polynomial of degree four is called biquadratic polynomial. The general form of biquadratic polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

## STANDARD FORM OF A POLYNOMIAL
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are standard form of the same polynomial in variable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, in which power of the variable are either increasing or decreasing.
- A symbol like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> in the above polynomial, which takes various numerical values is known as a variable.
- In a polynomial, powers of the variable are non-negative integer.
- Terms having same variable with same indices are called like terms.
- Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are real numbers. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are all integers then the above polynomial is said to be a polynomial over integers.
- If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then degree of the above polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.
Did You
Know
If we put any polynomial equal to zero then we get polynomial equation i.e. if we put <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then we get the polynomial equation as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>

## Examples :
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> is a polynomial of degree 7 .
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is an expression but not a polynomial, since it contains a term in which power of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, which is not a non-negative integer.
(iii) In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math> is the coefficient of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>;</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is the variable and 2 is the power or index of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> are like terms.

## DIFFERENT TYPES OF POLYNOMIALS
There are some important types of polynomial based on the numebr of terms in it. These are listed below:
(i) Monomial : A polynomial having one term is called a monomial. Example : 3, 5x, 6a etc.
(ii) Binomial : A polynomial having two terms is called a binomial. Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> etc.
(iii) Trinomial : A polynomial having three terms is called a trinomial. Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>30</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> etc.
There are some important types of polynomials based on degrees. These are listed below :
(i) Linear polynomials : A polynomial of degree one is called a linear polynomial. The general form of the linear polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are any real constant and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a linear polynomial.
(ii) Quadratic polynomials : A polynomial of degree two is called a quadratic polynomial. The general form of the quadratic polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is a quadratic polynomial.
(iii) Cubic polynomials : A polynomial of degree three is called a cubic polynomial. The general form of a cubic polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is a cubic polynomial.
(iv) Biquadratic polynomials : A polynomial of degree four is called biquadratic polynomial. The general form of biquadratic polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

## VALUE OF A POLYNOMIAL
A polynomial of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> can be represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, etc. The value of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> is obtained by substituting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> in the given polynomial and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Consider the polynomial : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
If we replace <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> by 1 everywhere in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
So, we say that the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is 4 .

## ZERO(ES) / ROOT(S) OF POLYNOMIALS
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> be a root or zero of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
In other words, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is a root or zero of a polynomial if it is a solution to the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
The process of finding the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is actually solving the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Let's first find the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math>. To find the zeroes, we simply solve the following equation.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
So, this second degree polynomial has two zeroes or roots -5 and 3 .

theory_sections.topics: GEOMETRICAL MEANING OF THE ZERO(ES) OF A POLYNOMIAL
theory_sections.markdown:
## GEOMETRICAL MEANING OF THE ZERO(ES) OF A POLYNOMIAL
Zero(es) of a polynomial is/are the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate of the point(s) where the graph of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> intersects the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-axis.

## GRAPHS OF POLYNOMIALS
Graph of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a smooth free hand curve passing through points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi></mrow></math>. etc., where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>. are the values of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi></mrow></math>. respectively. In order to draw the graph of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, we may follow the following algorithm.

theory_sections.topics: Algorithm to draw the graph of the polynomials :
theory_sections.markdown:
## Algorithm to draw the graph of the polynomials : Step 1: Find the values y1,y2,…….yn, that is value of polynomial f(x) at x1,x2,……..xn and prepare a table that gives values of y or f(x) for various values of x.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⋯</mo><mo>⋯</mo></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⋯</mo><mo>⋯</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⋯</mo><mo>⋯</mo></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⋯</mo><mo>·</mo><mo>·</mo></mrow></math>
Step 2: Plot these points (x1,y1),(x2,y2),(x3,y3),……….,(xn,yn),……… on rectangular coordinate system. In plotting these points you may use different scales on the x and y-axis. Step 3 : Draw a free hand smooth curve passing through the points plotted in step 2 to get the graph of the polynomial f(x).

## GRAPH OF A LINEAR POLYNOMIAL
Consider a linear polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. In class IX we have studied that the graph of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is a straight line that has exactly one zero. That is why <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is called a linear polynomial. Since two points determine a straight line, so only two points needed to plot or draw the line <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>. The line represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> crosses the x -axis at exactly one point, namely <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

## GRAPH OF A QUADRATIC POLYNOMIAL
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> be real numbers and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is known as quadratic polynomial in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and it has either no zero or two zeroes.

## Example :
1. There are no zeroes of quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and thus the graph of the polynomial doesn't intersect <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
2. There are two zeroes of quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> i.e., 2,2 ; which means both zeroes are same and thus the graph of this polynomial intersects <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-axis only once at 2 .
3. There are two zeroes of quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math> that is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, thus the graph of this polynomial intersect <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-axis at two places, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>&</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
Note : (i) The two zeroes of quadratic polynomial can be either both rational or both irrational.
(ii) Graph of a quadratic polynomial is always a parabola.
The graph shown in the illustration 5 and 6 are the parabola.
Some parabola are upward open as in illustration 5 and others are downward open as in illustration 6.
If the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> in the quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is positive, then the parabola is upward open. If the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> in the quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is negative, then the parabola is downward open.

## ILLUSTRATIOM : 6
Draw the graph of the quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Also find its zeroes.

## GRAPHS OF A CUBIC POLYNOMIAL
A cubic polynomial is a function of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>&</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> are real constants but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then graph of a cubic function looks similar to one of the graphs in Figures (i), (ii) and (iii).
fig. (i)
fig. (ii)
fig. (iii)
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then graph of the cubic function looks similar to one of the graphs in Figures (iv), (v) and (vi).
