theory_sections.topics: RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ZERO(ES) AND COEFFICIENT OF A POLYNOMIAL
theory_sections.markdown:
## RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ZERO(ES) AND COEFFICIENT OF A POLYNOMIAL
(i) Zero of a linear polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> constant term </mtext></mrow><mrow><mo>coefficient</mo><mtext> of </mtext><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(ii) If quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is any real constant; then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>β</mi></mrow></math> are zeroes of quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, i.e., sum of zeroes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> coefficient of </mtext><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> coefficient of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> i.e., product of zeroes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> constant term </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> coefficient of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
We can obtain the quadratic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> (sum of zeroes) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> (product of zeroes)]
(iii) If cubic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is any real constant; then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>γ</mi></mrow></math> are zeroes of cubic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>α</mi><mi>β</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi><mi>γ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>γ</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi><mi>β</mi><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

## ILLUSTRATIOM : 8
If zeroes of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, then find the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math>.

## Some useful formulas :
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>α</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>α</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>α</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>α</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>α</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow></math>
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>α</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>α</mi><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(v) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>α</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>α</mi><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## DIVISION OF POLYNOMIALS
On dividing a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> by a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, let the quotient be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and the remainder be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> or deg. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo><</mo><mo>deg</mo><mo>.</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Here, Dividend <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, Divisor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, Quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and Remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Division algorithm of a polynomial by a polynomial :
Step 1: Arrange the terms of the dividend and the divisor in descending order of their degrees.
Step 2 : Divide the first term of the dividend by the first term of the divisor to obtain the first term of the quotient.
Step 3 : Multiply all the terms of the divisor by the first term of the quotient and subtract the result from the dividend.
Step 4 : Consider the remainder as new dividend and proceed as before.
Step 5 : Repeat this process till we obtain a remainder which is either 0 or a polynomial of degree less than that of the divisor.

## Learn More
- Factor Theorem
(i) If ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ) is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is a root of polynomial equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
(ii) Conversely, if the polynomial equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> has a root <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
- Remainder Theorem:
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be any polynomial of degree greater than or equal to one and ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ' be any real number. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is divided by linear polynomial ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ), then remainder is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

Sol. We find that degree of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> and degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>.

stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Equating coefficients of various powers of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and constant term from both sides, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext> On equating the constant terms </mtext><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>
Solving these equations, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext> and </mtext><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
∴ Quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and, Remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Since, remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

## Think Out of the Box
Q. 1. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is a root of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, then find other root of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
[Hint: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>.</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Ans. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> ]
Q. 2. If the quotient obtained on dividing the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>34</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>106</mn></mrow></math> by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> using division algorithm is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>, then find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> and also the reminder.
[Hint: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>94</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>388</mn></mrow></math>.
Ans. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>94</mn></mrow></math>, remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>388</mn></mrow></math> ]

## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES
1. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>. Find the roots of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and sketch the graph of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Sol. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Therefore, the roots are -1 and 3 .
The graph intersects the X -axis at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and 3 .
2. How many real roots, i.e., roots that are real numbers, has the parabola of each graph ?
Sol. Graph (a) has two real roots. It has two x -intercepts (i.e., the graph intersects the X -axis at two different points)
Graph (b) has no real roots. It has no x-intercepts. Both roots are complex.
Graph (c) has two real roots which are equal.
3. Inspect the following graph to solve this equation : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Sol. The quadratic polynomial will have the value 0 at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and 5 .
4. Find the zero(es) of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold">−</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></math> and verify the relationship between the zero(es) and the coefficients.
Sol. Recall the identity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Using it, we can write:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
So, the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> is zero when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Therefore, the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Now, Sum of zeroes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Product of zeroes </mtext><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Constant term </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
5. Show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></math> is a root of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> is a root of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
6. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is a root of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>, then find the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></math> and if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is root of polynomial, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>27</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>128</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>176</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mn>12</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>128</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>356</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>228</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></math>
7. Find the remainder when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
Sol. Put <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

(i) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>; system is called consistent, having one or unique solution and pair of straight lines representing the above equations intersect at one point only. (ii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>; system is called dependent and have infinitely many solution. Pair of lines representing the equations coincide. (iii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>; system is called inconsistent and has no solution. ## Equations Reducible to a Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
By using the suitable substitution or simplification first we convert the given system into the system of a pair of linear equations in two variables. Then after using any algebraic or graphical method we solve the system.

topics.chapter_name: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
topics.summary:
## SOLUTION OF A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES To find two numbers such that their sum is 35 and their difference is 5 . We can represent the problem algebraically by letting x represents the large number and y represents the smaller number. The problem is indicated by the two equations as given below: &x+y=33&x−y=5 The two equations for which we seek a common solution are called simultaneous equations. The two equations, taken together, comprise a system of equations. The value of the variables x and y that satisfied the above system of equations is called its solution. Each of the above equations represents a straight line. Graphically solution of a system of a pair of linear equations in two variables is the coordinates of the point where the two lines intersect each other. ## CONSISTENT, DEPENDENT AND INCONSISTENT SYSTEM OF EQUATIONS System of a pair of linear equations in two variables : &a1x+b1y+c1=0&a2x+b2y+c2=0 The given system of a pair of linear equations in two variables has either one solution, infinite solutions or no solution. Note that the variables in both the equations are same. Case (i); If a1a2≠b1b2, then the system has only one (or unique) solution, and the system is called consistent. In this case, a pair of straight lines represented by the system of equations intersect each other exactly at one point. Example: Consider the system of linear equations 2x−3y=6 and x+y=1 Here, a1=2,a2=1,b1=−3,b2=1 Now, 21≠−31⇒a1a2≠b1b2 Intersecting lines So, the system has unique solution. Case (ii); If a1a2=b1b2=c1c2, then the given system has infinite many solutions and the system is called dependent. In this case, a pair of lines represented by the system of equations, coincides with each other. So they intersect each other at infinite number of points. Example: Consider the system of equations 3x−y+5=0 and 6x−2y+10=0 Here, a1=3,a2=6,b1=−1,b2=−2,c1=5,c2=10 Now, 36=−1−2=510⇒a1a2=b1b2=c1c2 Now, the system has infinite solutions. Case (iii); If a1a2=b1b2≠c1c2, then the given system has no solution and the system is called inconsistent. In this case, a pair of lines represented by the system are parallel to each other. So they do not intersect each other at any point. Example: Consider the system of equations x−5y−6=0 and 2x−10y−14=0 Here, a1=1,a2=2,b1=−5,b2=−10,c1=−6,c2=−14 Now, 12=−5−10≠−6−14⇒a1a2=b1b2≠c1c2 Hence, the system has no solution. ## GRAPHICAL METHOD TO SOLVE A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES Draw the graph of both the equations of a pair of equations in two variables using same pair of horizontal and vertical lines called X and Y -axis respectively. Coordinates of the point(s) of intersection of the two lines is/are the solution(s) of the given pair of linear equations in two variables. ## SOLUTION : Here, a1a2=12,b1b2=3−3=−1,∴a1a2≠b1b2 Hence, the given system of a pair of equations in two variable is consistent. Let us draw the graphs of the equations (i) and (ii). For this, we find two solutions of each of the equations, which are given below in the table. x+3y=6

Plot the points A(0,2),B(6,0),P(0,−4) and Q(3,−2) on graph paper, and join the points to form the lines AB and PQ. Point B(6,0) common to both the lines AB and PQ. So, the solution of the pair of linear equations is x=6 and y=0. ## SOLUTION : (i) a1a2=57,b1b2=2−4=−12 ∵a1a2≠b1b2 Hence, the given system is consistent. (ii) a1a2=53,b1b2=106=53,c1c2=162=81 ∵a1a2=b1b2≠c1c2 Hence, the given system is inconsistent. (iii) a1a2=1015=23,b1b2=23,c1c2=1624=23 ∵a1a2=b1b2=c1c2 Therefore, the given system is dependent. ## ALGEBRAIC METHODS OF SOLVING A PAIR OF CONSISTENT LINEAR EQUATIONS A system of a pair of linear equations can be solved algebraically by following three methods. (A) Substitution Method (B) Elimination Method (C) Cross-multiplication Method ## (A) First Method - Substitution Method In substitution method, you have to express one of the variables in terms of the other using either of the equations and substitute this in other equation. ## Algorithm to find the solution : A system of a pair of linear equations in two variables: &a1x+b1y+c1=0&a2x+b2y+c2=0 Step 1 : Find the value of one variable, say y in terms of the other variable, i.e., x from either equation, whichever is convenient. Consider this equation as equation (iii). Step 2 : Substitute this value of y getting from equation (iii) in either equation (i) or (ii). This gives an equation in one variable x, from which you can easily get the value of x. Step 3 : Substitute the value of x obtained in Step 2 in the equations (iii), and obtain the value of the other variable y. ## Find the solution of the following system by substitution method : 4x+y=11;x+2y=8 ## SOLUTION : &4x+y=11&x+2y=8 It is easy to find the value of y in terms of x from the equation or to find the value of x in terms of y from the second equation. Let us find the value of y in terms of x from the first equation. The result is y=11−4x Now putting the value of y in equation (ii), we get x+2(11−4x)=8 We now have one equation that is linear in x; i.e the equation contains only the variable x. On solving, we find that x+22−8x=8 or −7x=8−22 or −7x=−14 or x=2 To get the corresponding value of y, we substitute x=2 in equation (iii). The result is y=11−4(2)=11−8=3 Thus, the solution of the given pair of linear equations are x=2 and y=3. ## (B) Second Method - Elimination Method ## Algorithm to find the solution: Step 1 : If coefficients of one variable (either x or y ) in both the equations are equal, then go to step- 2 otherwise multiply one or both the equation(s) by some suitable non-zero constants to make the coefficients of one variable (either x or y ) numerically equal. Step 2 : Add one equation to other or subtract one equation from the other so that one variable gets eliminated. In this case, you get an equation in one variable. By solving this equation you can easily get the value of the variable involved in this equation. Step 3 : Substitute the value of the variable ( x or y ) obtained in step- 2 in either of the original equations to get the value of the other variable. The elimination method is preferred when the numerical coefficients of one variable in the original equations are same. ## ILLUSTRATIOM : 4 The ratio of incomes of two persons is 9:7 and the ratio of their expenditures is 4:3. If each of them manages to save ₹ 2000 per month, find their monthly incomes. ## SOLUTION : Let the income of the two person be ₹9x and ₹7x and their expenditures be ₹4y and ₹3y respectively. Then the equations formed for the given situation are given by :  and &9x−4y=2000&7x−3y=2000 Step 1 : Multiply equation (i) by 3 and Equation (ii) by 4 to make the coefficients of y equal. Then, we get the equations: &27x−12y=6000&28x−12y=8000 Step 2 : Subtract equation (iii) from equation (iv) to eliminate y, because the coefficients of y are the same in equation (iii) and (iv). So, we get &(28x−27x)−(12y−12y)=8000−6000⇒&x=2000 Step 3 : Substituting this value of x in (i), we get 9(2000)−4y=2000 i.e., y=4000 So, the solution of the equations: x=2000,y=4000. Therefore, the monthly incomes of the two persons are ₹ 18,000 and ₹ 14,000 , respectively. Verification : 18000:14000=9:7. Also, the ratio of their expenditures =18000−2000:14000−2000=16000:12000=4:3 ## (C) Third Method - Cross-multiplication Method ## Algorithm to find the solution: Step 1: Write the given equations in the form : &a1x+b1y+c1=0&a2x+b2y+c2=0 Step 2 : Taking the help of the diagram given below : The arrows between the two numbers indicate that they are to be multiplied and the second product is to be subtracted from the first product. Write equation as xb1c2−b2c1=yc1a2−c2a1=1a1b2−a2b1 Step 3 : If a1b2−a2b1≠0, then solve xb1c2−b2c1=1a1b2−a2b1 for x and solve yc1a2−c2a1=1a1b2−a2b1 for y. ## SOLUTION : &3x+2y+25=0&x+y+15=0 Here, &a1=3,b1=2,c1=25&a2=1,b2=1,c2=15 ∴ &x2×15−25×1=y25×1−15×3=13×1−2×1⇒x30−25=y25−45=13−2&⇒x5=y−20=11⇒x5=1,y−20=1⇒x=5,y=−20 - In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD,∠A=(x+2)∘,∠B=(y+3)∘,∠C=(3y+8)∘ and ∠D=(4x−8)∘, find four angles. ## SOLUTION OF A SYSTEM OF A PAIR OF EQUATIONS REDUCIBLE TO THE SYSTEM OF A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES By using the suitable substitution or simplification first we convert the given system into the system of a pair of linear equations in two variables. Then after using any algebraic or graphical method we solve the system. ## ILLUSTRATIOM : 6 Solve the equations : 2x+13+3y+25=2 and 2(2x+1)3−3(3y+2)5=−1 ## SOLUTION : Given equations are : 2x+13+3y+25=2 ...(i) and 2(2x+1)3−3(3y+2)5=−1 Let 2x+13=u and 3y+25=v Then the equations become u+v=2… (iii) 2u−3v=−1 Multiplying (iii) by 3, 3u+3v=6. Adding (iv) and (v), 5u=5⇒u=1 Substituting this value of u in (iii), 1+v=2⇒v=2−1=1 Then 2x+13=u=1 and 3y+25=v=1⇒x=1 and y=1 ## SOLVING THE WORD PROBLEMS Many problems can be solved quickly and easily by converting them into a system of a pair of linear equations in two variables as follows : (i) Represent the unknown quantities by any two variables say x and y, which are to be determined. (ii) Find the conditions given in the problem and translate the verbal conditions into a pair of simultaneous linear equations using the variables x and y. (iii) Solve these equations and obtain the required quantities with appropriate units. ## ILLUSTRATIOM : 7 Find the two numbers such that half of the first equals one third of the second and twice their sum exceeds three times the second by 4 . ## SOLUTION : Let x and y be the first and second numbers respectively. We can write two equations almost directly from the statements of the problem as x2=y3 .... (i) and 2(x+y)=3y+4 Find the value of x in terms of y from first equation, x=2y3 Now putting the value of x in terms of y in second equation, 2(2y3+y)=3y+4 ⇒4y3+2y=3y+4⇒4y+6y=9y+12⇒y=12 (second number) Now putting the value of x in equation (i), x2=123⇒x=8 (first number) ## APPLICATIONS OF A SYSTEM OF A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES It is used to solve real life problem having two unknown by converting the real life problem into a pair of linear equations. It will be more clear by the following Illustration. ## SOLUTION : Let A and B be the two cars. A starts from P1 with constant speed of x km/hr and B starts from P2 with constant speed y km/hr. Case I: When the two cars move in same direction as shown in figures, the cars meet at position Q. Here, P1Q=5x km i.e., the distance travelled by car A in 5 hours with x km/hr. and P2Q=5y km i.e. the distance travelled by car B in 5 hours with y km/hr. We have, P,Q−P2Q=250⇒5x−5y=250⇒x−y=50 Case II: When two cars move in opposite direction as shown in figure, the cars meet at the position R. Here, P1R=2513x km and P2R=2513y km So, P1R+P2R=250⇒2513x+2513y=250⇒x+y=130 Adding (i) and (ii), we get ; 2x=180⇒x=90 and y=130−90=40 Speed of car A=90 km/hr and speed of car B=40 km/hr ## Learn More Concurrent lines: A set of lines are said to be concurrent if they all intersect at the same point. i.e., The coordinate of intersecting point P(a,b) satisfy all equations.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>24</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Substitution Method
Elimination Method
Cross-multiplication Method

In a cyclic quadrilateral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, find four angles.

Represent the unknown quantities by any two variables say <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>, which are to be determined.

Find the conditions given in the problem and translate the verbal conditions into a pair of simultaneous linear equations using the variables <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.
Solve these equations and obtain the required quantities with appropriate units.

If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> years be the sum of ages of a group of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> persons, then the sum of ages of these persons after <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> years will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> years, because after <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> years, age of each person in the group is increased by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> years and hence age of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> persons is increased by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> years.

If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> years be the sum of ages of a group of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> persons, then the sum of ages of these <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> persons before <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> years will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> years, because before <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> years age of each person in the group is decreased by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> years and hence age of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> persons is decreased by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> years.

If the average age of a group of persons is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> years, then after <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> years, their average age will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> years and before <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> years, their average age will be ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> ) years.

When in the question, comparison between ages after some years or before some years are given and you have to assume these ages, then you first assume their present ages and then accordingly find their ages after or before some years.

Solve for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>:</mi><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>;</mi><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

If the digits of the number differ by 2 , find the number. How many such numbers are there?
Solve the following system of equations graphically:

theory_sections.topics: SOLUTION OF A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES
theory_sections.markdown:
## SOLUTION OF A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES
To find two numbers such that their sum is 35 and their difference is 5 . We can represent the problem algebraically by letting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> represents the large number and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> represents the smaller number. The problem is indicated by the two equations as given below:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>33</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
The two equations for which we seek a common solution are called simultaneous equations. The two equations, taken together, comprise a system of equations. The value of the variables <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> that satisfied the above system of equations is called its solution. Each of the above equations represents a straight line.
Graphically solution of a system of a pair of linear equations in two variables is the coordinates of the point where the two lines intersect each other.

theory_sections.topics: CONSISTENT, DEPENDENT AND INCONSISTENT SYSTEM OF EQUATIONS
theory_sections.markdown:
## CONSISTENT, DEPENDENT AND INCONSISTENT SYSTEM OF EQUATIONS
System of a pair of linear equations in two variables :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
The given system of a pair of linear equations in two variables has either one solution, infinite solutions or no solution. Note that the variables in both the equations are same.
Case (i); If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, then the system has only one (or unique) solution, and the system is called consistent.
In this case, a pair of straight lines represented by the system of equations intersect each other exactly at one point.
Example: Consider the system of linear equations <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Intersecting lines
So, the system has unique solution.
Case (ii); If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, then the given system has infinite many solutions and the system is called dependent.
In this case, a pair of lines represented by the system of equations, coincides with each other.
So they intersect each other at infinite number of points.
Example: Consider the system of equations <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Now, the system has infinite solutions.
Case (iii); If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, then the given system has no solution and the system is called inconsistent. In this case, a pair of lines represented by the system are parallel to each other.
So they do not intersect each other at any point.
Example: Consider the system of equations <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow></math>
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Hence, the system has no solution.

theory_sections.topics: GRAPHICAL METHOD TO SOLVE A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES
theory_sections.markdown:
## GRAPHICAL METHOD TO SOLVE A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES
Draw the graph of both the equations of a pair of equations in two variables using same pair of horizontal and vertical lines called X and Y -axis respectively. Coordinates of the point(s) of intersection of the two lines is/are the solution(s) of the given pair of linear equations in two variables.

theory_sections.topics: ALGEBRAIC METHODS OF SOLVING A PAIR OF CONSISTENT LINEAR EQUATIONS
theory_sections.markdown:
## ALGEBRAIC METHODS OF SOLVING A PAIR OF CONSISTENT LINEAR EQUATIONS
A system of a pair of linear equations can be solved algebraically by following three methods.
(A) Substitution Method
(B) Elimination Method
(C) Cross-multiplication Method

## (A) First Method - Substitution Method
In substitution method, you have to express one of the variables in terms of the other using either of the equations and substitute this in other equation.

## Algorithm to find the solution :
A system of a pair of linear equations in two variables:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Step 1 : Find the value of one variable, say <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> in terms of the other variable, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> from either equation, whichever is convenient. Consider this equation as equation (iii).
Step 2 : Substitute this value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> getting from equation (iii) in either equation (i) or (ii). This gives an equation in one variable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, from which you can easily get the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
Step 3 : Substitute the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> obtained in Step 2 in the equations (iii), and obtain the value of the other variable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.

theory_sections.topics: Find the solution of the following system by substitution method :
theory_sections.markdown:
## Find the solution of the following system by substitution method :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>;</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>
## (B) Second Method - Elimination Method

## Algorithm to find the solution:
Step 1 : If coefficients of one variable (either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ) in both the equations are equal, then go to step- 2 otherwise multiply one or both the equation(s) by some suitable non-zero constants to make the coefficients of one variable (either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ) numerically equal.
Step 2 : Add one equation to other or subtract one equation from the other so that one variable gets eliminated. In this case, you get an equation in one variable. By solving this equation you can easily get the value of the variable involved in this equation.
Step 3 : Substitute the value of the variable ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ) obtained in step- 2 in either of the original equations to get the value of the other variable.
The elimination method is preferred when the numerical coefficients of one variable in the original equations are same.

## ILLUSTRATIOM : 4
The ratio of incomes of two persons is 9:7 and the ratio of their expenditures is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>. If each of them manages to save ₹ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math> per month, find their monthly incomes.
## (C) Third Method - Cross-multiplication Method

## Algorithm to find the solution:
Step 1: Write the given equations in the form :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Step 2 : Taking the help of the diagram given below :
The arrows between the two numbers indicate that they are to be multiplied and the second product is to be subtracted from the first product.
Write equation as
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Step 3 : If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then solve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and solve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.

theory_sections.topics: SOLUTION OF A SYSTEM OF A PAIR OF EQUATIONS REDUCIBLE TO THE SYSTEM OF A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES
theory_sections.markdown:
## SOLUTION OF A SYSTEM OF A PAIR OF EQUATIONS REDUCIBLE TO THE SYSTEM OF A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES
By using the suitable substitution or simplification first we convert the given system into the system of a pair of linear equations in two variables. Then after using any algebraic or graphical method we solve the system.

## ILLUSTRATIOM : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Solve the equations : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>

## SOLVING THE WORD PROBLEMS
Many problems can be solved quickly and easily by converting them into a system of a pair of linear equations in two variables as follows :
(i) Represent the unknown quantities by any two variables say <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>, which are to be determined.
(ii) Find the conditions given in the problem and translate the verbal conditions into a pair of simultaneous linear equations using the variables <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.
(iii) Solve these equations and obtain the required quantities with appropriate units.

## ILLUSTRATIOM : 7
Find the two numbers such that half of the first equals one third of the second and twice their sum exceeds three times the second by 4 .

Sol. Let the ten's and the unit's digits in the first number be x and y, respectively. So, the first number may be written as 10x+y in the expanded form (for example, 56=10(5)+6 ). When the digits are reversed, x becomes the unit's digit and y becomes the ten's digit. This number, in the expanded notation is 10y+x (for example, when 56 is reversed, we get 65=10(6)+5 ). According to the given condition. In this case, we get the number 42 . If y−x=2, then solving (i) and (iii) by elimination, we get x=2 and y=4. In this case, we get the number 24 . Thus, there are two such numbers 42 and 24 .
