theory_sections.topics: COORDINATE OF A POINT IN XY-PLANE
theory_sections.markdown:
## COORDINATE OF A POINT IN XY-PLANE
The perpendicular distance of any point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis is called <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate (or abscissa) of the point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and the perpendicular distance of the point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis is called <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate (or ordinate) of the point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>. In the figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> are the perpendicular distances of the point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> units <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> units <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> the position of point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Here the ordered pair <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is called the coordinates of point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>. Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a point in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-plane which is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> unit distant from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis and y unit distant from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
In the ordered pair <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, the first entry ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ' is the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate and the second entry ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ' is the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate of the point. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is called an ordered pair because there is a pair of numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>, in which the first entry <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is always <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate and the second entry <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is always <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate of the point.

## SIGN CONVENTIONS IN THE XY-PLANE
(a) All the distances are measured from origin (O).
(b) All the distances measured along or parallel to X -axis and right side of Y -axis are taken as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math>.
(c) All the distances measured along or parallel to X -axis and left side of Y -axis are taken as -ve.
(d) All the distances measured along or parallel to Y -axis and above the X -axis are taken as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math>.
(e) All the distances measured along or parallel to Y -axis and below the X -axis are taken as -ve.

theory_sections.topics: According to the Above Sign Conventions
theory_sections.markdown:
## According to the Above Sign Conventions
(i) Coordinate of origin is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) Coordinate of any point on the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis and right side of origin is of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
(iii) Coordinate of any point on the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis and left side of origin is of the form ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
(iv) Coordinate of any point on the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis and above the origin is of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
(v) Coordinate of any point on the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis and below the origin is of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
(vi) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis divide the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> plane in four parts. Each part is called a quadrant.
The four quadrants are written as I-quadrant (xoy), II-quadrant (yox '), III- quadrant ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mi>o</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ') and (IV) quadrant ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mi>o</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> ). Each of these quadrants shows the specific quadrant of the xoy plane as shown below :
Note: (a) Any of the four quadrants does not include any part of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
(b) In first quadrant both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-coordinates of any point are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math>.
(c) In second quadrant, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math>.
(d) In third quadrant, both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-coordinates of any point are-ve.
(e) In fourth quadrant, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-coordinate is -ve as shown in the diagram.

topics.summary:
## PLOTTING OF A POINT WHOSE COORDINATES ARE KNOWN
The point can be plotted by measuring its proper distances from both the axes. Thus, any point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> can be plotted as follows :
(i) Measure <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> equal to h along the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
(ii) Now measure <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> perpendicular to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>.
The method of describing the location of points in a plane was proposed by the great French mathematician Rene' Descartes in 17th century. Rene' Descartes' Latinized name is Renatius Cartesius and from here the terminology "Cartisian plane" and "Cartisian coordinate system" are derived.
## DISTANCE BETWEEN TWO POINTS
Distance between any two points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> in the plane is the length of the line segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>.
From <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> draw perpendiculars <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> respectively on the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> perpendicular on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>.
Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is a right angled triangle,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>P</mi><msup><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>Q</mi><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(By the Pythagoras Theorem)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
i.e., Distance between any two points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> difference of abscissae </mtext><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> difference of ordinates </mtext><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Corollary : The distance of the point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> from the origin <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Coordinate geometry is used to manage and regulate the location of air transport. Coordinate system is used in the Global Positioning System (GPS) which provides location and time information in all weather conditions. In a GPS, the longitude and the latitude of a place are its coordinates. The distance formula is used to find the distance between two places in a GPS.
## APPLICATIONS OF DISTANCE FORMULA
(i) For given three points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> to decide whether they are collinear or vertices of a particular triangle. First we find the length of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> then we shall find that the point are
(a) Collinear, if the sum of two shorter distances is equal to the longest distance
(b) Vertices of an equilateral triangle if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>
(c) Vertices of an isosceles triangle if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>
(d) Vertices of a right angled triangle if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(ii) For given four points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>;
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>;</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is a square.
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>;</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is a rhombus.
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>;</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is a rectangle.
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>;</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is a parallelogram.
(iii) (a) Diagonal of square, rhombus, rectangle and parallelogram always bisect each other
(b) Diagonal of rhombus and square bisect each other at right angle.
(c) Three given points are collinear if area of the triangle formed from these three points is zero.
(d) Four given points are collinear, if area of quadrilateral formed from these four points is zero.
## SECTION FORMULA
To find the co-ordinates of a point, which divides a line segment joining two points internally in a given ratio :
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> be the two given points and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> be a point on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, which divides it internally in the given ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.
We have to find the co-ordinates of P . Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Draw the perpendiculars <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and B respectively on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-axis and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> from A and P on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> respectively. Then, from similar triangles AKP and PTB, we have, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>A</mi><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
From (i), we have, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mo>⇒</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Therefore, co-ordinates of a point which divides the line segment joining the points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> in the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> internally is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
The coordinates of a point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> which divides line segment joining two points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> externally in the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
## SOLUTION :
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be the required point. Then,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
So, the coordinates of P are ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>21</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> )
## MID-POINT FORMULA
The co-ordinates of the mid-point of the line segment joining two points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> can be obtained by taking <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> in the section formula given above. Putting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> in the section formula, we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mtext> and </mtext><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Hence, co-ordinates of the mid-point joining two points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Prove that the points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝐂</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are the vertices of an isosceles right-angled triangle. Find the coordinates of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> so that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is a square.
## SOLUTION :
Consider the given points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Now, by distance formula, we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>36</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>52</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>36</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>52</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>104</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>52</mn></mrow></msqrt><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>52</mn></mrow></msqrt><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>52</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>52</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>104</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>90</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Hence, it is proved that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are the vertices of an isosceles right-angled triangle.
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> be the midpoint of diagonal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> of the square <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>.
Then the coordinates of the mid point P of diagonal AC is
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Also the diagonals of a square bisect each other. So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is also the mid point of diagonal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>. Let the coordinates of the point D be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Then we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>
Hence, the coordinates of D are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
## POINTS OF TRISECTION
Trisection means a line is dividing into three equal parts.
This can be done by finding two points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> on the line segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>
Let us assume <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>
Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
Also, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Hence, we can conclude that, to find points of trisection, we find two points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> which divides AB in the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, respectively.

Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be the given points. Let the points of trisection be P and Q . Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow></math> (say).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>λ</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>λ</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mi>:</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>λ</mi><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow><mi>:</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>λ</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
So, P divides AB internally in the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> while Q divides internally in the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. Thus, the coordinates of P and Q are
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mtext> respectively </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
Hence, the two points of trisection are ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ) and ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> )

Prove analytically that if in a triangle, two medians are equal in length, then it is an isosceles triangle.
## SOLUTION :
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> be a triangle in which two medians <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> are equal in length, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> are the mid-points of sides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> respectively. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> be the mid-point of the side <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and length of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> as origin and axes as shown in the figure then
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>≡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>≡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext> and </mtext><mi>C</mi><mo>≡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then by mid-point formula,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
Since, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>, therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><msup><mi>E</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mn>9</mn><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∵</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
Hence, the point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> and </mtext><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
From (i) and (ii), we find that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is an isosceles triangle.
Hence, it is proved that, if in a triangle two medians are equal, then it is an isosceles triangle.

## 1. Centroid of a Triangle
The centroid G is the point of intersection of medians <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and CF , which are the lines joining a vertex with the mid-point of opposite side.

where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
## 2. Incentre of the Triangle
The incentre I is the centre of circle touching the sides of the triangle internally, called INCIRCLE and it is the point of intersection of the internal bisectors. AP, BQ, CR of the vertex angles.
The coordinates of incentre I are given by
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>,

3. Circumcentre of the Triangle
The circumcentre <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is the centre of the circle passing through the vertices of triangle and it is the point of intersection of perpendicular bisectors of the sides of triangle.
Thus, we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>
Circumcentre of a right angled triangle is the mid points of its hypotenuse.
4. Orthocentre: It is the point of intersection of perpendicular drawn from vertices on opposite sides of a triangle.
Remarks: (i) If the triangle is equilateral, the centroid, incentre, orthocentre, circumcentre coincides.
(ii) Orthocentre, centroid and cirumcentre are always collinear.
(iii) In an isosceles triangle, centroid, orthocentre, incentre, circumcentre lies on the same line.

CASE-I : To find distance between two places on earth by using latitude \& longitude
Latitude : It is a coordinate that specifies the north-south position of a point on Earth's surface.
Longitude : It is coordinate that specifies the east-west position of a point on the Earth's surface.
Illustration: The coordinates of Kolkata is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>22.6</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>88.4</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> and the coordinates of Bangalore is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>13</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>77.5</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>. Find the air distance between Bangalore and Kolkata.
(Consider the length of the latitude between two longitudes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> apart is 110 km and length of longitude between two latitudes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> apart is 104 km .)
Sol.
Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>22.6</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>13</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>9.6</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>88.4</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>E</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>77.5</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10.9</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>
where, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>9.6</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9.6</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>104</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>998.4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>10.9</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10.9</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>110</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1199</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Distance between Banglore and Kolkata <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>998.4</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1199</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>1560</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
CASE-II : Proof of geometrical theorem by used the formula of coordinate geometry.
Illustration: The line segment joining the middle points of two sides of a triangle is equal to half of its third side.
Sol.
Consider a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> whose vertex <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> is the origin and side <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is along + ve direction of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-axis. Suppose coordinate of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> be ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ) and coordinate of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> be ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> )
Also suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> are mid-points of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> respectively.
Using mid-point formula
Coordinate of C is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and D is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Using distance formula
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> units.

2. The distance between two points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is 5 . Find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
Sol. By using distance formula, we have the distance between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
It is given that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
Squaring both sides, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>±</mi><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
