## TO FIND THE HEIGHT AND THE DISTANCE OF TOWER STANDING ON A HORIZONTAL PLANE
Let AB be a tower and B be its foot. On the horizontal line through B , take two points P and Q . Measure the length PQ .
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>.
Let the angles of elevation of the top A of the tower as seen from P and Q be respectively <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>></mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></math>.
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.
From right angled <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>tan</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi></mrow></math>
From right angled <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>tan</mi><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow></math>
From equations (i) and (ii),
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Also, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
In the above case, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> are on the same side of the tower.
If the two points are on the opposite sides of the tower then from the adjoining figure, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>tan</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></mfrac><mtext> or </mtext><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mtext> and </mtext><mi>tan</mi><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></mfrac><mtext> or </mtext><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi><mo>.</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>∴</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>∴</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow></mfrac><mtext> and </mtext><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Note : Here, all the lines <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are in the same plane.
The angle of elevation of a cliff from a fixed point is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math>. After going up a distance of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mi></mrow></mrow></math> meters towards the top of the cliff at an angle of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></math>, it is found that the angle of elevation is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math>. Show that the height of the cliff is
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>cos</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>sin</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>cot</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi></mrow></mfrac><mtext> meters </mtext></mrow></math>

## CONNECTING TOPIC
Bearing : If the observer and the object are on same plane (level), then bearing is defined. A bearing is an angle , measured clockwise or anticlockwise from the any one of four standard direction East, West, North and South.
## Learn More

## Compass bearing:
Compass bearing always begin with North ( N ) or South ( S ) in clockwise or anti clockwise direction, which ever is smallest angle.
Two stations due south of a leaning tower which leans towards the north are at distances <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi></mrow></mrow></math> metres and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math> metres from its foot. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></math> be the elevations of the top of the tower from these stations, prove that inclination <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math> of the leaning tower to the horizontal is given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>cot</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>α</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>cot</mi><mi>β</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.

## Think Out of the Box
Q. 1. A bird is sitting on the top of a vertical pole 20 m high and its elevation from a point O on the ground is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. It flies off horizontally straight away from the point O . After one second, the elevaion of the bird from O is reduced to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>30</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Then, find the speed (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> ) of bird.
Ans. Speed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>.
Q. 2. A man is walking towards a vertical pillar in a straight path, at a uniform speed. At a certain point A on the path, he observes that the angle of elevation of the top of the pillar is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>30</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. After walking for 10 minutes from A in the same direction, at a point B , he observes that the angle of elevation of the top of the pillar is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Then find the time taken (in minutes) by him, from B to reach the pillar.
Ans. ## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES
1. The angles of elevation of the top of a tower from the top and the foot of a pole of height <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> respectively. Find the height of the tower.
Sol. Let AB and CD be the pole and tower respectively.
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>30</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>tan</mi><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mo>∴</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>
Again, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>tan</mi><msup><mn>30</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo>∵</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>h</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math>.
Hence, height of the tower <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
2. A man is standing on the deck of a ship, which is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">8</mn><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> above water level. He observes the angle of elevation of the top of a hill as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and the angle of depression of the base of the hill as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>30</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Calculate the distance of the hill from the ship and the height of the hill.
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> be the distance of hill from man and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> be the height of hill which is required.
In rt. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>tan</mi><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo>∵</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>
In rt. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>tan</mi><msup><mn>30</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Distance of ship from hill <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
∴ Height of hill <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>8</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
3. A vertical tower stands on a horizontal plane and is surmounted by a vertical flag staff of height 5 meters. At point on the plane, the angle of elevation of the bottom and the top of the flag staff are respectively <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold">∘</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold">∘</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Find the height of the tower.
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> be the tower of height <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> meter and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> be the height of flag staff surmounted on the tower.
Let the point of the plane be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> at a distance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> meter from the foot of the tower.
In rt. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>tan</mi><msup><mn>30</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mi>h</mi></mrow></math>
In rt. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>tan</mi><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
From (i) and (ii), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
So, the height of tower <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

The angle of elevation of an aeroplane from a point on the ground is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. After a flight of 15 sec , the elevation changes to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. If the aeroplane is flying at a height of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math> metres, find the speed of the aeroplane.
Sol. Let the point on the ground is E which is y metres from point B and let after 15 sec ., flight covers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> metres distance
In rt. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>tan</mi><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3000</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3000</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
In rt. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>tan</mi><msup><mn>30</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3000</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∵</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3000</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
From eqs. (i) and (ii)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3000</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3000</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3000</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3000</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1.732</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>⇒</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3000</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>0.732</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2196</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
Speed of aeroplane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Distance covered </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Time taken </mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2196</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>146.4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2196</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>18</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>527.04</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Hence, the speed of aeroplane is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>527.04</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

There is a small island in the middle of a 100 m wide river and a tall tree stands on the island. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> are points directly opposite to each other on the two banks, and in line with the tree. If the angles of elevation of the top of the tree from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> are respectively <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>30</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, find the height of the tree.
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> be the tree.
Let the height of the tree be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> metres, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

Sol. Let length of tower <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

Shadow of tower, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

In rt. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>tan</mi><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>
Putting the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> in (ii), we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>⇒</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>⇒</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>⇒</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1.73</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8.65</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>23.65</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>

In rt. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>tan</mi><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>⇒</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
In rt. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>tan</mi><msup><mn>30</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>

## 10. Circles Foundation ## (CONCEPT MAP) ## CIRCLE A circle is the set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance from a fixed point in the plane. The fixed point is called the centre of the circle. The fixed distance is called the radius of the circle. Usually a circle is named by its centre and radius. A circle with centre ' O ' and radius ' r ' is named as circle ( O,r ). OR A circle is the locus of a point which moves in a plane in such a way that its distance from a given fixed point in the plane is always constant. ## CONGRUENT AND CONCENTRIC CIRCLES We say that two circles are congruent if they have the same radius. Two or more circles with the same centre are called concentric circles. In the figure, circles (O,p),(O,q),(O,r) are three concentric circles. ## CYCLIC QUADRILATERAL If all vertices of a quadrilateral lie on a circle, then it is called a cyclic quadrilateral. Remark : Sum of opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is 180∘. In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD,∠A+∠C=180∘ and ∠B+∠D=180∘ ## Learn More An exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to its opposite interior angle. In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD,∠CBE=∠ADC ## TERMS RELATED TO A CIRCLE - A line segment that connects two distinct points on a circle is called a chord. - A chord that passes through the centre of a circle is called a diameter. Diameter is the longest chord of a circle. - A line that intersects the circle at exactly two points is called a secant (line). - A tangent to a circle is a straight line which touches the circle at only one point. The point where the tangent touches the circle is called the point of contact of the tangent to the circle. In the figure, P is the point of contact of the tangent to the circle. ## Learn More Segments : The chord of a circle divide it into two parts. Each part is called a segment. Smaller part is called minor segment and larger part is called major segment. Alternate segment and its angle: The segment of a circle opposite to the angle formed by a tangent and a chord through the point of contact is called the alternate segment for that angle. Theorem: An angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact is equal to the angle in the alternate segment. In the figure, ∠APC=∠CDP and ∠BPD=∠DCP Time to Check Your Knowledge In the given figure, two circles C1 and C2 intersect at S and Q.PQN and RQM are tangents drawn to C1 and C2 respectively at Q.MAB and ABN are the chords of the circles C1 and C2. If ∠NQR=85∘, then find ∠AQB. ## NUMBER OF TANGENTS FROM A POINT 'P' TO A CIRCLE ## Case I : When point ' P ' lies outside the circle Only two tangents can be drawn from an exterior point to a circle. In the figure, PQ and PR are the two tangents from an exterior point P to a circle. ## Case II : When point ' P ' lies on the circle Only one tangent can be drawn from a point lying on the circle. ## Case III : When point ' 𝐏 ' lies inside the circle No tangent can be drawn from a point lying inside the circle. ## LENGTH OF A TANGENT Length of the segment of the tangent from the external point ' P ' and the point of contact with the circle is called the length of the tangent from the point ' P ' to the circle. ## Theorem 1: Statement : The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. Given : PQ is a tangent of a circle at a point A and O is the centre of the circle. To prove : OA⟂PQ Construction : Take any point B on PQ . Join OB . Proof : Distance of centre from any point on tangent other than the point of contact is greater than its distance from point of contact. Since, point B is outside the circle. Therefore, OB>OA Hence, out of all the line segments joining the centre O to the points on the tangent, OA is the least. Since perpendicular from a point O on the tangent PQ is least of all line segments joining the centre to the points on the tangent. Hence OA⟂PQ. Note : Converse of Theorem-1 is also true. ## Remarks : The line containing the radius through the point of contact is called the 'normal' to the circle at the point. Normal to a circle at the point of contact of a tangent to the circle is perpendicular to the tangent. ## Theorem 2: Statement : The lengths of two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal. Given : O is the centre of the circle. RP and RQ are two tangents drawn from external point R to the circle. To prove: RP=RQ Construction : Join OP, OQ and OR. Proof: We know that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. ∠OPR=∠OQR=90∘ In △OPR and △OQR, &∠OPR=∠OQR=90∘[By(i)]&OR=OR( Common sides )&OP=OQ( Radii of the same circle ) So, from right angle-hypotenuse-side congruency ΔOPR≅△OQR Since corresponding sides of two congruent triangles are equal. ∴RP=RQ Corollary : Centre of the circle lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangent drawn from an exterior point. When two chords intersect each other inside a circle, the products of their segments are equal i.e. AP×PB=CP×PD. It is known as intersecting chord theorem. The product of the intercepts of two secants from an external point are equal. i.e. PA×PB=PC×PD. It is known as intersecting secants theorem. Find the length of the common chord PQ . ## COMMON TANGENTS - If a line is tangent to two circles in the same plane, then the line is called a common tangent to the circles. - If the two circles are on the same side of the tangent, then the common tangent is called Direct common tangent. - If the two circles are on the opposite side of the tangent, then the common tangent is called Indirect (or transverse) common tangent. In the figure (i), AB is the Direct common tangent and in figure (ii) AB is the Indirect (or transverse) common tangent. ## IMPORTANT POINTS TO BE REMEMBER
1The number of common tangents to the circles one lying inside the other is zero.
2The number of common tangents to two circles touching internally is one. i.e. one direct common tangent.
3The number of common tangents to two intersecting circles is two, i.e., two direct common tangents.
4The number of common tangents to two circles touching externally is three, out of which two are direct common tangents and one is indirect or transverse common tangent.
5The number of common tangents to two non-intersecting circles is four, out of which 2 are direct common tangents and 2 are indirect (or transverse) common tangents.
6When two circles touch each other internally or externally, then the line joining the centres is perpendicular to the tangent drawn at the point of contact of the two circles. key_points.text: A line segment that connects two distinct points on a circle is called a chord.
A chord that passes through the centre of a circle is called a diameter. Diameter is the longest chord of a circle.
A line that intersects the circle at exactly two points is called a secant (line).

A tangent to a circle is a straight line which touches the circle at only one point. The point where the tangent touches the circle is called the point of contact of the tangent to the circle. In the figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is the point of contact of the tangent to the circle.
The distance between two parallel tangents drawn to a circle is equal to the diameter of the circle.
If a line is tangent to two circles in the same plane, then the line is called a common tangent to the circles.
If the two circles are on the same side of the tangent, then the common tangent is called Direct common tangent.
If the two circles are on the opposite side of the tangent, then the common tangent is called Indirect (or transverse) common tangent.

## 10. Circles
Foundation
## (CONCEPT MAP)

## CIRCLE
A circle is the set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance from a fixed point in the plane. The fixed point is called the centre of the circle. The fixed distance is called the radius of the circle.
Usually a circle is named by its centre and radius. A circle with centre ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi></mrow></math> ' and radius ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ' is named as circle ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ).
OR
A circle is the locus of a point which moves in a plane in such a way that its distance from a given fixed point in the plane is always constant.

## CONGRUENT AND CONCENTRIC CIRCLES
We say that two circles are congruent if they have the same radius.
Two or more circles with the same centre are called concentric circles.
In the figure, circles <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are three concentric circles.

## CYCLIC QUADRILATERAL
If all vertices of a quadrilateral lie on a circle, then it is called a cyclic quadrilateral.
Remark : Sum of opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
In cyclic quadrilateral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

## Learn More
An exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to its opposite interior angle. In cyclic quadrilateral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>

## TERMS RELATED TO A CIRCLE
- A line segment that connects two distinct points on a circle is called a chord.
- A chord that passes through the centre of a circle is called a diameter. Diameter is the longest chord of a circle.
- A line that intersects the circle at exactly two points is called a secant (line).
- A tangent to a circle is a straight line which touches the circle at only one point. The point where the tangent touches the circle is called the point of contact of the tangent to the circle. In the figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is the point of contact of the tangent to the circle.

## Learn More
Segments : The chord of a circle divide it into two parts. Each part is called a segment. Smaller part is called minor segment and larger part is called major segment.
Alternate segment and its angle: The segment of a circle opposite to the angle formed by a tangent and a chord through the point of contact is called the alternate segment for that angle.
Theorem: An angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact is equal to the angle in the alternate segment.
In the figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

## Case III : When point ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝐏</mi></mrow></math> ' lies inside the circle
No tangent can be drawn from a point lying inside the circle.

## LENGTH OF A TANGENT
Length of the segment of the tangent from the external point ' P ' and the point of contact with the circle is called the length of the tangent from the point ' P ' to the circle.

## Theorem 1:
Statement : The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
Given : PQ is a tangent of a circle at a point A and O is the centre of the circle.
To prove : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mi>⟂</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Construction : Take any point B on PQ . Join OB .
Proof : Distance of centre from any point on tangent other than the point of contact is greater than its distance from point of contact. Since, point B is outside the circle. Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Hence, out of all the line segments joining the centre O to the points on the tangent, OA is the least.
Since perpendicular from a point O on the tangent PQ is least of all line segments joining the centre to the points on the tangent. Hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mi>⟂</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Note : Converse of Theorem-1 is also true.

## Remarks :
The line containing the radius through the point of contact is called the 'normal' to the circle at the point. Normal to a circle at the point of contact of a tangent to the circle is perpendicular to the tangent.

## Theorem 2:
Statement : The lengths of two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
Given : O is the centre of the circle. RP and RQ are two tangents drawn from external point R to the circle.
To prove: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Construction : Join OP, OQ and OR.
Proof: We know that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>90</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>90</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> Common sides </mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> Radii of the same circle </mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
So, from right angle-hypotenuse-side congruency
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mo>≅</mo><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Since corresponding sides of two congruent triangles are equal.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Corollary : Centre of the circle lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangent drawn from an exterior point.
When two chords intersect each other inside a circle, the products of their segments are equal i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow><mo>×</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow><mo>×</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. It is known as intersecting chord theorem.
The product of the intercepts of two secants from an external point are equal. i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>. It is known as intersecting secants theorem.

## COMMON TANGENTS
- If a line is tangent to two circles in the same plane, then the line is called a common tangent to the circles.
- If the two circles are on the same side of the tangent, then the common tangent is called Direct common tangent.
- If the two circles are on the opposite side of the tangent, then the common tangent is called Indirect (or transverse) common tangent.
In the figure (i), AB is the Direct common tangent and in figure (ii) AB is the Indirect (or transverse) common tangent.

## IMPORTANT POINTS TO BE REMEMBER
1The number of common tangents to the circles one lying inside the other is zero.
2The number of common tangents to two circles touching internally is one. i.e. one direct common tangent.
3The number of common tangents to two intersecting circles is two, i.e., two direct common tangents.
4The number of common tangents to two circles touching externally is three, out of which two are direct common tangents and one is indirect or transverse common tangent.
5The number of common tangents to two non-intersecting circles is four, out of which 2 are direct common tangents and 2 are indirect (or transverse) common tangents.
6When two circles touch each other internally or externally, then the line joining the centres is perpendicular to the tangent drawn at the point of contact of the two circles. Case (I) Two circles with centres <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> touch each other internally at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>.</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is the line drawn through the centres and XY is the common tangent drawn at P <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is perpendicular to XY Case (II) Two circles with centres <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> touch each other externally at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the line joining the centres of the circles and XY is the common tangent to the two circles at P .Y

## CONNECTING TOPIC
Consider two circles with centres <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and radii <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
Case I: If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>></mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, i.e. the distance between centres <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> the sum of radii.
Then, the circles neither touch nor intersect and one circle is out of other.
Case II : If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Then, the circles touch one another externally.
Case III : If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo><</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo><</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Then, the circles intersect at two distinct points. [Assuming <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>></mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ].
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo><</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo><</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Case IV : If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Then, the circle touch one another internally.
Case V : If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo><</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Then, the smaller circle completely lies inside the bigger circle.

## Incircle :
The largest circle that will fit inside the triangle i.e., the circle which touches all sides of a triangle is called incircle or inscribed circle and centre is called the triangle's incentre. Clearly, each side of the triangle is a tangent to the circle. Thus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> are tangents to the circle. Radius through the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>⟂</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>⟂</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>⟂</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
Also, lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>.
Let us understand the above concepts in a better way in different cases through the illustrative examples.
CASE-I : When radius of the incircle and two parts of one side (like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> of the side <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ) of a triangle are given and we have to find other two sides of a triangle.
Illustration: The radius of the incircle of a triangle is 3cm and the segments into which one side is divided by the point of contact are 5 cm and 9 cm . Determine the other two sides of the triangle.
Sol. A circle with centre ' O ' and radius 3 cm inscribed in a triangle ABC such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> [tangents from external points] <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
Area of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
We know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>Ar</mo><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>△</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mo>∴</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mi>;</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>

CASE-II : When all three sides of triangle are given and we have to find radius of the incircle.
Illustration: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> circle is inscribed in a triangle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Find the radius of circle.
Sol. Let radius of circle be r cm .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∵</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
Ar <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>21</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>84</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∵</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>△</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>84</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>×</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>×</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>×</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>84</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
CASE-III : When a circle inscribed in a triangle whose all sides are given and we have to find the portion of a side (like AD or BD of AB ) of a triangle.
Illustration: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> circle inscribed in a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> having sides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Sides, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> touches the circle at point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> respectively. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and
Now,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∵</mo><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>~</mi><mi>△</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> By </mtext><mi>A</mi><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>∴</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>

## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES
1. PQ is a chord of length 8 cm of a circle of radius 5 cm . The tangents at P and Q intersect at a point T (see Fig.). Find the length of TP.
Sol. Join OT . Let it intersect PQ at a point R . Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is isosceles triangle and TO is the angle bisector of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mi>⟂</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Therefore, OT bisects PQ which gives
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Also, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>90</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Therefore, right triangle TRP is similar to the right triangle
PRO (by AA similarity).
This gives, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

Find the length of tangent drawn from a point whose distance from the centre of a circle is 5 cm and the radius of the circle is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Sol. In figure, O is the centre of the circle and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
∵ The tangent is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. Hence, in right angled triangle OPA,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mtext> or </mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
Hence, the length of tangent is 4 cm .

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mtext> gives </mtext><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> from </mtext><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mtext> gives </mtext><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> from </mtext><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>

Clearly, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is a square
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>&</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>P</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>P</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>=</mo><mi>&</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
( ∵ Lengths of tangents drawn from an external point are same.)

Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

Given, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> are two perpendicular diameters.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are parallel tangents at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> respectively.
