(iv) Join <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>
(v) Draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>
(vi) Draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is the required <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi></mrow></math> with its sides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> of the corresponding sides of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
11.
Given, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. To construct a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Steps of construction :
(i) Draw a line <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(ii) Draw an angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(iii) Cut an arc of length 5 cm on AX , taking A as centre. The point obtained is B .
(iv) Join the points B and C .
To construct a triangle whose sides are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> of the corresponding sides of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(v) Draw any ray AY making an acute angle with AC on the opposite to the vertex <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
(vi) Locate 5 (the greater of 3 and 5 in 3/5) points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> on AY so that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
(vii) Join <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and draw a line through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mrow /><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> point, 3 being smaller of 3 and 5 in 3/5) parallel to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> to intersect AC at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(viii) Draw a line through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> parallel to the line CB to intersect AB at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is the required triangle.
For justification of the construction, note that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mi>~</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∵</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Therefore,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>,
i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Also, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is parallel to CB .
Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

## Steps of construction :
(i) Draw a line segment BC of 5 cm .
(ii) Draw a ray BX such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>30</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(iii) With centre B and radius 3 cm an arc is drawn which intersects the ray BX at point M .
(iv) Join M to C .
(v) Draw ray CY such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Y</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, which intersects ray AX at A to form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Clearly, AB is the largest side of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Now, we have to divide the line segment AB in the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
(vi) Mark three points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> on the line segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(vii) Join A to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
(viii) Draw a line through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> parallel to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow></mrow></math> which intersects BA at point T . This point T divides the longest side AB of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> in the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mi>:</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
3.

## Steps of construction :
(i) Draw a line segment AB of length 6 cm .
(ii) Draw a ray <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi></mrow><mi>⟂</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(iii) Mark a point P on the ray AX such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(iv) Join P to B .
(v) Draw BC such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, which intersects ray AX at C . Thus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is formed.
(vi) Draw ray CY making an acute angle with CB .
(vii) Mark <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or ray <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(viii) Join <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
(ix) Draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>M</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, which intersect CB at M .
Point M divides the hypotenuse CB in the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></mrow><mi>:</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>

## Steps of construction :
(i) Draw a line segment BC of length 7 cm .
(ii) With centre B and radius 5 cm , draw an arc above BC (or any one side of BC).
(iii) With centre C and radius 6 cm , draw an arc intersecting the arc drawn in step (ii) at A .
(iv) Join A to B and C .
(v) Draw a ray BX below BC (or opposite side of A with respect to BC ) making an acute angle with BC .
(vi) Draw 7 arcs intersecting the ray BX at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
(vii) Join <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to C .
(viii) Draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>, which intersects BC produced at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(ix) Draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, which intersects BA produced at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
Thus, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is the required triangle.
3.

## Steps of construction :
(i) Draw a line segment BC of length 8 cm .
(ii) Draw a ray BX perpendicular to BC at B .
(iii) With centre B and radius 6 cm , draw an arc intersecting the ray BX at A .
(iv) Join A to C.
(v) Draw perpendicular bisector of BC which intersects BC at point E .
(vi) With centre E and radius EB (or EC ), draw a circle, which intersects AC at point D and passes through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and D .
(vii) With centre A and radius AB , draw an arc intersecting the circle at point F opposite to point B with respect to AC
(viii) Draw ray AF and extend AB to form a ray.
Thus, AB and AF are required tangents.
4.

## Steps of construction :
(i) Draw a circle with the help of a bangle.
(ii) Take a point P outside the circle
(iii) Draw a secant PAB , which intersects the circle at point A and B .
(iv) Produce AP to C such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(v) Draw perpendicular bisector of BC , which intersects BC at point O .
(vi) With centre O and radius OB or OC , draw a semicircle.
(vii) Draw PD perpendicular to BC , which intersect the semi-circle drawn in step (vi) at D .
(viii) With centre P and radius PD , draw arcs intersecting the circle at point T and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(ix) Draw ray PT and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
Thus, PT and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> are required tangents.

## Single Option Correct
1. (d) We know that, to divide a line segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> in the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, first draw a ray <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> which makes an acute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> then, marked <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> points at equal distance. Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
∴ Minimum number of these points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>
2. (c) We know that, in a triangle sum of two sides of triangle is greater than the third side. Here, the sides of triangle given in option (c) does not satisfy this condition. So, with these sides the construction of a triangle is not possible.
3. (d)
4. (a)

## TERMS RELATED TO CIRCLE
Chord : A line segment joining any two points of a circle is called a chord. A chord passing through the centre of circle is called its diameter. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> both are chords but the chord <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> passes through the centre. Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is the diameter also.
Diameter of a circle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> twice the radius of the circle.
Note : Diameter is the longest chord of a circle.
Arc : A part of a circle is called an arc. In Figure (i), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo></mrow></math> and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow></math>
(i)
Semi-circle : A diameter of a circle divides a circle into two equal arcs, each known as a semi-circle. In Figure (ii), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is a diameter and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mo>⏜</mo></mover></mrow></math> is a semi-circle and so is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mo>⏜</mo></mover></mrow></math>.
Minor arc : An arc of a circle whose length is less than a semi-circle of the same circle is called a minor arc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is a minor arc.
Major arc : An arc of a circle whose length is greater than a semi-circle of the same circle is called a major arc. In figure (iii), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is a major arc.
Sector : The region bounded by an arc of a circle and two radii at its end points is called a sector. In the figure (iv), the shaded portion is a minor sector formed by the arc <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> and the unshaded portion is a major sector formed by the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>.
(iv)
Segment : A chord divides the interior of a circle into two parts, each part called a segment. The segment in which the centre of the circle does not lie is called minor segment and the segment in which the centre of the circle lies is called major segment. In the figure (v), the shaded region <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and the unshaded region <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> are both segments of the circle.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is called a minor segment and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is called a major segment.
(v)
Circumference : Take a wheel and mark a point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> on the wheel where it touches the ground. Rotate the wheel along a line till the point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> touches back on the ground. Measure the distance between the first and last position of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> along the line. This distance is equal to the circumference of the circle. Thus, the length of the boundary of a circle is the circumference of the circle.
The ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter is always a constant. This constant is universally denoted by Greek letter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow></math>.
Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is the circumference, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> its diameter and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is its radius of the circle. An approximate value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>. Circumference of a circle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is the radius and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is the diameter of the circle.
The distance travelled by a person sitting on a Ferris wheel can be determined by calculating the Know! circumference of the wheel.

## CONGRUENT CIRCLES AND ARCS
Two circles or arcs are said to be congruent if we can superpose (place) one over the other such that they cover each other completely.

## AREA OF COMBINATIONS OF PLANE FIGURES
Whenever a plane figure is made by combination of two or more plane figures, then the area of combination of plane figures is always equal to the sum of the areas of the constituent figures.
## IMPORTANT POINTS TO BE REMEMBER
(i) Distance moved by a wheel in 1 revolution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Circumference of a wheel
(ii) Number of revolutions in one minute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Distance covered in1minute </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Circumference </mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(iii) Angle described by minute hand in 60 minute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(iv) Angle described by hour hand in 12 hour <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(v) The sum of the arcs of major and minor sectors of a circle is equal to the circumference of the circle.
(vi) The sum of the areas of major and minor sectors of a circle is equal to the area of the circle.

## CASE-III : Combination of trapezium and sector.
Illustration: In fig., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is a trapezium with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is a sector of a circle with centre <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, then find the area of the shaded region. (Use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>1.732</mn></mrow></math> )
Sol. Clearly, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
In right <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> Area of trapezium </mtext><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>L</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>63</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>
and,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Area of sector </mtext><mi>B</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>7</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>77</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> be the area of the shaded region. Then,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>63</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>77</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>54.558</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>25.666</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>28.89</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES
1. A path of width 2 meters runs around a circular plot whose circumference is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>75</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> metres. Find (i) the area of path.
(ii) the cost of gravelling the path at ₹ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow></mrow></math> per square metre.
Sol. Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>75</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>528</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>528</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> i.e., the radius of the plot is 12 m .
(i) Area of path <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>14</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>12</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>52</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1144</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>.
(ii) Cost <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>₹</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1144</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>₹</mi><mn>1144</mn></mrow></math>
2. The inner perimeter of a racetrack (figure) is 400 m and the outer perimeter is 488 m . The length of each straight portion is 90 m . Find the cost of developing the track at the rate of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>₹</mi><mn>12.50</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
Sol. Length of each straight portion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>90</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, Outer perimeter of the track <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>488</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
∴ length of circular ends of outer perimeter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>488</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>308</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
The two circular ends make a complete circle
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>308</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>308</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>22</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>49</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Inner perimeter of the track <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>400</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
∴ length of circular ends of inner perimeter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>400</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>220</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>220</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>220</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>22</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
∴ width of the track <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>49</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Area of straight portion on the track <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>14</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2520</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Area of circular parts <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>49</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>35</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>49</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>35</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>84</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3696</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
∴ total area of track <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2520</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3696</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6216</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>∴</mo></mrow></math> cost of developing track <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6216</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>12.50</mn><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> ₹ 77,700
3. A chord of circle 14 cm makes an angle of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> at the centre of the circle. Find :

The diagonal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is the diameter of the circle
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>8</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>6</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>36</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow></math>

Radius of wheel <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Circumference of wheel <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1320</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

∴ Distance covered in 140 revolutions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1320</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>140</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>26400</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>264</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>264</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Now, distance covered in one minute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>264</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
∵ Distance covered in one minute = Distance covered in 140 revolutions)
