## 12 Areas Related to circle
(CONCEPT MAP)

## TERMS RELATED TO CIRCLE
Chord : A line segment joining any two points of a circle is called a chord. A chord passing through the centre of circle is called its diameter. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> both are chords but the chord <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> passes through the centre. Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is the diameter also.
Diameter of a circle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> twice the radius of the circle.
Note : Diameter is the longest chord of a circle.
Arc : A part of a circle is called an arc. In Figure (i), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo></mrow></math> and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow></math>
(i)
Semi-circle : A diameter of a circle divides a circle into two equal arcs, each known as a semi-circle. In Figure (ii), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is a diameter and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mo>⏜</mo></mover></mrow></math> is a semi-circle and so is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mo>⏜</mo></mover></mrow></math>.
Minor arc : An arc of a circle whose length is less than a semi-circle of the same circle is called a minor arc. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is a minor arc.
Major arc : An arc of a circle whose length is greater than a semi-circle of the same circle is called a major arc. In figure (iii), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is a major arc.
Sector : The region bounded by an arc of a circle and two radii at its end points is called a sector. In the figure (iv), the shaded portion is a minor sector formed by the arc <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> and the unshaded portion is a major sector formed by the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>.
(iv)
Segment : A chord divides the interior of a circle into two parts, each part called a segment. The segment in which the centre of the circle does not lie is called minor segment and the segment in which the centre of the circle lies is called major segment. In the figure (v), the shaded region <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> and the unshaded region <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> are both segments of the circle.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is called a minor segment and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is called a major segment.
(v)
Circumference : Take a wheel and mark a point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> on the wheel where it touches the ground. Rotate the wheel along a line till the point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> touches back on the ground. Measure the distance between the first and last position of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> along the line. This distance is equal to the circumference of the circle. Thus, the length of the boundary of a circle is the circumference of the circle.
The ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter is always a constant. This constant is universally denoted by Greek letter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow></math>.
Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is the circumference, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> its diameter and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is its radius of the circle. An approximate value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>. Circumference of a circle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is the radius and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is the diameter of the circle.
The distance travelled by a person sitting on a Ferris wheel can be determined by calculating the Know! circumference of the wheel.

## AREA OF A CIRCLE
Area of a circle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, where ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ' is the radius of the circle.

## AREA OF A SEMI-CIRCLE
Area of a semi-circle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

theory_sections.topics: AREA OF A QUADRANT OF A CIRCLE
theory_sections.markdown:
## AREA OF A QUADRANT OF A CIRCLE
Area of a quadrant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

## Learn More
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is an equilateral triangle and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> be the side of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
Then, radius of circumcircle is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
and Area of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> can be defined as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

## CONCENTRIC CIRCLES
Circles having the same centre but different radii are called concentric circles.

## AREA OF CIRCULAR PATH (RING)
If we have a circular field of radius ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ', surrounded by a path of uniform width ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> ' and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> then, the area of the circular path
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Area of the outer circle - Area of the inner circle
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> sq. unit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> sq. unit

## CONGRUENT CIRCLES AND ARCS
Two circles or arcs are said to be congruent if we can superpose (place) one over the other such that they cover each other completely.

theory_sections.topics: PERIMETER AND AREA OF SECTOR OF A CIRCLE
theory_sections.markdown:
## PERIMETER AND AREA OF SECTOR OF A CIRCLE
Two radii OA and OB enclose a portion of the circular region which makes a central angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math>. The region is called a sector of the circle. In fig., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the sector with central angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math>. Let ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> ' be the length of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo>⏜</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mtext> circumference </mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> [Corresponding arcs subtend proportional central angles] or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>180</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where r is the radius of the circle
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Perimeter of the sector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo>⏜</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>180</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Also, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Area of sector </mtext><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Area of the circle </mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Area of sector </mtext><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> or Area of sector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

## AREA OF A SEGMENT
In right <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mo>⇒</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Area of minor segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Area of sector OAQBO <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Area of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>360</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>360</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>×</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>360</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Area of major segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Area of the circle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Area of minor segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>360</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

theory_sections.topics: AREA OF COMBINATIONS OF PLANE FIGURES
theory_sections.markdown:
## AREA OF COMBINATIONS OF PLANE FIGURES
Whenever a plane figure is made by combination of two or more plane figures, then the area of combination of plane figures is always equal to the sum of the areas of the constituent figures.

## IMPORTANT POINTS TO BE REMEMBER
(i) Distance moved by a wheel in 1 revolution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Circumference of a wheel
(ii) Number of revolutions in one minute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Distance covered in1minute </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Circumference </mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(iii) Angle described by minute hand in 60 minute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(iv) Angle described by hour hand in 12 hour <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(v) The sum of the arcs of major and minor sectors of a circle is equal to the circumference of the circle.
(vi) The sum of the areas of major and minor sectors of a circle is equal to the area of the circle.

theory_sections.topics: CASE-I : Combination of square and circles.
theory_sections.markdown:
## CASE-I : Combination of square and circles.
Illustration: In fig., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is a square of side 10 cm . Semi-circles are drawn with each side of square as diameter. Find the area of (i) the unshaded region (ii) the shaded region Sol. Let us mark the four unshaded regions as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
Clearly,
Area of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> Area of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Area of square <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> - Area of two semi-circles having centres at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>3.14</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo>∵</mo></mrow></math> Radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3.14</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>25</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>78.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>21.5</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Similarly, we have
Area of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> Area of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>21.5</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(i) Area of the unshaded region
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext> Area </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext> Area </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext> Area </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext> Area </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mtext> Area </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext> Area </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mtext> Area </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext> Area </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>21.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>43</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) Area of the shaded region
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>=</mo><mtext> Area of square </mtext><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mtext> Area of </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext> Area of </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>43</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>57</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>+</mo><mtext> Area of </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mtext> Area of </mtext><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

## CASE-II : Combination of only circles.
Illustration: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> is a diameter of a circle of radius 6 cm . The lengths <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> are equal. Semi-circles are drawn on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> as diameters as shown in fig. Find the perimeter and area of the shaded region.
Sol. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Diameter of a circle of radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Q</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> be the perimeter and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> be the area of the shaded region.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Arc of semi-circle of radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> Arc of semi-circle of radius 4 cm
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>×</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>π</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
and,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Area of semi-circle with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> as diameter + Area of semi-circle with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> as diameter - Area of semi-circle with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> as diameter.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>6</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>264</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>37.71</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>

## Think Out of the Box
Q. 1. A circle has circumference 44 cm inscribed in a square. Find the side of square.
[Hint: Side of square <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ] Ans.
[Hint : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> ] Ans. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>37.68</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

## CASE-III : Combination of trapezium and sector.
Illustration: In fig., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is a trapezium with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>D</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is a sector of a circle with centre <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, then find the area of the shaded region. (Use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>1.732</mn></mrow></math> )
Sol. Clearly, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>E</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
In right <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> Area of trapezium </mtext><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>L</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>63</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>
and,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Area of sector </mtext><mi>B</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>7</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>77</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> be the area of the shaded region. Then,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>63</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>77</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>54.558</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>25.666</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>28.89</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Q. 2. A circle inscribed in an equilateral triangle of side 12 cm . Find the area of inscribed circle. (Use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3.14</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>1.73</mn></mrow></math> ).

## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES
1. A path of width 2 meters runs around a circular plot whose circumference is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>75</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> metres. Find (i) the area of path.
(ii) the cost of gravelling the path at ₹ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow></mrow></math> per square metre.
Sol. Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>75</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>528</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>528</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> i.e., the radius of the plot is 12 m .
(i) Area of path <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>14</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>12</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>52</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1144</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>.
(ii) Cost <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>₹</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1144</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>₹</mi><mn>1144</mn></mrow></math>
2. The inner perimeter of a racetrack (figure) is 400 m and the outer perimeter is 488 m . The length of each straight portion is 90 m . Find the cost of developing the track at the rate of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>₹</mi><mn>12.50</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
Sol. ## BASIC CONCEPTS
- Solid : A figure which occupies a portion of space by plane or curved surface is called a solid.
A solid has three dimensions - length, breadth and height.
- Volume of a solid : The measurement of the space enclosed by a solid is called its volume.
It is also known as capacity. It is measured in cubic units.
- Surface area of a solid : The sum of the areas of the plane and curved surfaces (faces) of a solid is called its (total) surface area.
It is measured in square units.
Total surface area of a solid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> curved (lateral) surface area + plane surface area
## PRISM
A prism is a solid object with
- identical ends
- flat sides and
- the same cross-section all along its length, where cross-section is the shape made by cutting straight across an object. In other words, we can say 'prism' is a solid geometric figure whose two ends are similar, equal and parallel rectilinear figures and whose sides are parallelogram.
In geometry, there are different types of prisms - Triangular prisms, Rectangular prisms, Square prisms, etc.
For eg : Cubes and cuboids are prisms but cylinder is not a prism.
BASES : The top and bottom faces of prism are called bases.
Some important types of prisms and their cross-sections are shown below :

## SPHERE
Sphere is a set of points in the space which are equidistant from a fixed point. The fixed point is called the centre of the sphere and the distance is called the radius of the sphere.
A football, a cricket ball, the earth are some examples of sphere.

If a cone is cut by a plane parallel to the base of the cone, then the portion between the plane and base is called the frustum of the cone.

## IMPORTANT POINTS TO BE REMEMBER
- Volume of water released by a pipe/canal = Area of cross-section × Rate of flow × Time
- The cross-section is a circle in the case of a pipe.
