## CASE-II : A right triangle rotates about its hypotenuse.
Illustration: A right triangle, whose sides (other than hypotenuse) are 15 cm and 20 cm is revolve about its hypotenuse. Find the volume of the two cones so formed. (use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3.14</mn></mrow></math> )
Sol. In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> right angled at A ,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mn>20</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>15</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Slant height of first cone is 15 cm and of second cone is 20 cm . Radius of the two cones are same.
In the figure, let radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>15</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>20</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
[In rt. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ]
[In rt. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> ]
From (i) and (ii), we get. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
∴ Volume of the two cones
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>3.14</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>12</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>25</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3768</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>
Q. 1 A kite which sides are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>15</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>15</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and 20 cm is rotates through longest diagonal. Find the volume of the two cones so formed.
[Hint: Slant height of first cone is 15 cm and second cone is 20 cm . Ans. : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3768</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ]
Q. 2 A right triangle which hypotenuse is 13 cm and other one side is 12 cm is rotated through the smallest side. Find the surface Area of the cone so formed.

## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES
1. The decorative block shown in figure is made of two solids-a cube and a hemisphere. The base of the block is a cube with edge 5 cm and the hemisphere fixed on the top has a diameter of 4.2 cm . Find the total surface area of the block. (Take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">π</mi></mrow><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold">=</mo></mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold">/</mo></mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow></mrow></math> )
Sol. Side of cube <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
∴ Total surface area of cube <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>ℓ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Radius of hemisphere, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4.2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2.1</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Surface area of the block <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> TSA of cube + CSA of hemisphere - Base area of hemisphere
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>2.1</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2.1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>4.41</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>13.86</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>163.86</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
2. A solid is in the form of a cylinder with hemispherical ends. The total height of the solid is 19 cm and the diameter of the cylinder is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Find the volume and surface area of the solid.
Sol. Diameter of cylinder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
∴ Radius of cylinder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Radius of each hemispherical end <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Height of solid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Height of cylinder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Volume of cylinder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>462</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Volume of each hemispherical end <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>539</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Total volume of solid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>462</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>539</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>539</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2772</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>539</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>539</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3850</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>641.67</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Curved surface area of cylinder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>264</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Curved surface area of each hemispherical end <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>77</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Total surface area of solid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>264</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>77</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>77</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>418</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
3. A closed cylindrical container, the radius of which is 7 cm and height 10 cm is to be made out of a metal sheet. Find
(i) the area of metal sheet required.
(ii) the volume of the cylinder made.
(iii) the cost of painting the lateral surface of the cylinder at the rate of ₹ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow></math> per <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
Sol. (i) The area of the metal sheet required <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> The total surface area of the cylinder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>44</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>17</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>748</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) Volume <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>70</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1540</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(iii) To find the cost of painting the lateral surface, we need to find the curved (lateral) surface area.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>440</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Cost of painting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>440</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>₹</mi><mn>1760</mn></mrow></math>.
4. Volume of two cubes are in the ratio <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>27</mn></mrow></math>, find the ratio of their surface areas.
Sol. Let sides of two cubes be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> respectively.
Volume of first cube <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and Volume of second cube <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>27</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Now, surface area of first cube <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and surface area of second cube <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mtext> Now, </mtext><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> from equation (i)) </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> Ratio of surface are </mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>9</mn><mo>.</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
5. The height of a cylinder is 80 cm and diameter of the base is 14 cm . Find its curved surface area, total surface area and volume.
Sol. Height <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>80</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, Diameter of base <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> radius of base <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> curved surface area of cylinder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>80</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>44</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>80</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3520</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Total surface area (TSA) = C.S.A + Area of two ends
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>80</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>87</mn></mrow></math>
T.S.A of cylinder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3828</mn><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">q</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Volume (V) of cylinder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>80</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>154</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>80</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12320</mn><mtext> cubic units. </mtext></mrow></math>
6. Find the slant height, curved surface area and the whole surface area of a cone of radius 21 cm and height 28 cm .
Sol. Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>21</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>28</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
∴ Slant height, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>21</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>28</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1225</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Curved surface area <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>21</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>35</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2310</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Total surface area <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2310</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>21</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>21</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>3696</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
7. A hemispherical tank of radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is full of water. It is connected with a pipe which empties it at the rate of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow></mrow></math> liters per second. How much time will it take to empty the tank completely?
Sol. Radius of the hemisphere <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>175</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
∴ Volume of the hemisphere <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>×</mo><mn>175</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>175</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>175</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
The cylindrical pipe empties it at the rate of 7 litres i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>7000</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> of water per second.
Hence, the required time to empty the tank <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>175</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>175</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>175</mn><mo>÷</mo><mn>7000</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>175</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>175</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>175</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7000</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1925</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>72</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>26.74</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mtext> nearly. </mtext></mrow></math>
8. Water in a canal, 30 dm wide and 12 dm deep, is flowing with a speed of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo></mrow></math> hour. How much area will it irrigate in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">n</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">t</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mo mathvariant="bold">,</mo><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext></mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">8</mn><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. of standing water is required for irrigation.
Sol. Speed of water in the canal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10000</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>60</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>500</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
∴ The volume of the water flowing out of the canal in 1 minute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>500</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>600</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> In 30 min , the amount of water flowing out of the canal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>600</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>30</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>18000</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
If the required area of the irrigated land is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, then the volume of water to be needed to irrigate the land
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>25</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>25</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>18000</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>18000</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>25</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>225000</mn></mrow></math>
Hence, the required area is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>225000</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
9. The earth dug out of a well is spread evenly all around it to form an embankment which is 2 m wide. Find the height of the embankment if the diameter of the well is 2 m and its depth is 20 m .
Sol. Given, diameter of well <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and depth of well <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Volume of earth dug out <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></math>
Given, that the width of the embankment is 2 m . Let the height of the embankment be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math>.
Then, volume of embankment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> external volume - internal volume <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>h</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></math>
But, volume of embankment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> volume of earth taken out <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mi>π</mi><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
10. A piece of copper of volume <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is melted down and recast into a bar which is 36 m long and has a square crosssection. An exact cube is cut off from one end of the bar. Find the cost of this cube, if the original piece of copper cost ₹ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mo mathvariant="bold">,</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">8</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>.
Sol. Given, volume of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and length of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>36</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Area of cross-section <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> volume </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> length </mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>36</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Side of square cross-section <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
∴ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Volume of cube cut off from bar <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>216</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Cost of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> of copper <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>₹</mi><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>800</mn></mrow></math> (Given) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> cost of cube <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>216</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>10800</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>₹</mi><mn>50</mn></mrow></math>
11. Hanumappa and his wife Gangamma are busy making jaggery out of sugarcane juice. They have processed the sugarcane juice to make the molasses, which is poured into moulds in the shape of a frustum of a cone having the diameters of its two circular faces as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn></mrow></mrow></math> cm and the vertical height of the mould is 14 cm (see Fig.). If each cm3 of molasses has mass about 1.2 g , find the mass of the molasses that can be poured into each mould. (Take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">π</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> )
Sol. Since, the mould is in the shape of a frustum of a cone, the quantity (volume) of molasses that can be poured into it is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the radius of the larger base and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the radius of the smaller base.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>14</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>11641.7</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
It is given that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> of molasses has mass 1.2 g .
So, the mass of the molasses that can be poured into each mould
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>11641.7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1.2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13970.04</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>13.97</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></mrow><mtext> (approx.) </mtext></mrow></math>
12. A bucket is 40 cm in diameter at the top and 28 cm in diameter at the bottom. Find the capacity of the bucket in litres, if it is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> deep. Also, find the cost of tin sheet used in making the bucket, if the cost of tin is ₹ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo mathvariant="bold">.</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math> per sq. dm.
Sol. Given : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>21</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Now, the required capacity (i.e., volume) of the bucket <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>21</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>20</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>14</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>876</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>19272</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>19272</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mtext> litres </mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>19.272</mn><mtext> litres </mtext></mrow></math>
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>21</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mn>6</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>21</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>36</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>441</mn></mrow></msqrt><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>477</mn></mrow></msqrt><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>21.84</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
∴ Total surface area of the bucket (which is open at the top) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mi>ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>π</mi><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mn>21.84</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>14</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2949.76</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

Water flows at the rate of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> per minute through a cylindrical pipe having its diameter as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. How much time will it take to fill a conical vessel whose diameter of the base is 40 cm and depth 24 cm .

Diameter of the pipe <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo></mrow></math>. Radius of the pipe <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
In 1 minute, the length of the water column in the cylindrical pipe <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1000</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Volume of water that flows out of the pipe in 1 minute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>1000</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

Hence, the time needed to fill up this conical vessel
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> minutes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>256</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> minutes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>51.2</mn></mrow></math> minutes
Hence, the required time is 51.2 minutes.

## DATA
The word 'data' means information in the form of numerical figure or a set of given facts.
- Raw Data: Data obtained from direct observation and experience.
Example: Marks of 5 students in unit test is raw data or ungrouped data.
- Grouped Data : The data can be represented into classes or groups. Such a presentation is known as grouped data.
- Class Limits : Suppose, marks obtained by all of the students are divided into seven classes namely, 25-35, 35-45 and so on. In class <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>25</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow></math> is called Lower class limit and 35 is called Upper class limit.
- Class Size : The difference between upper and lower class limit is called Class size.
Here, class size <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>.
- Class Mark : Class mark <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Upper limit </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> lower limit </mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
## GROUPED AND UNGROUPED DATA / DISCRETE AND CONTINUOUS FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTION
(i) Discrete Frequency Distribution : If each data is given with their frequency, then this type of frequency distribution is called Discrete Frequency Distribution.
(ii) Continuous Frequency Distribution : If the data is given in the form of class interval with frequency, then this type of frequency distribution is called Continuous Frequency Distribution.
(iii) Measures of Central Tendency : A certain numerical values representatives of the ungrouped data is called Measures of Central Tendency, namely mean, median and mode.
## MEAN OF DISCRETE FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTION
Mean of discrete frequency distribution may be computed by any one of the following methods :
(i) Direct method
(ii) Assume mean method (Short-cut method)
(iii) Step-Deviation method

## MODE
The mode is that value of the observation which occurs most frequently, i.e., an observation with the maximum frequency is called the mode.
The term "mode" originates with Karl Pearson in 1895. He uses the term mode interchangeably with maximum-ordinate.
Note : It is not effected by presence of extremely large or small items.

120 has the maximum frequency. Hence, the mode is 120 .

## MEDIAN
The median is that value of the given number of observations, which divides it into exactly two parts.
Median is the middle most or the central value of the variate in a set of observations, when the observations are arranged either in ascending or in descending order of their magnitudes.
- Methods to Find Median : When the data is arranged in ascending (or descending) order, the median of ungrouped data is calculated as follows:
(i) When the number of observations (n) is odd, the median is the value of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> th observation.
(ii) When the number of observations ( n ) is even, the median is the mean of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> th and the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> th observations. value in 1869 and the medium in 1880.

## CUMULATIVE FREQUENCY CURVE (OGIVE)
Cumulative frequency curve or an ogive is the graphical representation of a cumulative frequency distribution. There are two methods of constructing an ogive:
(i) Less than method (ii) More than method
(i) Less Than Method: Following are the steps for construction of an ogive:
(a) Construct a cumulative frequency table of less than type.
(b) Mark upper class limits along <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
(c) Mark the corresponding cumulative frequency along <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
(d) Plot the points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the upper limit of a class and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the corresponding c.f. and join them by a smooth free hand curve.
The curve, we get is the Less Than Type Ogive.

## MEDIAN BY GRAPH
We can find the median graphically in two ways :
(i) By drawing more than and less than Ogives on same graph simultaneously.
(ii) By drawing only less than Ogive.
(i) Median by Drawing Both More Than and Less Than Ogives:
If we draw the two types of curves i.e. Less Than type Ogive and More Than type Ogive on same pair of axes, then these two curves intersects each other at a point. From this point of intersection, if we draw a perpendicular to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis, it will intersect the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis at some point. The X -coordinate of this point is the Median.
(ii) Median by Drawing Only Less than Ogive :
Generally, we use only Less Than type Ogive to calculate the median. Steps are as follows:
(a) First prepare a less than type cumulative frequency distribution table.
(b) Draw less than cumulative frequency curve (ogive).
(c) If total number of observations is N , then locate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> on cumulative frequency axis i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
(d) From this point on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis, draw a horizontal line parallel to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis which meet the ogive at some point.
(e) Through this point on the curve, draw a perpendicular to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
(f) The perpendicular meets the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis at some point. X-coordinate of this point is the required median.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Correct mean <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> correct value of </mtext><mo>∑</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3970</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>39.7</mn></mrow></math>

## SOME BASIC TERMS
- Probability as a Measure of Uncertainity
(i) Experiment : An operation which can produce some well defined outcomes, is known as an experiment.
(ii) Trial : Performing of an experiment is called a trial. For example : Tossing a coin, throwing a dice.
(iii) Sample space : The set of all possible outcomes in a trial is called sample space.
- If a fair coin is tossed, there are two possible outcomes, namely head (H) \& Tail (T).
∴ Sample space <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
- When two coins are tossed ;
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
- Sample space, when three coins are tossed together.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
- When an unbiased die is thrown, then sample space,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
(iv) Elementary event : An event having only one outcome is called an elementary event.
(v) Compound event : An event having two or more outcomes is called compound event.
(vi) Equally likely event : Outcomes of trial are said to be equally likely if taking into consideration all the relevant evidences, there is no reason to expect one in preference to the others, i.e., probability of each elementary event is same.
For example : In throwing an unbiased die, all the six faces are equally likely to come.

## DATA
The word 'data' means information in the form of numerical figure or a set of given facts.
- Raw Data: Data obtained from direct observation and experience.
Example: Marks of 5 students in unit test is raw data or ungrouped data.
- Grouped Data : The data can be represented into classes or groups. Such a presentation is known as grouped data.
- Class Limits : Suppose, marks obtained by all of the students are divided into seven classes namely, 25-35, 35-45 and so on. In class <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>25</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow></math> is called Lower class limit and 35 is called Upper class limit.
- Class Size : The difference between upper and lower class limit is called Class size.
Here, class size <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>.
- Class Mark : Class mark <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Upper limit </mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext> lower limit </mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

theory_sections.topics: GROUPED AND UNGROUPED DATA / DISCRETE AND CONTINUOUS FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTION
theory_sections.markdown:
## GROUPED AND UNGROUPED DATA / DISCRETE AND CONTINUOUS FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTION
(i) Discrete Frequency Distribution : If each data is given with their frequency, then this type of frequency distribution is called Discrete Frequency Distribution.
(ii) Continuous Frequency Distribution : If the data is given in the form of class interval with frequency, then this type of frequency distribution is called Continuous Frequency Distribution.
(iii) Measures of Central Tendency : A certain numerical values representatives of the ungrouped data is called Measures of Central Tendency, namely mean, median and mode.

## MEAN OF DISCRETE FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTION Mean of discrete frequency distribution may be computed by any one of the following methods : (i) Direct method (ii) Assume mean method (Short-cut method) (iii) Step-Deviation method (i) Direct Method: For the discrete frequency distribution, we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
then arithmetic mean of values x1,x2,….,xn is given by Mean(x¯)=f1x1+f2x2+…………+fnxnf1+f2+…………+fn=∑i=1nfixiΣfi Note : If xi and fi are sufficiently small, then direct method is an appropriate choice.

## MEAN OF CONTINUOUS FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTION In case of continuons frequency distribution with class intervals mean may be computed by applying any of the methods discussed above. Note : The values of x1,x2,−−xn are taken as the mid-points or class marks of the various classes. Let us understand the mean of Continuous frequency distribution by following illustrations. (i)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

theory_sections.topics: IMPORTANT POINTS TO BE REMEMBER ABOUT A MEAN
theory_sections.markdown:
## IMPORTANT POINTS TO BE REMEMBER ABOUT A MEAN
(i) The algebraic sum of deviations taken about the mean is zero. i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mover><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
(ii) The value of the mean depends on all the observations.
(iii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow></math> is the mean of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, then the mean of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> for all values of ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> '.

## MODE
The mode is that value of the observation which occurs most frequently, i.e., an observation with the maximum frequency is called the mode.
The term "mode" originates with Karl Pearson in 1895. He uses the term mode interchangeably with maximum-ordinate.
Note : It is not effected by presence of extremely large or small items.
## CONNECTING TOPIC

## WEIGHTED AVERAGE
If we have two or more groups of numbers whose individual averages are known, then combined average of all the numbers of all the groups is known as Weighted Average. Thus, if there are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> groups having number of numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> with averages <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> respectively; then weighted average
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∑</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∑</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

## MODE OF CONTINUOUS FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTION
Mode <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></math>, where
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> lower limit of the modal class*
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> size of the class interval
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> frequency of the modal class
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> frequency of the class preceeding the modal class
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> frequency of the class succeeding the modal class.
Note : Modal class is the class having maximum frequency.

## MEDIAN
The median is that value of the given number of observations, which divides it into exactly two parts.
Median is the middle most or the central value of the variate in a set of observations, when the observations are arranged either in ascending or in descending order of their magnitudes.
- Methods to Find Median : When the data is arranged in ascending (or descending) order, the median of ungrouped data is calculated as follows:
(i) When the number of observations (n) is odd, the median is the value of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> th observation.
(ii) When the number of observations ( n ) is even, the median is the mean of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> th and the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> th observations. value in 1869 and the medium in 1880.

## CUMULATIVE FREQUENCY CURVE (OGIVE)
Cumulative frequency curve or an ogive is the graphical representation of a cumulative frequency distribution. There are two methods of constructing an ogive:
(i) Less than method (ii) More than method
(i) Less Than Method: Following are the steps for construction of an ogive:
(a) Construct a cumulative frequency table of less than type.
(b) Mark upper class limits along <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
(c) Mark the corresponding cumulative frequency along <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
(d) Plot the points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the upper limit of a class and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the corresponding c.f. and join them by a smooth free hand curve.
The curve, we get is the Less Than Type Ogive.
