## MEDIAN BY GRAPH
We can find the median graphically in two ways :
(i) By drawing more than and less than Ogives on same graph simultaneously.
(ii) By drawing only less than Ogive.
(i) Median by Drawing Both More Than and Less Than Ogives:
If we draw the two types of curves i.e. Less Than type Ogive and More Than type Ogive on same pair of axes, then these two curves intersects each other at a point. From this point of intersection, if we draw a perpendicular to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis, it will intersect the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis at some point. The X -coordinate of this point is the Median.
(ii) Median by Drawing Only Less than Ogive :
Generally, we use only Less Than type Ogive to calculate the median. Steps are as follows:
(a) First prepare a less than type cumulative frequency distribution table.
(b) Draw less than cumulative frequency curve (ogive).
(c) If total number of observations is N , then locate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> on cumulative frequency axis i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
(d) From this point on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-axis, draw a horizontal line parallel to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis which meet the ogive at some point.
(e) Through this point on the curve, draw a perpendicular to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis.
(f) The perpendicular meets the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>-axis at some point. X-coordinate of this point is the required median.

## Learn More
If a frequency distribution's graph is having a symmetrical frequency curve, the mean, median and mode will be equal, i.e., mean <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> mode <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> median

## SOME BASIC TERMS
- Probability as a Measure of Uncertainity
(i) Experiment : An operation which can produce some well defined outcomes, is known as an experiment.
(ii) Trial : Performing of an experiment is called a trial. For example : Tossing a coin, throwing a dice.
(iii) Sample space : The set of all possible outcomes in a trial is called sample space.
- If a fair coin is tossed, there are two possible outcomes, namely head (H) \& Tail (T).
∴ Sample space <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
- When two coins are tossed ;
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
- Sample space, when three coins are tossed together.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
- When an unbiased die is thrown, then sample space,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
(iv) Elementary event : An event having only one outcome is called an elementary event.
(v) Compound event : An event having two or more outcomes is called compound event.
(vi) Equally likely event : Outcomes of trial are said to be equally likely if taking into consideration all the relevant evidences, there is no reason to expect one in preference to the others, i.e., probability of each elementary event is same.
For example : In throwing an unbiased die, all the six faces are equally likely to come.

## MEASUREMENT OF PROBABILITY
- Experimental (Empirical) Approach of Probability
(i) A trial is an action which results in one or several outcomes.
(ii) The probability <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> of happening an event E , is given by
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Number of trials in which the event happened </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> The total number of trials </mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Note: The empirical probability depends on the number of trials.
## A Theoritical Approach (Classical Probability) of Probability
If an event ' A' happen in ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ' ways and does not happen in ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ' ways, then the probability of occurrence of event ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> ', denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is given by,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Number of favourable outcomes of the event </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Number of all possible outcomes of the experiment </mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
and probability of not happening this event ' A ' is given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Number of unfavourable outcomes </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Number of all possible outcomes </mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
The basic difference between experimental and theoretical approaches probability is that, in the experimental approach, the probability of an event is based on what has been actually happened while in theoretical approach, we predict what will happen without actually performing the experiments.

## IMPOSSIBLE EVENT
## Consider an Example
In throwing a die, there are only six possible outcomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> and 6 . Let we are interested in getting a number 7 on throwing a die. Since no face of the die is marked with 7 . So, 7 cannot come under any circumstances. Hence getting a number 7 is impossible, this type of event is called an impossible event.
- It is also called a null event.
- Probability of an impossible event is always zero.
## SURE EVENT OR CERTAIN EVENT
Suppose, we want to find the probability of getting a number less than 7 in a single throw of a die. We are sure that we shall always get a number less than 7 , whenever we throw a die. So the above event is a sure event.
Also, we can say the entire sample space is favour to occur a sure event.
- Probability of a sure event is always 1.
- From above discussion and various examples, we can conclude that probability of any event lies in the range from 0 to 1 . Mathematically, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
- The sum of the probabilities of all the elementary events of an experiment is 1 . Knowledge

## CONNECTING TOPIC
## INDEPENDENT EVENTS
Two or more events are said to be independent if the happening (or non-happening) of one event is not affected by the happening or non-happening of others.
- For any two Independent events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
- Also, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then two events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are called independent events.

key_points.text: Experimental (Empirical) Approach of Probability
A trial is an action which results in one or several outcomes.

The probability <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> of happening an event E , is given by
It is also called a null event.
Probability of an impossible event is always zero.
Probability of a sure event is always 1.

From above discussion and various examples, we can conclude that probability of any event lies in the range from 0 to 1 . Mathematically, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
The sum of the probabilities of all the elementary events of an experiment is 1 . Knowledge

Son is on one end : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>

Father is in middle : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">F</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>

For any two Independent events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

Also, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then two events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are called independent events.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>

Here getting 4, 5 or 6 in the first throw and getting 1, 2, 3 or 4 in the second throw are the independent events. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be the probability of the events. Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and B<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>·</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

The event " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> " denoted by " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ", which occurs when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> or both occur.

The event "Not <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> " denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow></math>, occurs when and only when A does not occur. Thus

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>∩</mo><mover><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow></math> denotes the "non-occurrence of both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> " or "neither <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> nor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ".

## A Theoritical Approach (Classical Probability) of Probability
If an event ' A' happen in ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ' ways and does not happen in ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ' ways, then the probability of occurrence of event ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> ', denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is given by,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Number of favourable outcomes of the event </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Number of all possible outcomes of the experiment </mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
and probability of not happening this event ' A ' is given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Number of unfavourable outcomes </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Number of all possible outcomes </mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
The basic difference between experimental and theoretical approaches probability is that, in the experimental approach, the probability of an event is based on what has been actually happened while in theoretical approach, we predict what will happen without actually performing the experiments.
## IMPOSSIBLE EVENT

## Consider an Example
In throwing a die, there are only six possible outcomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> and 6 . Let we are interested in getting a number 7 on throwing a die. Since no face of the die is marked with 7 . So, 7 cannot come under any circumstances. Hence getting a number 7 is impossible, this type of event is called an impossible event.
- It is also called a null event.
- Probability of an impossible event is always zero.

## SURE EVENT OR CERTAIN EVENT
Suppose, we want to find the probability of getting a number less than 7 in a single throw of a die. We are sure that we shall always get a number less than 7 , whenever we throw a die. So the above event is a sure event.
Also, we can say the entire sample space is favour to occur a sure event.
- Probability of a sure event is always 1.
- From above discussion and various examples, we can conclude that probability of any event lies in the range from 0 to 1 . Mathematically, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
- The sum of the probabilities of all the elementary events of an experiment is 1 . Knowledge
Mother, father and son line up at random for a family picture. Find the probability (i) Son is on one end (ii) Father is in middle.
## CONNECTING TOPIC

## INDEPENDENT EVENTS
Two or more events are said to be independent if the happening (or non-happening) of one event is not affected by the happening or non-happening of others.
- For any two Independent events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
- Also, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then two events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are called independent events.
Did You Know!
Two or more balls are drawn with replacement from a bag is a case of independent events.

If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow></mrow></math> of the players are already selected and the other are selected at random, then the probability that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow></math> particular players of the remaining <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></math> will be selected.

## ALGEBRA OF EVENTS
Let A and B be two events related to a random experiment. We define
(i) The event " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> " denoted by " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ", which occurs when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> or both occur.
Thus, the event " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ", denoted by " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ", which occurs when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> both occur.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Probability that at least one of the two events occur <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
(ii) The event "Not <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> " denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow></math>, occurs when and only when A does not occur. Thus
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Probability of non-occurrence of the event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>∩</mo><mover><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow></math> denotes the "non-occurrence of both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> " or "neither <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> nor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ".
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>∩</mo><mover><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>∪</mo><mover><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow></math> denotes the "non-occurence of both A and B " or "not A or not B ".
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>∪</mo><mover><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

## MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE EVENTS
If two events cannot occur simultaneously, then they are mutually exclusive. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are mutually exclusive events, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></math>.
Ex. In drawing a card from a well shuffled pack of 52 cards, consider the following events:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> the card is a spade and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> the card is a heart.
The two events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are mutually exclusive. Because, both have no common card.
Again, consider other events
(a) The card is a heart. (b) The card is a king.
These two events are not mutually exclusive. Because, the card can be king of heart.

(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> wins) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>. (iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> (neither <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> nor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.

## CASE-III : Winning the game when one coin and a die is thrown together.
Illustration: Mohit plays a game by throwing a coin and a die. On getting a tail and an even number, he wins ₹50 and on getting a head and even number, he wins ₹100. Which one has more chance to get ₹50 or ₹ 100 .
Sol. Number of possible outcomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math>
Outcomes of a tail and an even number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> win ₹50 <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Outcomes of a head and an even number = \{H2, H4, H6\};
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> win ₹ 100<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
CASE-II : Winning the game when a coin tossed three times
Case-2
∴ More chance to win ₹50 and ₹100 are same.
Q. 2 A coin is tossed 3 times, find the probability of getting exactly two head.
[Hint : Two head <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Ans. 3/8]

## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES
1. Suppose we throw a die once. (i) What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4 ? (ii) What is the probability of getting a number less than or equal to 4 ?
Sol. (i) Here, let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> be the event 'getting a number greater than 4 '. The number of possible outcomes is six : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> and 6, and the outcomes favourable to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> are 5 and 6 . Therefore, the number of outcomes favourable to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> is 2 . So,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> number greater than </mtext><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(ii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> be the event 'getting a number less than or equal to 4 '.
Number of possible outcomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>
Outcomes favourable to the event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>.
So, the number of outcomes favourable to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> is 4 .
Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
2. A box contains 3 blue, 2 white, and 4 red marbles. If a marble is drawn at random from the box, what is the probability that it will be (i) white? (ii) blue? (iii) red?
Sol. Saying that a marble is drawn at random is a short way of saying that all the marbles are equally likely to be drawn. Therefore, the number of possible outcomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> denote the event 'the marble is white', <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> denote the event 'the marble is blue' and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> denote the event 'marble is red'.
(i) The number of outcomes favourable to the event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>. So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>. Similarly,
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and (iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
3. One card is drawn at random from a shuffled standard deck of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></math> cards. Find the probability that the card selected is not a king.
Sol. There are 52 different possible outcomes. There are 4 kings in a deck, so the other 48 cards are not kings, and these are the favourable outcomes. Hence, the probability that the card selected is not a king is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>48</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>52</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.

## Alternate Solution :
The probability of selecting a king is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>52</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>. Therefore, the probability that the selected card is not a king is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> not <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
4. One hundred cards are numbered from 1 to 100 . Find the probability that a card chosen at random has the digit 5 .
Sol. Total number of cases <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow></math>
All the numbers from 50 to 59 have the digit 5 . They are 10 in number.
Besides these numbers the numbers 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 65, 75, 85, 95 have the digit 5. These are 9 in number.
Number of favourable cases <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Number of numbers which have the digit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Probability <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>19</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
5. A die is thrown. Find the probability of
(a) prime number
(b) multiple of 2 or 3
(c) a number greater than 3
Sol. In a single throw of die any one of six numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> can be obtained. Therefore, the total number of elementary events is 6 .
(a) The event "Getting a prime no." Occurs if any one of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> comes as out come.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Favourable number of elementary events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Getting a prime no. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(b) A multiple of 2 or 3 is obtained if we obtain one of the numbers 2, 3, 4, 6 as outcomes.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Favourable number of elementary events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Getting multiple of 2 or 3<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(c) The event "Getting a number greater than 3" will occur, if we obtain one of number 4, 5, 6 as an outcome.
∴ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Favourable number of outcomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
Hence, required probability <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
6. A box contains 20 balls bearing numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>_</mi><mi>_</mi><mi>_</mi><mi>_</mi></mrow></math> 20. A ball is drawn at random from the box. What is the probability that the number on the ball is
(a) an odd number
(b) divisible by 2 or 3
(c) prime number
Sol. Total number of balls <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></math>.
∴ Total number of all elementary events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></math>
(a) Odd numbers are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></math>
∴ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Favourable number of elementary events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>
Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> an odd number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(b) Number divisible by 2 or 3 are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></math>
∴ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Favourable number of elementary events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> Number divisible by </mtext><mn>2</mn><mtext> or </mtext><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(c) There are 8 prime number form 1 to 20, i.e., 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Favourable number of elementary events <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>

## SOLVED EXAMPLE BASED ON CONNECTING TOPICS
7. A club holds an election for the post of chairperson. The probabilities that the candidates Anjani and Laxmi will be elected are 0.36 and 0.47 respectively. Find the probability that
(a) either Anjani or Laxmi will be elected,
(b) neither Anjani nor Laxmi will be elected.
Sol. (a) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> be the event that Anjani will be elected, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> be the event that Laxmi will be elected.
Since there is only 1 chairperson, so the events, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are mutually exclusive.
P (either Anjani or Laxmi will be elected) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0.36</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0.47</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0.83</mn></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> (neither Anjani nor Laxmi will be elected) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> (either Anjani or Laxmi will be elected) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>0.83</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0.17</mn></mrow></math>
8. Sol. ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> ' speaks truth in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> cases. ∴ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> (' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> ' speaks truth) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
Similarly, ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ' speaks truth in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>50</mn><mi>%</mi></mrow></math> cases. ∴ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> ' speaks truth <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>50</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Both contradict each other <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
9. In a class of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math> students, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math> opted for NCC, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></math> opted for NSS and 24 opted for both NCC and NSS. If one of these student is selected at random. Find the probability that the student opted for NCC or NSS.
Sol. Total number of students <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> be the event that a student opts for NCC <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> be the event that a student opts for NSS <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>∴</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
24 students opt for NCC and NSS both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>24</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Probability that a student opts for NSS or NCC <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>24</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>38</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>19</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
10. The probability that Guru will hit a target is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>. The probability that Srinu will hit the same target is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>. If each of them fires once, find the probability that the target will be hit by

Sol. (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> (Guru will miss) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> (Guru will hit) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Similarly, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> Srinu will miss) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Hence, we have a tree diagram as shown below.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> the target will be hit by both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> (the target will be hit by only one of them)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Guru will hit and Srinu will miss <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Guru will miss and Srinu will hit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Probability that die will land inside the circle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>24</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

## 16. Binomial Theorem
Foundation
## (CONCEPT MAP)
as 2 n is even.
## Independent Term
In the expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, the middle term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term,
It is given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (constant)
This term is called term independent of x or the constant term. So, Independent term is the term in binomial expansion whose power of x is zero.
## Middle Terms in the Expansion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐛</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>𝐧</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
which is even. So there will be two middle terms.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup><mtext> term and </mtext><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup><mtext> term. </mtext></mrow></math>
If a and b are real numbers, then for all <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> above expansion are called binomial coefficients. beginning.
## Binomial Theorem for Any Positive Integer n
## General Term
denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>…</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> The coefficients <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi></mrow></math> occuring in the
The general term in the expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Note that in the binomial expansion, the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term from the end is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term from the
(i) If n is even, then the number of terms in the expansion will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> which is odd. So, middle term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term
(ii) If n is odd, then the number of terms in the expansion will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
## BINOMIAL THEOREM

key_points.text: If n is even, then the number of terms in the expansion will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> which is odd. If n is odd, then the number of terms in the expansion will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
The expansion of a binomial for any positive integral power <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is given by Binomial theorem, which is

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>720</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>19</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow></math> !
Number of terms are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are called binomial coefficients of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mtext>st </mtext></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext>nd </mtext></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term respectively.

The general term of an expansion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

In the expansion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is even, then the middle term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term.
It has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> terms.

The sum of the indices of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and a in each term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.
The coefficients of terms equidistant from the beginning and the end are equal.

## 16. Binomial Theorem
Foundation

## (CONCEPT MAP)
as 2 n is even.

## Independent Term
In the expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, the middle term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term,
It is given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (constant)
This term is called term independent of x or the constant term. So, Independent term is the term in binomial expansion whose power of x is zero.

## Middle Terms in the Expansion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐛</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>𝐧</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
which is even. So there will be two middle terms.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup><mtext> term and </mtext><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup><mtext> term. </mtext></mrow></math>
If a and b are real numbers, then for all <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo></mrow></math> above expansion are called binomial coefficients. beginning.

theory_sections.markdown: ## Binomial Theorem for Any Positive Integer n

## General Term
denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>…</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> The coefficients <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi></mrow></math> occuring in the
The general term in the expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Note that in the binomial expansion, the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term from the end is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term from the
(i) If n is even, then the number of terms in the expansion will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> which is odd. So, middle term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term
(ii) If n is odd, then the number of terms in the expansion will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>

## BINOMIAL THEOREM
(i) The expansion of a binomial for any positive integral power <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is given by Binomial theorem, which is
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>a</mi><mo>.</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mi>;</mi></mrow></math>
where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>!</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mn>2.1</mn><mi>;</mi><mn>0</mn><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is a non-negative integer.
