- <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>720</mn></mrow></math>
- <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>19</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow></math> !

## Write the expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

## BINOMIAL EXPANSION
For the expansion,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mi>;</mi></mrow></math>
- Number of terms are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
- <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are called binomial coefficients of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mtext>st </mtext></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext>nd </mtext></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term respectively.

## GENERAL TERM
(ii) The general term of an expansion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

theory_sections.markdown:
## Find the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term in the expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math>.
SOLUTION :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in the expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>·</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>·</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>220</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>·</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msup><mo>·</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1760</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>

## MIDDLE TERMS
(iii) In the expansion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is even, then the middle term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term.
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is odd, then the middle terms are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> terms.

## <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>𝐫</mi><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> TERM FROM THE END
In the binomial expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term from the end is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mtext>th </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> term from the beginning.

(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>n</mi><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>

## Note:
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">[</mo></mrow></math> where, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(v) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(vi) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow /><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
DIRECTIONS : This section contains multiple choice questions. Each question has 4 choices (a), (b), (c) and (d) out of which ONLY ONE is correct.
1. The term independent of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> in the expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext>nd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
2. In the expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mroot><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mn>3</mn></mroot><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, the constant term is
(a) -70
(b) 70
(c) 210

## 17. Sets, Relations and Functions ## SETS In everyday life, we often speak about the collection of objects of particular kind such as a cricket team, the river of India, the vowels in the English alphabet etc. Each of these collection is well-defined collection of objects in the sense that we can definitely decide whether a given particular object belongs to a given collection or not. In mathematics, we call such collections as sets. For example, we say that 10 does not belong to the given collection of all odd natural numbers. On the other side, 15 belongs to the given collection. The following points may be noted : (i) Objects, elements and members of a set are synonymous terms. (ii) Sets are usually denoted by capital letters A,B,C,D,E,F, etc. (iii) The elements of a set are represented by small letters a,b,c,d,e,f, etc. (iv) Each element in a set comes only once i.e. repetition of any element is not allowed. The Greek symbol ∈ (epsilon) is used to denote the phrase 'belongs to'. If ' a ' is an element of a set A, we say that " a belongs to A ". Thus, we write a∈A. If ' b ' is not an element of a set A, we write b∉A and read " b does not belong to set A ". Eg : In the set V of vowels in the English alphabet, a∈V but b∉V. In the set P of prime factors of 30,3∈P but 15∉P. ## REPRESENTATIONS OF SETS There are two methods of representing a set : (i) Roster or tabular form (ii) Set-builder form. ## Roster or Tabular Form (i) In roster form, all the elements of a set are listed, the elements are being separated by commas and are enclosed within braces }. For example, the set of all even positive integers less than 7 is described in roster form as {2,4,6}. (ii) In roster form, the order in which the elements are listed is immaterial. ## Set-Builder Form In this form, a set is described by using a representative and stating the common property or properties which the elements of the set satisfy, through the representative. The set {a,e,i,o,u} in roster form can be written in set builder form as {x:x is a vowel in English alphabet }. Z : Set of all integers R : Set of all real numbers Q+: Set of all positive rational numbers, and ## TYPES OF SETS ## Empty Set A set which does not contain any element is called the empty set, null set or void set. The empty set is denoted by the symbol ϕ or }. Given below are few examples of empty sets. (i) If A={x:1<x<2,x is a natural number }. Then A is the empty set, because there is no natural number between 1 and 2 . (ii) If B={x:x2−2=0 and x is rational number }. Then B is the empty set, because the equation x2−2=0 is not satisfied by any rational value of x. (iii) If C={x:x is an even prime number greater than 2}. Then C is the empty set, because 2 is the only even prime number. (iv) If D={x:x2=4,x is odd }. Then D is the empty set, because the equation x2=4 is not satisfied by any odd value of x. ## Singleton Set A set, consisting of a single element is called a singleton set. For example: The sets {0},{5},{−7} are singleton sets. {x:x+6=0,x∈Z} is a singleton set, because this set contains only one integer -6 . ## Finite and Infinite Sets A set which is empty or consists of a definite number of elements is called finite otherwise, the set is called infinite. ## Consider some examples : (i) Let W be the set of the days of the week. Then, W is finite. (ii) Let S be the set of solutions of the equation x2−16=0. Then, S is finite. (iii) Let G be the set of points on a line. Then, G is infinite. We represent the infinite set in the roster form by writing a few elements which clearly indicate the structure of the set followed (or preceded) by multiple of three dots. For example, {1,2,3,…} is the set of natural numbers, {1,3,5,7,……} is the set of odd natural numbers, {……,−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3,……} is the set of integers. All these sets are infinite. Note : All infinite sets can not be described in the roster form. The three dots ( … ) are called an ellipsis and it means "Continue on". ## Equal Sets Two sets A and B are said to be equal if they have exactly the same elements. Two equal set A and B are represented as A=B. Otherwise, the sets are said to be unequal and we write A≠B. For example : Let A={1,2,3,4} and B={3,1,4,2}. Then, A=B. ## ILLUSTRATIOM : 3 Which of the following pairs of sets are equal? Justify your answer. (i) X, the set of letters in "ALLOY" and B, the set of letters in "LOYAL". Since some elements −2,1,0 of A do not belong to B, therefore A and B are not equal sets. ## DISJOINT SETS Two sets A and B are said to be disjoint, if they have no elements in common. For example: Let A={1,2,3} and B={4,6,9}. Then, A& B are disjoint sets. ## Subsets A set A is said to be a subset of a set B if every element of set A is also an element of set B. Here, set B is called superset of set A. Symbolically, A⊂B if whenever a∈A, then a∈B. Here ' A⊂B ' is read as A is the subset of set B. Note : It is often convenient to use the symbol "⇒" which means implies. Using this symbol, we can write the definition of subset as follows: A⊂B if a∈A⇒a∈B. We read the above statement as " A is a subset of B if a is an element of A implies that a is also an element of B ". If A is not a subset of B, we write A⊄B. For example : (i) The set Q of rational numbers is a subset of the set R of real numbers, so we write Q⊂R. (ii) If A is the set of all divisors of 56 and B the set of all prime divisors of 56 , then B is a subset of A. So we write B⊂A. (iii) Let A={a,e,i,o,u} and B={a,b,c,d}. Then, A is not a subset of B, also B is not a subset of A. ## IMPORTANT POINTS ABOUT SUBSETS (i) Every set is a subset of itself. (ii) The empty set is a subset of every set. (iii) Number of subsets of a set =2n, where n is number of elements in the given set. ## INTERVALS AS SUBSETS OF SET OF REAL NUMBERS (R) Let a,b∈R and a<b. Then, the set of real numbers {y:a<y<b} is called an open interval and is denoted by (a,b) as interval. All the points between a and b belong to the open interval (a,b) but a,b themselves do not belong to this interval. The interval which contains the end points also, is called closed interval and is denoted by [a,b]. Thus [a,b]={x:a≤x≤b} We can also have intervals closed at one end and open at the other, i.e., [a,b)={x:a≤x<b} is a semi-open interval from a to b, including a but excluding b. (a,b]={x:a<x≤b} is a semi-open interval from a to b including b but excluding a. Note that in P(A), every element is a set. If A has n elements, then its power set has 2n elements. Ex. : Let A={a,b}, then P(A)={ϕ,{a},{b},{a,b}} Here, number of elements of P(A)=4 ## UNIVERSAL SET If there are some sets under consideration, and out of these sets, there is a set which is the superset of each one of the given sets. That is all other sets under consideration are subsets of this set. Such a set is known as the universal set, denoted by U. For example : (i) In the context of human population studies, the universal set consists of all the people in the world. theory_sections.markdown: ## 17. Sets, Relations and Functions

## SETS
In everyday life, we often speak about the collection of objects of particular kind such as a cricket team, the river of India, the vowels in the English alphabet etc. Each of these collection is well-defined collection of objects in the sense that we can definitely decide whether a given particular object belongs to a given collection or not. In mathematics, we call such collections as sets. For example, we say that 10 does not belong to the given collection of all odd natural numbers. On the other side, 15 belongs to the given collection.
The following points may be noted :
(i) Objects, elements and members of a set are synonymous terms.
(ii) Sets are usually denoted by capital letters <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>, etc.
(iii) The elements of a set are represented by small letters <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>, etc.
(iv) Each element in a set comes only once i.e. repetition of any element is not allowed.
The Greek symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∈</mo></mrow></math> (epsilon) is used to denote the phrase 'belongs to'. If ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ' is an element of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>, we say that " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> belongs to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> ". Thus, we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>. If ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ' is not an element of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>, we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∉</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and read " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> does not belong to set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> ".
Eg : In the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> of vowels in the English alphabet, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∉</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>.
In the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> of prime factors of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>∈</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>∉</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>.

## REPRESENTATIONS OF SETS
There are two methods of representing a set :
(i) Roster or tabular form
(ii) Set-builder form.

## Roster or Tabular Form
(i) In roster form, all the elements of a set are listed, the elements are being separated by commas and are enclosed within braces <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. For example, the set of all even positive integers less than 7 is described in roster form as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>.
(ii) In roster form, the order in which the elements are listed is immaterial.

## Set-Builder Form In this form, a set is described by using a representative and stating the common property or properties which the elements of the set satisfy, through the representative. The set {a,e,i,o,u} in roster form can be written in set builder form as {x:x is a vowel in English alphabet }. Here the set written in set builder form read as ' x ' is an element of the set such that x is a vowel of English alphabet'. Here the colon (:) read as 'such that'. And in set-builder form after ':' a common property which possess all the elements of the set is written. Comparison Table

## TYPES OF SETS

## Empty Set
A set which does not contain any element is called the empty set, null set or void set.
The empty set is denoted by the symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>.
Given below are few examples of empty sets.
(i) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mn>1</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a natural number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is the empty set, because there is no natural number between 1 and 2 .
(ii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is rational number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the empty set, because the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> is not satisfied by any rational value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
(iii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is an even prime number greater than 2<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is the empty set, because 2 is the only even prime number.
(iv) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> is odd <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is the empty set, because the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> is not satisfied by any odd value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.

## Singleton Set
A set, consisting of a single element is called a singleton set. For example: The sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> are singleton sets. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is a singleton set, because this set contains only one integer -6 .

## Finite and Infinite Sets
A set which is empty or consists of a definite number of elements is called finite otherwise, the set is called infinite.

## Consider some examples :
(i) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> be the set of the days of the week. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> is finite.
(ii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> be the set of solutions of the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> is finite.
(iii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> be the set of points on a line. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> is infinite.
We represent the infinite set in the roster form by writing a few elements which clearly indicate the structure of the set followed (or preceded) by multiple of three dots. For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is the set of natural numbers, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is the set of odd natural numbers,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is the set of integers. All these sets are infinite.
Note : All infinite sets can not be described in the roster form.
The three dots ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>…</mi></mrow></math> ) are called an ellipsis and it means "Continue on".

## Equal Sets
Two sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are said to be equal if they have exactly the same elements. Two equal set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are represented as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. Otherwise, the sets are said to be unequal and we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
For example : Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.

## ILLUSTRATIOM : 3
Which of the following pairs of sets are equal? Justify your answer.
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>, the set of letters in "ALLOY" and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, the set of letters in "LOYAL".
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>≤</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

## DISJOINT SETS
Two sets A and B are said to be disjoint, if they have no elements in common.
For example: Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>&</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are disjoint sets.

## Subsets
A set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is said to be a subset of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> if every element of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is also an element of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. Here, set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is called superset of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.
Symbolically, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> if whenever <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Here ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ' is read as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is the subset of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Note : It is often convenient to use the symbol "⇒" which means implies. Using this symbol, we can write the definition of subset as follows: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
We read the above statement as " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is an element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> implies that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is also an element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ". If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is not a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⊄</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. For example :
(i) The set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> of rational numbers is a subset of the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> of real numbers, so we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>.
(ii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is the set of all divisors of 56 and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> the set of all prime divisors of 56 , then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>. So we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.
(iii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is not a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, also <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is not a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.

## IMPORTANT POINTS ABOUT SUBSETS
(i) Every set is a subset of itself.
(ii) The empty set is a subset of every set.
(iii) Number of subsets of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is number of elements in the given set.

theory_sections.topics: INTERVALS AS SUBSETS OF SET OF REAL NUMBERS (R)
theory_sections.markdown:
## INTERVALS AS SUBSETS OF SET OF REAL NUMBERS (R)
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>. Then, the set of real numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>y</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>y</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is called an open interval and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as interval. All the points between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> belong to the open interval <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> themselves do not belong to this interval.
The interval which contains the end points also, is called closed interval and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>. Thus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>a</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
We can also have intervals closed at one end and open at the other, i.e.,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>a</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is a semi-open interval from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, including <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> but excluding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is a semi-open interval from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> including <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> but excluding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>.
These sets can be shown by the dark portion of the number line and use dark circle for included number and hollow circle for not included point.

## POWER SET OF A SET
The set of all subsets of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is called the power set of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>. It is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Note that in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, every element is a set.
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> elements, then its power set has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> elements.
Ex. : Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
Here, number of elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>

## UNIVERSAL SET
If there are some sets under consideration, and out of these sets, there is a set which is the superset of each one of the given sets. That is all other sets under consideration are subsets of this set. Such a set is known as the universal set, denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math>. For example :
(i) In the context of human population studies, the universal set consists of all the people in the world.
(ii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> are sets under consideration, then set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> can be considered as universal set because all other three sets are the subset of this set.

## ILLUSTRATIOM : 5
What universal set would you propose for each of the following :
(i) The set of right triangles.
(ii) The set of isosceles triangles.

## VENN DIAGRAMS
In order to illustrate universal sets, subsets and certain operations on sets in a clear and simple way, we make use of geometric figures. These figures are called Venn-Diagrams. In Venn Diagrams, a universal set is represented by a rectangle and any other set is represented by a circle in it.
In the Venn-diagrams, the elements of the sets are written in their respective circles.
In the Venn-diagram, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is the universal set of which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> are subsets.
## OPERATION ON SETS

## Union of Sets
The union of two sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the set which consists of all those elements which are either in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> or in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> (including those which are in both). In symbols, we write
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
The union of two sets can be represented by a Venn diagram as shown in Figure.
The shaded portion in Figure represents <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.

## Intersection of Sets
The intersection of two sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the set of all those elements which belong to both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. Symbolically, we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
The shaded portion in Figure indicates the intersection of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.

## ILLUSTRATIOM : 7
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>, then find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

## Difference of Two Sets
The difference of the sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the set of elements which belong to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> but not to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. Symbolically, we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and read as " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> minus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ".
Using the setbuilder notation, we can rewrite the definition of difference as
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∉</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
The difference of two sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> can be represented by Venn diagram as shown in the figure. The shaded portion represents the difference of sets A and B i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.

## Complement of a Set
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> be the universal set and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> be a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math>. Then, the complement of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is the set of all elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> which are not the elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>. Symbolically, we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> to denote the complement of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> with respect to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math>. Thus, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∉</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>.
Obviously, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>
The complement <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> can be represented by a Venn diagram as shown in the figure. The shaded portion represents the complement of the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.

theory_sections.topics: Some Properties of Complement of a Set
theory_sections.markdown:
## Some Properties of Complement of a Set
1. Complement laws: (i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> (ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></math>
2. De Morgan's law: (i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>∩</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> (ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>∪</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
3. Law of double complementation : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>
4. Laws of empty set and universal set : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></math>.

## CARDINAL NUMBER
Number of element in a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is called cardinal number of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.
It is represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
For Example: If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>

## FORMULA TO SOLVE PRACTICAL PROBLEM
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are finite sets, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## ILLUSTRATIOM : 9
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> are two sets such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> has 50 elements, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> has 28 elements and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> has 32 elements, then how many elements does <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> have ?
## RELATION

## Ordered Pair
Two elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> listed in a specific order form an ordered pair denoted by ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ).
In general, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≠</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
Two ordered pairs are equal, if and only if the corresponding first elements are equal and the second elements are also equal.

## Cartesian Product of Sets
If A and B are two non-empty sets, then the set of all ordered pairs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is called the Cartesian product of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Thus, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>:</mi><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>, then we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>.

## Relation
A relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> from a non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> to a non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is a subset of the cartesian product <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. The subset is derived by describing a relationship between the first element and the second element of the ordered pairs in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
A relation from a non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> to non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is symbolically represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Eg : Consider two non-empty sets:

## Complex Numbers
If a and b are two real numbers, then a number of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is called a complex number. Here <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is the real part denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>Re</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> \& b is the imaginary part denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>Im</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, here <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
## Algebra of Complex Numbers
I. Addition : Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
II. Difference : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
III. Multiplication : Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
## COMPLEX NUMBER
A number of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are real numbers is called a complex number, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is the real part and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is the imaginary part of the complex number. E.g : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, etc.
Note : (i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is read as iota. (ii) A complex number is usually represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>. i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>
(iii) Real part of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> is denoted by " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>Re</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> " and imaginary part of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> is denoted by " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>Im</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> "

So <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>

## CONJUGATE OF A COMPLEX NUMBER
The conjugate of a complex number is also a complex whose real and imaginary part are same but sign of imaginary part are opposite.
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> be a complex number, then its conjugate denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow></math> is defined as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>
## Properties of Conjugate of Complex Number
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>±</mi><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mi>±</mi><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>·</mo><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math>
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
## ALGEBRAIC OPERATIONS WITH COMPLEX NUMBER
For any complex numbers, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, we have
