The solutions of quadratic equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, are given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>±</mi><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is called the discriminant of the quadratic equation. ## Complex Numbers
If a and b are two real numbers, then a number of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is called a complex number. Here <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is the real part denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>Re</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> \& b is the imaginary part denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>Im</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, here <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

## Algebra of Complex Numbers
I. Addition : Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
II. Difference : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
III. Multiplication : Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>

## COMPLEX NUMBER
A number of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are real numbers is called a complex number, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is the real part and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is the imaginary part of the complex number. E.g : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, etc.
Note : (i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is read as iota. (ii) A complex number is usually represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>. i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>
(iii) Real part of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> is denoted by " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>Re</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> " and imaginary part of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> is denoted by " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>Im</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> "

## INTEGRAL POWERS OF IOTA
We have, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. So <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>
The values of the negative integral powers of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> are found as given below :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Remarks : A complex number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is said to be
(i) Purely real, if imaginary part of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
(ii) Purely imaginary, if real part of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>

## CONJUGATE OF A COMPLEX NUMBER
The conjugate of a complex number is also a complex whose real and imaginary part are same but sign of imaginary part are opposite.
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> be a complex number, then its conjugate denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow></math> is defined as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>

theory_sections.topics: Properties of Conjugate of Complex Number
theory_sections.markdown:
## Properties of Conjugate of Complex Number
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>±</mi><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mi>±</mi><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>·</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>·</mo><mover><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math>
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>

## ALGEBRAIC OPERATIONS WITH COMPLEX NUMBER
For any complex numbers, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, we have
(a) Addition : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(b) Subtraction : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(c) Multiplication : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(d) Division : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> ( when at least one of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is non-zero) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

## MODULUS OF A COMPLEX NUMBER <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>
The modulus of a complex number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></math> and read as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>mod</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. It is defined as the distance of point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> from origin in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>-plane (called Argand plane)
i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>Re</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>Im</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

## ILLUSTRATIOM : 2
Find the modulus of the complex number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>

## Properties of Modulus of Complex Number
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>z</mi><mo>·</mo><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>z</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>·</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(v) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mover><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></math>
(vi) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></math>
(vii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(viii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

## MULTIPLICATIVE INVERSE OF A COMPLEX NUMBER
For any non-zero complex number, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, there exists the complex number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> called the multiplicative inverse of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>

## Solution of a Quadratic Equation
The solutions of quadratic equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, are given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>±</mi><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is called the discriminant of the quadratic equation. The value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> may be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></mrow></mrow></math> or 0.
When <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, roots of the quadratic equation are complex (i.e., non-real).
DIRECTIONS: This section contains multiple choice questions. Each questions has 4 choices (a), (b), (c) and (d) out of which ONLY ONE is correct.
1. Value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>
2. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, then
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
3. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, then
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
4. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>57</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>25</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, when simplified has the value
(a) 0
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>
(d) 2
5. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>⋯</mo><mo>·</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is
(a) positive
(b) negative
(c) 0
(d) cannot be determined
6. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">|</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> lies on
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-axis
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>-axis
(c) line <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
(d) None of these
7. The multiplicative inverse of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, is
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
8. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, then
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math>
9. Find the multiplicative inverse of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>
10. Express the complex number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> in the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>

## 19. Matrices | Symmetric \& Skew Symmetric Matrices | | :--- | | Symmetric Matrix A square matrix A=[aij] is called a symmetric matrix, if aij=aji for all i,j or AT=A Skew Symmetric Matrix A square matrix A=[aij ] is called a skew-symmetric matrix, if aij=−aji for all i,j or AT=−A. | A matrix is an ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions. The numbers or functions are called the elements of the matrix. For example [125346] is a matrix. The horizontal lines of elements in the above matrix are said to constitute, rows of the matrix \& vertical lines of elements are said to constitute columns of the matrix. Thus above matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns. ## Matrix be mn. ## Order of a Matrix A matrix having m rows and n columns is called a matrix of order m×n or simply m×n matrix. or A=[aij]m×n,1≤i≤m,1≤j≤ni,j∈Naij is an element lying in the ith  row \& j th column. The number of elements in m×n matrix will ## Multiplication of a Matrix by a Scalar Let A=[aij]m×n be a matrix \& k be a number. Then, kA=Ak=[kaij]m×n ## MATRICES Suppose your school organizes an inter-school debate competition, where any participant can speak in either of the six languages Hindi, English, Malayalam, Telugu, Tamil or Marathi. Various schools send the list of their students who wish to participate in the debate competition. Out of all the list received, let us consider the list of participants received from three schools A,B and C . The list received from the school A consists of 2 participants in English, 4 in Hindi, 1 in Malayalam and 1 in Telugu. In the list of school B, 5 participants are in English, 3 are in Hindi, 1 in Malayalam, 2 in Telugu and 1 in Marathi. As per the list received from the school C, 6 participants are in English, 1 in Hindi, 2 each in Malayalam and Telugu, 3 in Tamil and 4 in Marathi. The information given in the above example, can be put in a compact way in a tabular form as follows:
Name of the SchoolNumber of speakers (language wise)
EnglishHindiMalayalamTeluguTamilMarathi
A241100
B531201
C612234
The above arranged form of numbers is known as rectangular array. In the array, the lines from top to bottom are called columns whereas the lines from left to right are called rows. Thus in the above arrangement of numbers there are 3 rows and 6 columns and therefore, total number of elements is 3×6=18. Now, we write the numbers given in the above arrangement in the form given below. [241100531201612234] The above arrangement of numbers in a square bracket is an example of a matrix. Example : A=[21−3120] is a matrix having 2 rows and 3 columns. ## ORDER OF A MATRIX If a matrix ' A ' has ' m ' rows and ' n ' columns, then m×n is called the order of matrix A and is denoted as Am×n. Example : Let B=(abc) is a matrix consisting of 3 rows and 1 column. So, its order is 3×1. Each number or entry in the matrix is called an element of the matrix. An element of a matrix is generally denoted by aij, where the first subscript i of aij denotes the row number and the second subscript j of aij denotes the column number. Example : a13 denote the element of 1st  row and 3rd  column. Similarly, a32 denotes the element of 3rd  row and 2nd  column. Thus in a 3×3 matrix, the elements can be symbolically written as under : [a11a12a13a21a22a23a31a32a33] Note : You can also represent a matrix by using the symbols [aij] or (aij). Generally, we use the notation [aij] to denote a matrix. However, this notation is incomplete unless we talk about the number of rows and numbers of columns of the matrix. Therefore, to have a clear cut idea of a matrix, we write [aij]m×n, where m×n is the order of the matrix which mean, there are m rows and n columns in the matrix. ## TYPES OF MATRICES ## Row Matrix A matrix, in which there is only one row, is called a row matrix. For example, [36 62 ] is a row matrix. ## Column Matrix A matrix, in which there is only one column, is called a column matrix. For example, [259] is a column matrix. ## Square Matrix A matrix in which the number of rows equal to the number of columns is called a square matrix. For example, [10−36172i5],[1725−3514] and [100010001] are square matrices. ## Null or (Zero) Matrix A matrix having all the elements zero is called zero matrix (null matrix). ## Diagonal Matrix A square matrix is called diagonal matrix if all its non-diagonal elements are zero. The diagonal elements may or may not be zero. For example, X=[2000500011] is a diagonal matrix. ## Scalar Matrix A diagonal matrix in which all the diagonal element are equal and all other elements equal to zero is called a scalar matrix. For example, [−300−3] is a scalar matrix of order 2. ## Unit or Identity Matrix A square matrix, in which all the diagonal elements are unity and all other elements are zero, is called a unit matrix. For example, E=[100010001] is a unit matrix of order 3×3. Note : If number of rows and columns of a matrix are equal, then we inspite of writing both number of rows and columns to write the order of the matrix as m×m, we write only m. In other words, we can say that any square matrix [aij] is called a unit matrix, aij={1, whenever i=j0, whenever i≠j Identity matrix is represented by the English capital letter ' I '. ## EQUALITY OF TWO MATRICES Two matrices are said to be equal if they are of same order and each element of one matrix is equal to the corresponding element of other matrix. For example, [2−3153−2] and [2−3a53b] will be equal matrices if a=1 and b=−2 because both matrices have same order. ## ALGEBRA OF MATRICES ## Addition of Matrices Let there be two matrices A and B of the same order m×n. Then their sum denoted by A+B, is defined to be the matrix of order m×n obtained by adding the corresponding elements of A and B. Thus, if A=[aij]m×n and B=[bij]m×n, then A+B=[aij+bij]m×n Example : A=[172−459608] and B=[142−4365−21], then A+B=[1+17+42+2(−4)+(−4)5+39+66+50+(−2)8+1]=[2114−881511−29] Note : Similarly, subtraction of two matrices can be defined. ## Multiplication of a Matrix by a Scalar If X is a matrix and k is a scalar (or say k is any number), then kX is a matrix, each element of which is k times the corresponding element of the matrix X. Thus, if X=[125−4365−21], then kX=[k2k5k−4k3k6k5k−2kk] ## Multiplication of Two Matrices If A and B are two matrices, then the multiplication of two matrices A and B (i.e. product AB ) is possible only when number of columns in the first matrix A is equal to the number of rows in the second matrix B. For example, if A is a 2×2 matrix and B is a 2×3 matrix, then the number of columns 2 of matrix A is equal to the number of rows of matrix B and hence A.B is defined and it will be of order 2×3. But B.A is not possible because the number of columns 3 of matrix B is not equal to number of rows of matrix A. ## SOLUTION : If AB=[x11x12x21x22x31x32], then x11=[11][21]=1×2+1×1=3,x12=[11][34]=1×3+1×4=7 &x21=[23][21]=2×2+3×1=7,x22=[23][34]=2×3+3×4=18&x31=[12][21]=1×2+2×1=4,x32=[12][34]=1×3+2×4=11&∴AB=[37718411] ## TRANSPOSE OF A MATRIX If the rows and corresponding columns of a matrix A of order m×n are interchanged, we get a new matrix of the order n×m, which is called the transpose of the matrix A. The transpose of a matrix A is denoted by A′ or AT. For example: If A=[17225−6341], then the transpose of A can be expressed as A′=[1237542−61] ## Properties of Transpose of a Matrix (i) The transpose of the sum of two matrices is the sum of their transpose, i.e., (A+B)′=A′+B′. (ii) The transpose of the transpose of a matrix is the matrix itself, i.e., (A′)′=A. (iii) If A is a matrix of any order and k is a scalar, then (kA)′=kA′. (iv) The transpose of the product of two matrices is the product in reverse order of their transpose, i.e., (AB)′=B′A′. ## SYMMETRIC MATRIX A square matrix A=[aij] is called symmetric if aij=aji, for all values of i and j. In other words, we can say that a square matrix A is symmetric matrix if A′=A For example, A=[140425057] is a symmetric matrix Note : If A is a symmetric matrix, then kA is also symmetric, where k is a scalar. ## SKEW-SYMMETRIC MATRIX A square matrix A=[aij] is called skew-symmetric matrix if aij=−aji, for all values of i and j. In other words, we can say that a square matrix A is skew-symmetric if A′=−A For example, A=[0−2320−5−350] is a skew-symmetric matrix. Note: (i) If A is a skew-symmetric matrix, then kA is also skew-symmetric, where k is a scalar. (ii) Each diagonal element of a skew-symmetric matrix is 0 . key_points.text: The transpose of the sum of two matrices is the sum of their transpose, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

The transpose of the transpose of a matrix is the matrix itself, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.

The transpose of the product of two matrices is the product in reverse order of their transpose, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
