Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">j</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>

## MATRICES Suppose your school organizes an inter-school debate competition, where any participant can speak in either of the six languages Hindi, English, Malayalam, Telugu, Tamil or Marathi. Various schools send the list of their students who wish to participate in the debate competition. Out of all the list received, let us consider the list of participants received from three schools A,B and C . The list received from the school A consists of 2 participants in English, 4 in Hindi, 1 in Malayalam and 1 in Telugu. In the list of school B, 5 participants are in English, 3 are in Hindi, 1 in Malayalam, 2 in Telugu and 1 in Marathi. As per the list received from the school C, 6 participants are in English, 1 in Hindi, 2 each in Malayalam and Telugu, 3 in Tamil and 4 in Marathi. The information given in the above example, can be put in a compact way in a tabular form as follows:
Name of the SchoolNumber of speakers (language wise)
EnglishHindiMalayalamTeluguTamilMarathi
A241100
B531201
C612234
The above arranged form of numbers is known as rectangular array. In the array, the lines from top to bottom are called columns whereas the lines from left to right are called rows. Thus in the above arrangement of numbers there are 3 rows and 6 columns and therefore, total number of elements is 3×6=18. Now, we write the numbers given in the above arrangement in the form given below. [241100531201612234] The above arrangement of numbers in a square bracket is an example of a matrix. Example : A=[21−3120] is a matrix having 2 rows and 3 columns.

## ORDER OF A MATRIX
If a matrix ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> ' has ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> ' rows and ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> ' columns, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is called the order of matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and is denoted as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
Example : Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>a</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>b</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>c</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a matrix consisting of 3 rows and 1 column. So, its order is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
Each number or entry in the matrix is called an element of the matrix. An element of a matrix is generally denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, where the first subscript <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denotes the row number and the second subscript <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denotes the column number.
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denote the element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>1</mn><mrow><mtext>st </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> row and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> column. Similarly, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denotes the element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mtext>rd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> row and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext>nd </mtext></mrow></msup></mrow></math> column. Thus in a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> matrix, the elements can be symbolically written as under :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>23</mn></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>33</mn></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Note : You can also represent a matrix by using the symbols <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. Generally, we use the notation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> to denote a matrix. However, this notation is incomplete unless we talk about the number of rows and numbers of columns of the matrix. Therefore, to have a clear cut idea of a matrix, we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is the order of the matrix which mean, there are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> rows and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> columns in the matrix.
## TYPES OF MATRICES

## Row Matrix
A matrix, in which there is only one row, is called a row matrix. For example, [36 62 ] is a row matrix.

theory_sections.topics: Column Matrix A matrix, in which there is only one column, is called a column matrix. For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>5</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>9</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a column matrix.
theory_sections.markdown: ## Column Matrix A matrix, in which there is only one column, is called a column matrix. For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>5</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>9</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a column matrix.

## Square Matrix
A matrix in which the number of rows equal to the number of columns is called a square matrix.
For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>6</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>7</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mi>i</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> are square matrices.

## Null or (Zero) Matrix
A matrix having all the elements zero is called zero matrix (null matrix).

## Diagonal Matrix
A square matrix is called diagonal matrix if all its non-diagonal elements are zero. The diagonal elements may or may not be zero.
For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>11</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a diagonal matrix.

## Scalar Matrix
A diagonal matrix in which all the diagonal element are equal and all other elements equal to zero is called a scalar matrix.
For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a scalar matrix of order 2.

## Unit or Identity Matrix
A square matrix, in which all the diagonal elements are unity and all other elements are zero, is called a unit matrix.
For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a unit matrix of order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.
Note : If number of rows and columns of a matrix are equal, then we inspite of writing both number of rows and columns to write the order of the matrix as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>, we write only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>.
In other words, we can say that any square matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is called a unit matrix, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext> whenever </mtext><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext> whenever </mtext><mi>i</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> Identity matrix is represented by the English capital letter ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> '.

## EQUALITY OF TWO MATRICES
Two matrices are said to be equal if they are of same order and each element of one matrix is equal to the corresponding element of other matrix.
For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>5</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi>a</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>5</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mi>b</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> will be equal matrices if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> because both matrices have same order.
## ALGEBRA OF MATRICES

## Addition of Matrices
Let there be two matrices <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> of the same order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. Then their sum denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, is defined to be the matrix of order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> obtained by adding the corresponding elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Thus, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
Example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>7</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>9</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>6</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>8</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>4</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>6</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>8</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>11</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>4</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>8</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>15</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>11</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>9</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Note : Similarly, subtraction of two matrices can be defined.

theory_sections.topics: Multiplication of a Matrix by a Scalar
theory_sections.markdown:
## Multiplication of a Matrix by a Scalar
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> is a matrix and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is a scalar (or say <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is any number), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> is a matrix, each element of which is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> times the corresponding element of the matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>. Thus, if
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>6</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mtext>, then </mtext><mi>k</mi><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mi>k</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn><mi>k</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>k</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn><mi>k</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>6</mn><mi>k</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn><mi>k</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mi>k</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

## Multiplication of Two Matrices
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are two matrices, then the multiplication of two matrices <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> (i.e. product <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ) is possible only when number of columns in the first matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is equal to the number of rows in the second matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
For example, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> matrix and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> matrix, then the number of columns 2 of matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is equal to the number of rows of matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is defined and it will be of order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>. But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is not possible because the number of columns 3 of matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is not equal to number of rows of matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.

## TRANSPOSE OF A MATRIX
If the rows and corresponding columns of a matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> of order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> are interchanged, we get a new matrix of the order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>, which is called the transpose of the matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>. The transpose of a matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. For example:
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>7</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>4</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, then the transpose of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> can be expressed as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>7</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>4</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

theory_sections.topics: Properties of Transpose of a Matrix
theory_sections.markdown:
## Properties of Transpose of a Matrix
(i) The transpose of the sum of two matrices is the sum of their transpose, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(ii) The transpose of the transpose of a matrix is the matrix itself, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.
(iii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is a matrix of any order and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is a scalar, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>A</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(iv) The transpose of the product of two matrices is the product in reverse order of their transpose, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

## SYMMETRIC MATRIX
A square matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is called symmetric if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, for all values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>.
In other words, we can say that a square matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is symmetric matrix if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>
For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>4</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>4</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>5</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>7</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a symmetric matrix
Note : If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is a symmetric matrix, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is also symmetric, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is a scalar.

## SKEW-SYMMETRIC MATRIX
A square matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is called skew-symmetric matrix if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, for all values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>.
In other words, we can say that a square matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is skew-symmetric if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>
For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a skew-symmetric matrix.
Note: (i) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is a skew-symmetric matrix, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is also skew-symmetric, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is a scalar.
(ii) Each diagonal element of a skew-symmetric matrix is 0 .
DIRECTIONS: This section contains multiple choice questions. Each questions has 4 choices (a), (b), (c) and (d) out of which only one is correct.
1. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mi>cos</mi><mi>α</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mi>sin</mi><mi>α</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mi>sin</mi><mi>α</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mi>cos</mi><mi>α</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow></math>, then the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> is
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
2. For any square matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is a
(a) Unit matrix
(b) Symmetric matrix
(c) Skew symmetric matrix
(d) Diagonal matrix
3. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>4</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is equal to
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>8</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>20</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>7</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>9</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>8</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>7</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>20</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>9</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(d) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>8</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>7</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
4. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>5</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>x</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>y</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, then
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>
(d) None of these
5. A matrix in which the number of columns is equal to the number of rows, is called
(a) Row matrix
(b) Column matrix
(c) Square matrix
(d) Diagonal matrix
6. A square matrix in which all elements except the diagonal elements are zero is known as
(a) Row matrix
(b) Column matrix
(c) Square matrix
(d) Diagonal matrix
7. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a diagonal matrix of order
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 1
rows.question:
Find the quotient and remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> for the pairs of positive integers given below :
(i) 23, 4
(ii) 81, 3
(iii) 12, 5
SOLUTION :
(i) 23,4
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>23</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>;</mi><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>;</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
When 23 is divided by 4 , quotient is 5 and remainder is 3 .
(ii) 81,3
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>81</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>27</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
When 81 is divided by 3 , quotient is 27 and remainder is 0 .
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>27</mn><mi>;</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mn>27</mn></mrow></math>
(iii) 12,5
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
On dividing 12 by 5 , we have quotient 2 and remainder 2 .
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>;</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
Remark : The above Euclid's lemma is nothing but a restatement of the long division process.
## TO FIND THE H.C.F. OF TWO POSITIVE INTEGERS USING EUCLID'S DIVISION ALGORITHM
To obtain the H.C.F. of two positive integers, say <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>></mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, follow the step below :
Step (i) : Apply Euclid's division lemma, to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
So, we find whole numbers, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>
Step (ii) : If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is the H.C.F. of a and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, apply the division lemma to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>.
Step (iii) : Continue the process till the remainder become zero.
The divisor at this stage will be the required H.C.F.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 2
rows.question: ## Let us find the H.C.F. of 60 and 108 using the Euclid's Division Algorithm.
rows.answer:
Step (i) : Since, 108 > 60 applying Euclid's Lemma to 60 and 108, we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>108</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>48</mn></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mn>48</mn><mo><</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math>
Step (ii) : Since, remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>48</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
So, again applying the division lemma to 60 and 48, we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>48</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mn>12</mn><mo><</mo><mn>48</mn></mrow></math>.
Step (iii) : Again remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> so applying division lemma to 48 and 12, we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>48</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, Here remainder is zero.
Therefore, 12 is the required H.C.F.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 3
rows.question: Let us find H.C.F. of three numbers 140, 90 and 54 using the Euclid's Division Algorithm.
rows.answer:
Since 140 > 90, applying Euclid's Lemma
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>140</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow></math>
Since, remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
So, again applying Euclid's Lemma to 90 and 50, we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>90</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>40</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>50</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>40</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Here, remainder is zero.
Therefore, H.C.F. of 140 and 90 is 10
Now, find the H.C.F. of 10 and the third number 54.
Since, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>54</mn><mo>></mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>, then by Euclid's Lemma
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>54</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Here, remainder is zero. Therefore, 2 is H.C.F. of 10 and 54.
Hence, required H.C.F. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>140</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>54</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
## FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ARITHMETIC
Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes and this factorisation is unique, except the order in which the prime factors occur.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 4
rows.question:
Express the following numbers as the product of prime factors.
(i) 36
(ii) 156
SOLUTION :
(i) 36
In each of the cases, product of prime factors of 36 is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.
(ii) 156
So, in each of the cases prime factors of 156 is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math>.
Hence, we can conclude that the prime factorisation of a number is unique.
## TO FIND THE H.C.F. AND L.C.M. BY PRIME FACTORISATION METHOD
## Algorithm
(i) Factorize and express integers as a product of primes with powers.
(ii) To find H.C.F. find the product of each common prime factor(s) with smallest power involved in the numbers.
(iii) To find L.C.M. find the product of each prime factors with greatest power involved in the numbers.
(iv) For any two positive numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and b, H.C.F. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo></mrow></math> L.C.M. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> be some fractions, then
(a) LCM of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>LCM</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>HCF</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

rows.question: Find the L.C.M. and H.C.F. of the following integers by applying the prime factorisation method. 8, 9 and 25
rows.answer:
First we write the prime factorisation of each of the given numbers.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
∴ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> L.C.M. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1800</mn></mrow></math> and H.C.F. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Remark : The product of two positive integers is equal to the product of their H.C.F. and L.C.M., but the same is not true for three or more positive integers.

Know!
The symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow></math> is called pi and this is a famous irrational number. The symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow></math> was introduced by an Anglo-Welsh philogist William Jones in 1706.
## CONSEQUENCE OF FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> be a prime number and ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ' be a positive integer. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> divides ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> '.
## PROVING IRRATIONALITY OF NUMBERS
In proving a number is an irrational number or not, we will use the 'consequence of fundamental theorem of Arithmetic'.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 6
rows.question: Prove that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is irrational.
rows.answer:
Let us assume, to the contrary, that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is rational. So, we can find integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> have a common factor other than 1 . Then, we divide by the common factor to get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are co-prime i.e. they have no common.
Factor other than 1 . So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>
Squaring on both sides and rearranging, we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Here we see that, 2 divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Since 2 is a prime number and divides square of a positive number ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ', therefore according to consequence of fundamental theorem 2 divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> also. So, we can write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> for some integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>.
Substituting for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>, we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, that is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
This means that 2 divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, and so 2 divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> (again using consequence of fundamental theorem)
Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> have at least 2 as a common factor.
But this contradicts the fact that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> have no common factors other than 1 .
This contradiction, has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is rational.
So, we conclude that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is irrational.
Some properties of Rational and Irrational numbers.
(a) Sum or difference of two or more irrational number is either zero or an irrational number
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> (irrational)
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> (irrational)
(v) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> (irrational)
(b) Product of two or more irrational numbers can be rational or irrational
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>×</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> (rational)
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>·</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>·</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> (rational)
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>·</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>·</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> (irrational)
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>·</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> (irrational)
(c) Division of one irrational number by another irrational number can be rational or irrational.
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> (rational)
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> (irrational)
## DECIMAL EXPANSION OF RATIONAL NUMBERS
(i) If a number in the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> are co-prime (i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> have no common factor other than 1 ) and prime factorisation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> is of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> are non-negative integers then decimal expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> terminates
i.e. when we divide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>, then we get an integer or a number upto a certain decimal place. i.e. when we divide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>, then we get an integer or a number upto a certain decimal place.
(ii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> be a rational number whose decimal expansion terminates. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> can be expressed in the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> are co-prime, and the prime factorisation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> is of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>; where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> are non-negative integers.
(iii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> be a rational number, such that the prime factorisation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> is not of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>; where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> are non-negative integers. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> has a decimal expansion which is non-terminating repeating (recurring) i.e. decimal expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> has infinite digits after decimal point but no part of digits after decimal point repeat continuously.
