Also show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> is in the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> are nonnegative integers.
rows.answer: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6.235</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>6235</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1247</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>200</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, which is in the form of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>. Also <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, which is in the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Note: We can also convert a rational number which is non-terminating reccuring (i.e., repeating) in the form of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> are co-prime (but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ).

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 9
rows.question: Convert <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>23</mn><mo>.</mo><mover><mrow><mn>426</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math> into <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> form, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> are coprime (but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> ).
rows.answer:
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>.</mo><mover><mrow><mn>426</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mspace width="1em" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23.426426426</mn><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>.
Multiply equation (i) by 1000 , so that in the right hand side of the equation (i), the point (.) comes just after the first repeating part (426).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mn>1000</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23426.426426</mn><mi>…</mi></mrow></math>.
Subtracting equation (i) from (ii), we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>999</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23403</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>23403</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>999</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7801</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>333</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mn>23</mn><mo>.</mo><mover><mrow><mn>426</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7801</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>333</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, which is in the required form of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
## - Show that there is no positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is rational.
We assume that there is a positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is rational and equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are positive integers.
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></math>
Rationalising RHS by multiplying numerator and denominator by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
or, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Adding equations (i) and (ii), we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Subtracting eqn. (ii) from (i), we get, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
From (iii) and (iv), we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> are both rational as a and b are both positive integer.
This is possible only when both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> are perfect squares of some positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> differ by 2 . But two perfect squares never differ by 2 , hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> both cannot be perfect square. So, there is no positive number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is a rational number.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 1
rows.question:
Find the quotient and remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> for the pairs of positive integers given below :
(i) 23, 4
(ii) 81, 3
(iii) 12, 5
SOLUTION :
(i) 23,4
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>23</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>;</mi><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>;</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
When 23 is divided by 4 , quotient is 5 and remainder is 3 .
(ii) 81,3
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>81</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>27</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
When 81 is divided by 3 , quotient is 27 and remainder is 0 .
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>27</mn><mi>;</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mn>27</mn></mrow></math>
(iii) 12,5
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
On dividing 12 by 5 , we have quotient 2 and remainder 2 .
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>;</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
Remark : The above Euclid's lemma is nothing but a restatement of the long division process.
## TO FIND THE H.C.F. OF TWO POSITIVE INTEGERS USING EUCLID'S DIVISION ALGORITHM
To obtain the H.C.F. of two positive integers, say <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>></mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, follow the step below :
Step (i) : Apply Euclid's division lemma, to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
So, we find whole numbers, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>
Step (ii) : If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is the H.C.F. of a and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, apply the division lemma to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>.
Step (iii) : Continue the process till the remainder become zero.
The divisor at this stage will be the required H.C.F.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 2
rows.question: ## Let us find the H.C.F. of 60 and 108 using the Euclid's Division Algorithm.
rows.answer:
Step (i) : Since, 108 > 60 applying Euclid's Lemma to 60 and 108, we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>108</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>48</mn></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mn>48</mn><mo><</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math>
Step (ii) : Since, remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>48</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
So, again applying the division lemma to 60 and 48, we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>48</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mn>12</mn><mo><</mo><mn>48</mn></mrow></math>.
Step (iii) : Again remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> so applying division lemma to 48 and 12, we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>48</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, Here remainder is zero.
Therefore, 12 is the required H.C.F.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 3
rows.question: Let us find H.C.F. of three numbers 140, 90 and 54 using the Euclid's Division Algorithm.
rows.answer:
Since 140 > 90, applying Euclid's Lemma
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>140</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow></math>
Since, remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
So, again applying Euclid's Lemma to 90 and 50, we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>90</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>40</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>50</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>40</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Here, remainder is zero.
Therefore, H.C.F. of 140 and 90 is 10
Now, find the H.C.F. of 10 and the third number 54.
Since, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>54</mn><mo>></mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>, then by Euclid's Lemma
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>54</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Here, remainder is zero. Therefore, 2 is H.C.F. of 10 and 54.
Hence, required H.C.F. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>140</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>54</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
## FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ARITHMETIC
Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes and this factorisation is unique, except the order in which the prime factors occur.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 4
rows.question:
Express the following numbers as the product of prime factors.
(i) 36
(ii) 156
SOLUTION :
(i) 36
In each of the cases, product of prime factors of 36 is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.
(ii) 156
So, in each of the cases prime factors of 156 is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math>.
Hence, we can conclude that the prime factorisation of a number is unique.
## TO FIND THE H.C.F. AND L.C.M. BY PRIME FACTORISATION METHOD
## Algorithm
(i) Factorize and express integers as a product of primes with powers.
(ii) To find H.C.F. find the product of each common prime factor(s) with smallest power involved in the numbers.
(iii) To find L.C.M. find the product of each prime factors with greatest power involved in the numbers.
(iv) For any two positive numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and b, H.C.F. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo></mrow></math> L.C.M. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> be some fractions, then
(a) LCM of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>LCM</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>HCF</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(b) HCF of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>HCF</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>LCM</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 5
rows.question: Find the L.C.M. and H.C.F. of the following integers by applying the prime factorisation method. 8, 9 and 25
rows.answer:
First we write the prime factorisation of each of the given numbers.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
∴ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> L.C.M. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1800</mn></mrow></math> and H.C.F. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Remark : The product of two positive integers is equal to the product of their H.C.F. and L.C.M., but the same is not true for three or more positive integers.
Did You
Know!
The symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow></math> is called pi and this is a famous irrational number. The symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow></math> was introduced by an Anglo-Welsh philogist William Jones in 1706.
## CONSEQUENCE OF FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> be a prime number and ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ' be a positive integer. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> divides ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> '.
## PROVING IRRATIONALITY OF NUMBERS
In proving a number is an irrational number or not, we will use the 'consequence of fundamental theorem of Arithmetic'.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 6
rows.question: Prove that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is irrational.
rows.answer:
Let us assume, to the contrary, that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is rational. So, we can find integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> have a common factor other than 1 . Then, we divide by the common factor to get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are co-prime i.e. they have no common.
Factor other than 1 . So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>
Squaring on both sides and rearranging, we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Here we see that, 2 divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Since 2 is a prime number and divides square of a positive number ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> ', therefore according to consequence of fundamental theorem 2 divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> also. So, we can write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> for some integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>.
Substituting for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>, we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, that is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
This means that 2 divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, and so 2 divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> (again using consequence of fundamental theorem)
Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> have at least 2 as a common factor.
But this contradicts the fact that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> have no common factors other than 1 .
This contradiction, has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is rational.
So, we conclude that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is irrational.
Some properties of Rational and Irrational numbers.
(a) Sum or difference of two or more irrational number is either zero or an irrational number
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> (irrational)
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> (irrational)
(v) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> (irrational)
(b) Product of two or more irrational numbers can be rational or irrational
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>×</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> (rational)
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>·</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>·</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> (rational)
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>·</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>·</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> (irrational)
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>·</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>56</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> (irrational)
(c) Division of one irrational number by another irrational number can be rational or irrational.
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> (rational)
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> (irrational)
## DECIMAL EXPANSION OF RATIONAL NUMBERS
(i) If a number in the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> are co-prime (i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> have no common factor other than 1 ) and prime factorisation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> is of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> are non-negative integers then decimal expansion of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> terminates
i.e. when we divide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>, then we get an integer or a number upto a certain decimal place. i.e. when we divide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>, then we get an integer or a number upto a certain decimal place.
(ii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> be a rational number whose decimal expansion terminates. rows.answer:
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>.</mo><mover><mrow><mn>426</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mspace width="1em" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23.426426426</mn><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>.
Multiply equation (i) by 1000 , so that in the right hand side of the equation (i), the point (.) comes just after the first repeating part (426).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mn>1000</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23426.426426</mn><mi>…</mi></mrow></math>.
Subtracting equation (i) from (ii), we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>999</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23403</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>23403</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>999</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7801</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>333</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mn>23</mn><mo>.</mo><mover><mrow><mn>426</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7801</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>333</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, which is in the required form of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
## - Show that there is no positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is rational.
We assume that there is a positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is rational and equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are positive integers.
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></math>
Rationalising RHS by multiplying numerator and denominator by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
or, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Adding equations (i) and (ii), we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Subtracting eqn. (ii) from (i), we get, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
From (iii) and (iv), we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> are both rational as a and b are both positive integer.
This is possible only when both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> are perfect squares of some positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> differ by 2 . But two perfect squares never differ by 2 , hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> both cannot be perfect square. So, there is no positive number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> is a rational number.

rows.question:
Write down the degree of the following polynomials.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
SOLUTION :
(a) The highest power term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and exponent of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo><mo>∴</mo></mrow></math> degree of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> is 1
(b) The highest power term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>9</mn><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and exponent of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> is 4 . So, degree of the given polynomial is 4 .
(c) The highest power term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and exponent of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is 8 .
## VALUE OF A POLYNOMIAL
A polynomial of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> can be represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, etc. The value of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> is obtained by substituting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> in the given polynomial and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Consider the polynomial : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
If we replace <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> by 1 everywhere in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
So, we say that the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is 4 .
## ZERO(ES) / ROOT(S) OF POLYNOMIALS
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> be a root or zero of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
In other words, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is a root or zero of a polynomial if it is a solution to the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
The process of finding the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is actually solving the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Let's first find the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math>. To find the zeroes, we simply solve the following equation.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
So, this second degree polynomial has two zeroes or roots -5 and 3 .

rows.question: If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> are roots of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>. Find the values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
rows.answer:
Since, 2 is a root, therefore f(2)=2(2)3−5(2)2+a(2)+b=0⇒16−20+2a+b=0⇒2a+b=4 Since 0 is also a root, therefore f(0)=2(0)3−5(0)2+a(0)+b=0⇒b=0⇒2a=4⇒a=2,b=0 Time to Check Your Knowledge If the zeroes of p(x)=x3+2x2+a, are also the zeroes of polynomial q(x)=x5−x4−4x3+3x2+3x+b; then find the values of a and b. Which zeroes of q(x) are not the zeroes of p(x) ? If zeroes of p(x) are also the zeroes of q(x), then q(x) is divisible by p(x). Let us now divide q(x) by p(x) to obtain the remainder. \[ \] If q(x) is divisible by p(x), then remainder must be 0 . Now, remainder =0 ⇒(−1−a)x2+3x(1+a)+b−2a=0 for all x. ⇒(−1−a)=0,3(1+a)=0 and b−2a=0⇒a=−1 and b=−2 Substituting a=−1 in p(x), we obtain p(x)=x3+2x2+1 Now, x2−3x+2=(x−1)(x−2). So, zeroes of x2−3x+2 are 1 and 2 . q(1)=2≠0 and q(2)=15≠0 So, zeroes of the x2−3x+2 are not the zeroes of p(x). Hence, 1 and 2 are zeroes of q(x) which are not the zeroes of p(x). ## GEOMETRICAL MEANING OF THE ZERO(ES) OF A POLYNOMIAL Zero(es) of a polynomial is/are the x-coordinate of the point(s) where the graph of y=f(x) intersects the x-axis. ## GRAPHS OF POLYNOMIALS Graph of a polynomial f(x) is a smooth free hand curve passing through points (x1,y1),(x2,y2),(x3,y3),………. etc., where y1, y2,y3,…….. are the values of the polynomial f(x) at x1,x2,x3,……. respectively. In order to draw the graph of a polynomial f(x), we may follow the following algorithm. ## Algorithm to draw the graph of the polynomials : Step 1: Find the values y1,y2,…….yn, that is value of polynomial f(x) at x1,x2,……..xn and prepare a table that gives values of y or f(x) for various values of x.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⋯</mo><mo>⋯</mo></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⋯</mo><mo>⋯</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⋯</mo><mo>⋯</mo></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⋯</mo><mo>·</mo><mo>·</mo></mrow></math>
Step 2: Plot these points (x1,y1),(x2,y2),(x3,y3),……….,(xn,yn),……… on rectangular coordinate system. In plotting these points you may use different scales on the x and y-axis. Step 3 : Draw a free hand smooth curve passing through the points plotted in step 2 to get the graph of the polynomial f(x). ## GRAPH OF A LINEAR POLYNOMIAL Consider a linear polynomial f(x)=ax+b,a≠0. In class IX we have studied that the graph of y=ax+b is a straight line that has exactly one zero. That is why f(x)=ax+b is called a linear polynomial. Since two points determine a straight line, so only two points needed to plot or draw the line y=ax+b. The line represented by y=ax+b crosses the x -axis at exactly one point, namely (−ba,0).

Draw the graph of the polynomial f(x)=2x−5. Also, find its zero. SOLUTION : Let y=2x−5 The following table list the values of y corresponding to different values of x.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></mrow></math>14
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-33
The points A(1,−3) and B(4,3) are plotted on the graph paper on a suitable scale. A line is drawn passing through these points to obtain the graphs of the given polynomial. The line intersects the X-axis at x=52. Hence, zero or root of the given polynomial is 52. ## GRAPH OF A QUADRATIC POLYNOMIAL Let a,b,c be real numbers and a≠0. Then f(x)=ax2+bx+c is known as quadratic polynomial in x and it has either no zero or two zeroes. ## Example : 1. There are no zeroes of quadratic polynomial f(x)=x2+1 and thus the graph of the polynomial doesn't intersect x-axis. 2. There are two zeroes of quadratic polynomial p(x)=x2−4x+4 i.e., 2,2 ; which means both zeroes are same and thus the graph of this polynomial intersects x-axis only once at 2 . 3. There are two zeroes of quadratic polynomial g(x)=x2−9 that is +3,−3, thus the graph of this polynomial intersect x-axis at two places, 3&−3 Note : (i) The two zeroes of quadratic polynomial can be either both rational or both irrational. (ii) Graph of a quadratic polynomial is always a parabola. The graph shown in the illustration 5 and 6 are the parabola. Some parabola are upward open as in illustration 5 and others are downward open as in illustration 6. If the value of a in the quadratic polynomial ax2+bx+c is positive, then the parabola is upward open. If the value of a in the quadratic polynomial ax2+bx+c is negative, then the parabola is downward open.

Also find its zero(es).
rows.answer:
Let y=f(x)=x3−4x. The values of y for few values of x are listed in the following table :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>-3-2-10123

Since the graph of the given polynomial intersects x -axis at −2,0 and 2 . Therefore, zeroes of the given cubic polynomial are −2,0 and 2 . Cubic polynomial has either all roots are rational or one is rational and two are irrational. Irrational roots always occur in conjugate pairs. ## RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ZERO(ES) AND COEFFICIENT OF A POLYNOMIAL (i) Zero of a linear polynomial ax+b, is x=−ba or x=− constant term coefficient of x (ii) If quadratic polynomial ax2+bx+c=k(x−α)(x−β), where k is any real constant; then α and β are zeroes of quadratic polynomial ax2+bx+c, where a,b,c∈R and a≠0. α+β=−ba, i.e., sum of zeroes =− coefficient of x coefficient of x2 and α.β=−ca i.e., product of zeroes = constant term  coefficient of x2 We can obtain the quadratic polynomial p(x) as p(x)=k[x2− (sum of zeroes) x+ (product of zeroes)] (iii) If cubic polynomial ax3+bx2+cx+d=k(x−α)(x−β)(x−γ), where k is any real constant; then α,β and γ are zeroes of cubic polynomial ax3+bx2+cx+d where a,b,c,d∈R and a≠0, then α+β+γ=−ba,αβ+βγ+γα=ca and αβγ=−da ## ILLUSTRATIOM : 8 If zeroes of the polynomial x2+4x+2a are α and 2α, then find the value of α. Given, α and - are the zeroes of x2+4x+2a. Now, product of zeroes = constant term  coefficient of x2 ⇒α×2α=2a⇒2=2α⇒α=1 ## Some useful formulas : (i) α2+β2=(α+β)2−2αβ (ii) α2−β2=(α+β)(α−β)=α+β(α+β)2−4αβ (iii) (α−β)2=(α+β)2−4αβ (iv) α3+β3=(α+β)3−3αβ(α+β) (v) α3−β3=(α−β)3+3αβ(α−β) ## DIVISION OF POLYNOMIALS On dividing a polynomial p(x) by a polynomial d(x), let the quotient be q(x) and the remainder be r(x), then p(x)=d(x).q(x)+r(x), where either r(x)=0 or deg. r(x)<deg.d(x) Here, Dividend =p(x), Divisor =d(x), Quotient =q(x) and Remainder =r(x). Division algorithm of a polynomial by a polynomial : Step 1: Arrange the terms of the dividend and the divisor in descending order of their degrees. Step 2 : Divide the first term of the dividend by the first term of the divisor to obtain the first term of the quotient. Step 3 : Multiply all the terms of the divisor by the first term of the quotient and subtract the result from the dividend. Step 4 : Consider the remainder as new dividend and proceed as before. Step 5 : Repeat this process till we obtain a remainder which is either 0 or a polynomial of degree less than that of the divisor.
