rows.question: Divide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow></math> by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
rows.answer:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>\longdiv</mi><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>30</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>÷</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 10
rows.question: Find the remainder obtained on dividing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
rows.answer:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>\longdiv</mi><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mo>−</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>+</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mo>−</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></math>
Hence, remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
Alternate Method : To find remainder we can use remainder theorem.
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
Put Divisor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Then remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
So, 2 is the remainder.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 11
rows.question: Find all the zero(es) of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></math>, if you know that two of its zero(es) are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>.
rows.answer:
Two zeroes are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>. Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are the factors of given polynomial.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, is a factor of the given polynomial.
Now, we divide the given polynomial by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mi>&</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mi>&</mi><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> (First term of quotient is </mtext><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mtext> ) </mtext></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>−</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>+</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable><mtext> (Third term of quotient is </mtext><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext> ) </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
Now, by splitting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, we factorise <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
So, the remaining two zero(es) are given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. Therefore, the zero(es) of the given polynomial are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and 1 .
# CASE STUDY : Division Algorithm, Factor Theorem, Remainder Theorem and zero(es) of the Polynomial
- Division Algorithm :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Dividend <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Divisor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
- Factor Theorem :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
- Remainder Theorem :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
If polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
If polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
If polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
- Zeroes of a Polynomial
If polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Zeroes of a Polynomial
A number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> is a zero of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
Number of zero(s) of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Degree of the polynomial.
Hence number zero(s) of alinear polynomial, quadratic polynomial, cubic polynomial and biquadratic polynomial are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> and 4 respectively.
CASE-II : To find the quotient and remainder using division algorithm
Illustration: Apply the division algorithm to find the quotient and remainder on dividing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>, by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
Sol. We have,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
We find that degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> and degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. Therefore, quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is of degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and the remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is of degree zero.
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>.
By using division algorithm, we obtain
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>&</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>&</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Equating the coefficients of like powers of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and can start term on both sides, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>&</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>&</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>&</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mtext> and </mtext><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>&</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients terms </mtext><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
Solving these equations, we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>27</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>27</mn></mrow></math> and, Remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math>.
CASE-I : To find the remaining zeroes of a polynomial when some of its zeroes are given
Illustration: Obtain all the zeroes of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>, if two of its zeroes are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>.
Sol. It is given that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> are two zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a factor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. But, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a factor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Let us now divide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>. Using long division method, we obtain
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>\longdiv</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mn>0</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>+</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mo>+</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow></math>
Clearly, Quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and Remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
By division algorithm, we obtain
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Thus, the factors of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
Equating each factor to zero, we obtain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. Hence,
the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and -1 .
## CASE-III : To check whether a given polynomial in a factor of the other polynomial by applying the Division Algorithm
Illustration: By applying division algorithm prove that the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is a factor of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
Sol. We find that degree of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> and degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>. Therefore, quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is of degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and the remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is of degree 1 or less. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>.
Using division algorithm, we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo ## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES
1. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>. Find the roots of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and sketch the graph of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Sol. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Therefore, the roots are -1 and 3 .
The graph intersects the X -axis at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and 3 .
2. How many real roots, i.e., roots that are real numbers, has the parabola of each graph ?
Sol. Graph (a) has two real roots. It has two x -intercepts (i.e., the graph intersects the X -axis at two different points)
Graph (b) has no real roots. It has no x-intercepts. Both roots are complex.
Graph (c) has two real roots which are equal.
3. Inspect the following graph to solve this equation : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Sol. The quadratic polynomial will have the value 0 at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and 5 .
4. Find the zero(es) of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold">−</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></math> and verify the relationship between the zero(es) and the coefficients.
Sol. Recall the identity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Using it, we can write:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
So, the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> is zero when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Therefore, the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Now, Sum of zeroes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Product of zeroes </mtext><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Constant term </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
5. Show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></math> is a root of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> is a root of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
6. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is a root of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>, then find the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Sol. rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 2
rows.question:
Write down the degree of the following polynomials.
(a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
(b) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(c) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
SOLUTION :
(a) The highest power term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and exponent of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo><mo>∴</mo></mrow></math> degree of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> is 1
(b) The highest power term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>9</mn><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and exponent of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> is 4 . So, degree of the given polynomial is 4 .
(c) The highest power term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and exponent of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is 8 .
## VALUE OF A POLYNOMIAL
A polynomial of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> can be represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, etc. The value of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> is obtained by substituting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> in the given polynomial and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Consider the polynomial : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
If we replace <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> by 1 everywhere in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
So, we say that the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is 4 .
## ZERO(ES) / ROOT(S) OF POLYNOMIALS
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> be a root or zero of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
In other words, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is a root or zero of a polynomial if it is a solution to the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
The process of finding the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is actually solving the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Let's first find the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math>. To find the zeroes, we simply solve the following equation.

rows.question: If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> are roots of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>. Find the values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
rows.answer:
Since, 2 is a root, therefore f(2)=2(2)3−5(2)2+a(2)+b=0⇒16−20+2a+b=0⇒2a+b=4 Since 0 is also a root, therefore f(0)=2(0)3−5(0)2+a(0)+b=0⇒b=0⇒2a=4⇒a=2,b=0 Time to Check Your Knowledge If the zeroes of p(x)=x3+2x2+a, are also the zeroes of polynomial q(x)=x5−x4−4x3+3x2+3x+b; then find the values of a and b. Which zeroes of q(x) are not the zeroes of p(x) ? If zeroes of p(x) are also the zeroes of q(x), then q(x) is divisible by p(x). Let us now divide q(x) by p(x) to obtain the remainder. \[ \] If q(x) is divisible by p(x), then remainder must be 0 . Now, remainder =0 ⇒(−1−a)x2+3x(1+a)+b−2a=0 for all x. ⇒(−1−a)=0,3(1+a)=0 and b−2a=0⇒a=−1 and b=−2 Substituting a=−1 in p(x), we obtain p(x)=x3+2x2+1 Now, x2−3x+2=(x−1)(x−2). So, zeroes of x2−3x+2 are 1 and 2 . q(1)=2≠0 and q(2)=15≠0 So, zeroes of the x2−3x+2 are not the zeroes of p(x). Hence, 1 and 2 are zeroes of q(x) which are not the zeroes of p(x). ## GEOMETRICAL MEANING OF THE ZERO(ES) OF A POLYNOMIAL Zero(es) of a polynomial is/are the x-coordinate of the point(s) where the graph of y=f(x) intersects the x-axis. ## GRAPHS OF POLYNOMIALS Graph of a polynomial f(x) is a smooth free hand curve passing through points (x1,y1),(x2,y2),(x3,y3),………. etc., where y1, y2,y3,…….. are the values of the polynomial f(x) at x1,x2,x3,……. respectively. In order to draw the graph of a polynomial f(x), we may follow the following algorithm. ## Algorithm to draw the graph of the polynomials : Step 1: Find the values y1,y2,…….yn, that is value of polynomial f(x) at x1,x2,……..xn and prepare a table that gives values of y or f(x) for various values of x.

Step 2: Plot these points (x1,y1),(x2,y2),(x3,y3),……….,(xn,yn),……… on rectangular coordinate system. In plotting these points you may use different scales on the x and y-axis. Step 3 : Draw a free hand smooth curve passing through the points plotted in step 2 to get the graph of the polynomial f(x). ## GRAPH OF A LINEAR POLYNOMIAL Consider a linear polynomial f(x)=ax+b,a≠0. In class IX we have studied that the graph of y=ax+b is a straight line that has exactly one zero. That is why f(x)=ax+b is called a linear polynomial. Since two points determine a straight line, so only two points needed to plot or draw the line y=ax+b. The line represented by y=ax+b crosses the x -axis at exactly one point, namely (−ba,0).

Let y=f(x)=x3−4x. The values of y for few values of x are listed in the following table :

Since the graph of the given polynomial intersects x -axis at −2,0 and 2 . Therefore, zeroes of the given cubic polynomial are −2,0 and 2 . Cubic polynomial has either all roots are rational or one is rational and two are irrational. Irrational roots always occur in conjugate pairs. ## RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ZERO(ES) AND COEFFICIENT OF A POLYNOMIAL (i) Zero of a linear polynomial ax+b, is x=−ba or x=− constant term coefficient of x (ii) If quadratic polynomial ax2+bx+c=k(x−α)(x−β), where k is any real constant; then α and β are zeroes of quadratic polynomial ax2+bx+c, where a,b,c∈R and a≠0. α+β=−ba, i.e., sum of zeroes =− coefficient of x coefficient of x2 and α.β=−ca i.e., product of zeroes = constant term  coefficient of x2 We can obtain the quadratic polynomial p(x) as p(x)=k[x2− (sum of zeroes) x+ (product of zeroes)] (iii) If cubic polynomial ax3+bx2+cx+d=k(x−α)(x−β)(x−γ), where k is any real constant; then α,β and γ are zeroes of cubic polynomial ax3+bx2+cx+d where a,b,c,d∈R and a≠0, then α+β+γ=−ba,αβ+βγ+γα=ca and αβγ=−da ## ILLUSTRATIOM : 8 If zeroes of the polynomial x2+4x+2a are α and 2α, then find the value of α. Given, α and - are the zeroes of x2+4x+2a. Now, product of zeroes = constant term  coefficient of x2 ⇒α×2α=2a⇒2=2α⇒α=1 ## Some useful formulas : (i) α2+β2=(α+β)2−2αβ (ii) α2−β2=(α+β)(α−β)=α+β(α+β)2−4αβ (iii) (α−β)2=(α+β)2−4αβ (iv) α3+β3=(α+β)3−3αβ(α+β) (v) α3−β3=(α−β)3+3αβ(α−β) ## DIVISION OF POLYNOMIALS On dividing a polynomial p(x) by a polynomial d(x), let the quotient be q(x) and the remainder be r(x), then p(x)=d(x).q(x)+r(x), where either r(x)=0 or deg. r(x)<deg.d(x) Here, Dividend =p(x), Divisor =d(x), Quotient =q(x) and Remainder =r(x). Division algorithm of a polynomial by a polynomial : Step 1: Arrange the terms of the dividend and the divisor in descending order of their degrees. Step 2 : Divide the first term of the dividend by the first term of the divisor to obtain the first term of the quotient. Step 3 : Multiply all the terms of the divisor by the first term of the quotient and subtract the result from the dividend. Step 4 : Consider the remainder as new dividend and proceed as before. Step 5 : Repeat this process till we obtain a remainder which is either 0 or a polynomial of degree less than that of the divisor.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>\longdiv</mi><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mo>−</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>+</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mo>−</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></math>

Then remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
So, 2 is the remainder.

rows.question: Find all the zero(es) of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></math>, if you know that two of its zero(es) are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>.
rows.answer:
Two zeroes are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>. Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are the factors of given polynomial.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, is a factor of the given polynomial.
Now, we divide the given polynomial by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt><mi>&</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mi>&</mi><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> (First term of quotient is </mtext><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mtext> ) </mtext></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>−</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>+</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable><mtext> (Third term of quotient is </mtext><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext> ) </mtext></mrow></mrow></math>
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
Now, by splitting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, we factorise <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
So, the remaining two zero(es) are given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. Therefore, the zero(es) of the given polynomial are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and 1 .
# CASE STUDY : Division Algorithm, Factor Theorem, Remainder Theorem and zero(es) of the Polynomial
- Division Algorithm :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Dividend <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Divisor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
- Factor Theorem :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
- Remainder Theorem :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a factor of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
If polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
If polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
If polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
- Zeroes of a Polynomial
If polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Zeroes of a Polynomial
A number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow></math> is a zero of polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
Number of zero(s) of a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Degree of the polynomial.
Hence number zero(s) of alinear polynomial, quadratic polynomial, cubic polynomial and biquadratic polynomial are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> and 4 respectively.
CASE-II : To find the quotient and remainder using division algorithm
Illustration: Apply the division algorithm to find the quotient and remainder on dividing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>, by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
Sol. We have,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
We find that degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> and degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. Therefore, quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is of degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and the remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is of degree zero.
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>.
By using division algorithm, we obtain
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>&</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>&</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
Equating the coefficients of like powers of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and can start term on both sides, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>&</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>&</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>&</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients of </mtext><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mtext> and </mtext><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>&</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext> On equating the coefficients terms </mtext><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>

It is given that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> are two zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Find the roots of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and sketch the graph of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
