Therefore, the roots are -1 and 3 .
The graph intersects the X -axis at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and 3 .
2. How many real roots, i.e., roots that are real numbers, has the parabola of each graph ?
Sol. Graph (a) has two real roots. It has two x -intercepts (i.e., the graph intersects the X -axis at two different points)
Graph (b) has no real roots. It has no x-intercepts. Both roots are complex.
Graph (c) has two real roots which are equal.

4. Find the zero(es) of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold">−</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></math> and verify the relationship between the zero(es) and the coefficients.
Sol. Recall the identity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Using it, we can write:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
So, the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> is zero when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Therefore, the zeroes of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
Now, Sum of zeroes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Product of zeroes </mtext><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Constant term </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Coefficient of </mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
5. Show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></math> is a root of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> is a root of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
6. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is a root of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>, then find the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Sol. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></math> and if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is root of polynomial, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>27</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>128</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>176</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mn>12</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>128</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>356</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>228</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn></mrow></math>
7. Find the remainder when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
Sol. Put <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is a factor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, then find the values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>.

rows.chapter_name: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 1
rows.question:
Check whether the pair of equations
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>
and
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math>
is consistent. If so, solve them graphically.
rows.answer:
Here, a1a2=12,b1b2=3−3=−1,∴a1a2≠b1b2 Hence, the given system of a pair of equations in two variable is consistent. Let us draw the graphs of the equations (i) and (ii). For this, we find two solutions of each of the equations, which are given below in the table. x+3y=6
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></mrow></math>06
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></mrow></math>20
2x−3y=12
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></mrow></math>03
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-4-2
Plot the points A(0,2),B(6,0),P(0,−4) and Q(3,−2) on graph paper, and join the points to form the lines AB and PQ. Point B(6,0) common to both the lines AB and PQ. So, the solution of the pair of linear equations is x=6 and y=0.

rows.chapter_name: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
rows.question:
In each of the following, find whether the system is consistent, inconsistent or dependent :
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
rows.answer:
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∵</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Hence, the given system is consistent.
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∵</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Hence, the given system is inconsistent.
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>24</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∵</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Therefore, the given system is dependent.
## ALGEBRAIC METHODS OF SOLVING A PAIR OF CONSISTENT LINEAR EQUATIONS
A system of a pair of linear equations can be solved algebraically by following three methods.
(A) Substitution Method
(B) Elimination Method
(C) Cross-multiplication Method
## (A) First Method - Substitution Method
In substitution method, you have to express one of the variables in terms of the other using either of the equations and substitute this in other equation.
## Algorithm to find the solution :
A system of a pair of linear equations in two variables:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Step 1 : Find the value of one variable, say <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> in terms of the other variable, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> from either equation, whichever is convenient. Consider this equation as equation (iii).
Step 2 : Substitute this value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> getting from equation (iii) in either equation (i) or (ii). This gives an equation in one variable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, from which you can easily get the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
Step 3 : Substitute the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> obtained in Step 2 in the equations (iii), and obtain the value of the other variable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.

rows.chapter_name: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 3
rows.question:
## Find the solution of the following system by substitution method :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>;</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>
rows.answer:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
It is easy to find the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> in terms of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> from the equation or to find the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> in terms of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> from the second equation. Let us find the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> in terms of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> from the first equation. The result is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>
Now putting the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> in equation (ii), we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>
We now have one equation that is linear in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>; i.e the equation contains only the variable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
On solving, we find that
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> or </mtext><mspace width="1em" /><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>22</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> or </mtext><mspace width="1em" /><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>14</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> or </mtext><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
To get the corresponding value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>, we substitute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> in equation (iii). The result is
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
Thus, the solution of the given pair of linear equations are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.
## (B) Second Method - Elimination Method
## Algorithm to find the solution:
Step 1 : If coefficients of one variable (either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ) in both the equations are equal, then go to step- 2 otherwise multiply one or both the equation(s) by some suitable non-zero constants to make the coefficients of one variable (either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ) numerically equal.
Step 2 : Add one equation to other or subtract one equation from the other so that one variable gets eliminated. In this case, you get an equation in one variable. By solving this equation you can easily get the value of the variable involved in this equation.
Step 3 : Substitute the value of the variable ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> ) obtained in step- 2 in either of the original equations to get the value of the other variable.
The elimination method is preferred when the numerical coefficients of one variable in the original equations are same.
## ILLUSTRATIOM : 4
The ratio of incomes of two persons is 9:7 and the ratio of their expenditures is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>. If each of them manages to save ₹ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow></mrow></math> per month, find their monthly incomes.
Let the income of the two person be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>₹</mi><mn>9</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>₹</mi><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and their expenditures be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>₹</mi><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>₹</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> respectively. Then the equations formed for the given situation are given by :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> and </mtext><mspace width="1em" /><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>9</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2000</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2000</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Step 1 : Multiply equation (i) by 3 and Equation (ii) by 4 to make the coefficients of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> equal. Then, we get the equations:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>27</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6000</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>28</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8000</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Step 2 : Subtract equation (iii) from equation (iv) to eliminate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>, because the coefficients of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> are the same in equation (iii) and (iv). So, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>28</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>27</mn><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>8000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6000</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2000</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Step 3 : Substituting this value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> in (i), we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2000</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2000</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> i.e., </mtext><mspace width="1em" /><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4000</mn></mrow></math>
So, the solution of the equations: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2000</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4000</mn></mrow></math>. Therefore, the monthly incomes of the two persons are ₹ 18,000 and ₹ 14,000 , respectively.
Verification : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>18000</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>14000</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>.
Also, the ratio of their expenditures <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>18000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2000</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>14000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2000</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>16000</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>12000</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
## (C) Third Method - Cross-multiplication Method
## Algorithm to find the solution:
Step 1: Write the given equations in the form :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Step 2 : Taking the help of the diagram given below :
The arrows between the two numbers indicate that they are to be multiplied and the second product is to be subtracted from the first product.
Write equation as
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Step 3 : If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, then solve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and solve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.

rows.chapter_name: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 5
rows.question:
Solve the following equations by cross-multiplication method:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
rows.answer:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Here,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
∴
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>25</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>25</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>45</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
- In a cyclic quadrilateral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, find four angles.
In a cylic quadrilateral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
[sum of opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ]
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>170</mn></mrow></math>
... (i) and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>185</mn></mrow></math>
Using elimination method, multiply equation (i) by (4), we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>170</mn></mrow></math>
On subtracting equation (iii) from (ii), we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>495</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>35</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>37</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>;</mi><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>48</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>143</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>132</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
## SOLUTION OF A SYSTEM OF A PAIR OF EQUATIONS REDUCIBLE TO THE SYSTEM OF A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES
By using the suitable substitution or simplification first we convert the given system into the system of a pair of linear equations in two variables. Then after using any algebraic or graphical method we solve the system.
## ILLUSTRATIOM : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
Solve the equations : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Given equations are : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
...(i) and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></math>
Then the equations become
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mi>…</mi><mtext> (iii) </mtext><mspace width="1em" /><mn>2</mn><mi>u</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Multiplying (iii) by 3, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>.
Adding (iv) and (v), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Substituting this value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> in (iii), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
## SOLVING THE WORD PROBLEMS
Many problems can be solved quickly and easily by converting them into a system of a pair of linear equations in two variables as follows :
(i) Represent the unknown quantities by any two variables say <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>, which are to be determined.
(ii) Find the conditions given in the problem and translate the verbal conditions into a pair of simultaneous linear equations using the variables <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.
(iii) Solve these equations and obtain the required quantities with appropriate units.
## ILLUSTRATIOM : 7
Find the two numbers such that half of the first equals one third of the second and twice their sum exceeds three times the second by 4 .
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> be the first and second numbers respectively. We can write two equations almost directly from the statements of the problem as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
.... (i) and
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
Find the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> in terms of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> from first equation, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Now putting the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> in terms of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> in second equation, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math> (second number)
Now putting the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> in equation (i), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> (first number)
## APPLICATIONS OF A SYSTEM OF A PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES
It is used to solve real life problem having two unknown by converting the real life problem into a pair of linear equations. It will be more clear by the following Illustration.

rows.chapter_name: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 8
rows.question:
On a national highway, place <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are 250 km apart from each other.
A car starts from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> \& another from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> at the same time. If they go in the same direction then they meet in 5 hours and if they go in opposite directions they meet in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> hours. Find their speeds.
rows.answer:
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> be the two cars. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> starts from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> with constant speed of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> starts from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> with constant speed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Case I: When the two cars move in same direction as shown in figures, the cars meet at position <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>.
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> i.e., the distance travelled by car <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> in 5 hours with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>y</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> i.e. the distance travelled by car <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> in 5 hours with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
We have, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>250</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>250</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow></math>
Case II: When two cars move in opposite direction as shown in figure, the cars meet at the position <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>.
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>25</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>25</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>y</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
So, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>R</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>250</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>25</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>25</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>250</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>130</mn></mrow></math>
Adding (i) and (ii), we get ; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>90</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>130</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow></math>
Speed of car <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>90</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and speed of car <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

rows.title: Exercise 2 — Text-book Questions — Q2
rows.question:
Let Aftab's present age be x years. Daughter's present age be y years. Now, seven years ago, Aftab's age =(x−7) years. Daughter's age =(y−7) years. After three years, Aftab's age =(x+3) years. Daughter's age =(y+3) years. Now, according to the question, (i) Seven years ago, Aftab's age =7 times the age of the daughter ⇒x−7=7(y−7) ⇒x−7=7y−49 ⇒x−7y=−42 (ii) Three years from now, Aftab's age =3 times the age of the daughter ⇒(x+3)=3(y+3) ⇒x+3=3y+9 ⇒x−3y=6 Thus, algebraic representation of given situation is given by the equations (i) and (ii). Now, represent this situation graphically, we find two solutions of each equation. x−7y+42=0
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></mrow></math>-420
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></mrow></math>06
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></mrow></math>60
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></mrow></math>0-2
Now, we plot these points A ( −42,0 ), B ( 0,6 ) and C(6,0),D(0,−2) to get the lines, on graph. Thus, in the above graph, the two lines representing the two equations intersecting at the point (42,12). Hence, x=42 and y=12 ∴ Aftab's present age =42 years. His daughter's present age =12 years. Also, when his daughter was, born, Aftab's age =42−12=30 years.

rows.question:
(i) Let Nuri's present age <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> years.
Let Sonu's present age <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> years.
According to the question,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>
and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>

Since, coefficients of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> are same in both the equations therefore, subtract equation (ii) from equation (i), we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></math>.
Put value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> in (i), we get, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow></math>
So, Nuri's present age <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow></math> years
and Sonu's present age <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow></math> years.
(ii) Let the fixed charges for 3 days be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>₹</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and additional charges for each day be ₹ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>27</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∵</mo><mtext> additional days </mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext> and </mtext><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>21</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∵</mo><mtext> additional days </mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math>
Subtract equation (ii) from equation (i), we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>27</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>21</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>&</mi><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>27</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>21</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mrow></math>

Hence, fixed charge <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>₹</mi><mn>15</mn></mrow></math> and additional charge <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>₹</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo>∵</mo><mtext> Area of rectangle </mtext><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>

Now, divide each one of the given equation by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mtext> and </mtext><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> then equations becomes
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>

Now, subtract equation (i) from equation (ii), we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>v</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>v</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
Put value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> in equation (i), we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
On adding (i) \& (ii)
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>

rows.chapter_name: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q1
rows.question:
(a) If the lines are parallel, then
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Taking II and III part of equation (i), we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>≠</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>
So, option (a) is correct.
rows.answer: consistent

rows.chapter_name: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.title: Assertion \& Reason — Multiple Choice Questions — Q2
rows.question:
(c) Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
For a pair of linear equations to have infinitely many solutions:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
So, we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> which gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>36</mn></mrow></math> i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>±</mi><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>
Also, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, which means <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>.
Therefore, the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> that satisfies both the conditions, is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>. For this value, the pair of linear equations has infinitely many solutions.
rows.answer: 4 and 1

Given equations are
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>;</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> We know that equations represent coincident lines if they are consistent with many solutions.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>28</mn></mrow></math>
Hence, for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>28</mn></mrow></math>, given equations represent coincident lines.

Given equations are
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>;</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> We know that equations represent coincident lines if they are consistent with many solutions.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>28</mn></mrow></math>
Hence, for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>28</mn></mrow></math>, given equations represent coincident lines.

rows.question:
Since, system of equations,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>;</mi><mn>12</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> has infinitely many solutions.
Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Take first two parts, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>12</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>36</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>±</mi><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>.
Therefore, the values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>±</mi><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>.
But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> does not satisfy the equation (i).
Hence, the required value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is only 6 .

Thus, we have either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mtext> or </mtext><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mn>23</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> The number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>41</mn></mrow></math>
or

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>23</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>
Solving these equations, we get
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>19</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>137</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>137</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
But this is not possible since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> are digits
Hence the number is 41 .
