## CONSTRUCTION OF A TANGENT TO A CIRCLE (AT A GIVEN POINT)
Case (a): To draw the tangent to a circle at a given point on it, when the centre of the circle is known :
Required : To draw the tangent to the circle at P .
Steps of construction :
(i) Take a point O as centre and draw a circle of given radius.
(ii) Take a point P on the circle.
(iii) Join OP.
(iv) Draw a line AB perpendicular to OP at the point P . Line APB is the required tangent at P .

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 5
rows.question: Draw a circle of diameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> with centre <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝐎</mi></mrow></math>. Through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow></math>, draw tangent to the circle.
rows.answer:
Given : A circle of diameter AB with centre O .
Required : To draw tangent to the circle at B .
Steps of construction :
(i) Draw a circle with O as centre and radius equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(ii) Draw a diameter AOB .
(iii) Draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mi>⟂</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>90</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
So, CD is the required tangent.
Case (b) : To draw the tangent to a circle at a given point on it, when the centre of the circle is
not known.
Given : A circle and a point P on it.
Required : To draw the tangent to the circle at P .
Steps of construction :
(i) Draw any chord PQ through P and join P and Q to a point R in major <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>⏜</mo></mover></mrow></math> (or minor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>⏜</mo></mover></mrow></math> ).
(ii) Construct <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></math> equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and on opposite side of R with respect to chord PQ .
Produce BP to A to get the required tangent APB
## To draw the circum-circle of a given triangle.
## Steps of Construction
Step 1: Draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> with the given measurements.
Step 2: Draw perpendicular bisectors of the two of the sides, say AB and AC to intersect at O .
Step 3: Taking O as centre, and the radius equal to AO or BO or CO , draw a circle. The circle passes through all the vertices <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and C of the triangle. ∴ The circle drawn is the required circum-circle.
## CONSTRUCTION OF TANGENTS TO A CIRCLE FROM A POINT OUTSIDE THE CIRCLE
In this situation, when the point lies outside the circle, there will be two tangents to the circle from this point.
In this construction, again we have two different situations:
Case (a) : To draw the tangents to a circle from a point outside it (external point), when its centre is known.
Given : A circle with centre O and a point P outside it.
Required : To construct the tangents to the circle from point P .
Steps of construction :
(i) Join OP and bisect it. Let M be the mid-point of OP .
(ii) Taking M as centre and MO as radius, draw a circle which intersect the given circle in two points, say A and B .
(iii) Join P to A and P to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>.</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and PB are the required tangents from P to given circle .

rows.question: Draw a circle of radius 2.5 cm . From a point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. apart from the centre of the circle, draw two tangents to the circle.
rows.answer:
Given : A point P is at a distance of 6 cm . from the centre of a circle with radius 2.5 cm .
Required : To draw two tangents to the circle from the given point P .
Steps of construction :
(i) Draw a line segment OP of length 6 cm .
(ii) With centre O and radius equal to 2.5 cm , draw a circle.
(iii) Draw the right bisector of OP , which intersects OP at M .
(iv) Taking M as centre and MO as radius, draw a circle, which intersect the given circle in two points, say A and B .
(v) Join PA and PB . These are the required tangents from P to the given circle.
Case (b): To draw the tangents to a circle from a point outside it (external point), when its centre is not known.
Given : A circle and a point P outside it.
Required : To construct the tangents to the circle from point P .
Step of construction :
(i) Through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> draw a secant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, which intersects the circle at points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> (say).
(ii) Produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> to a point C such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is the mid-point of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
(iii) Draw a semi-circle with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> as diameter.
(iv) Draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>⟂</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, which intersects the semi-circle at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>.
(v) With <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> as centre and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> as radius draw arcs to intersect the given circle at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(vi) Join P to T and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Then PT and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> are the required tangents.

rows.answer:
Given : A circle with radius 4 cm and a point P outside it.
Required : To draw two tangents to the circle from the given point P .
## Step of construction :
(i) Draw a circle of radius 4 cm .
(ii) Take a point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> outside the circle and draw a secant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, which intersects the circle at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
(iii) Produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>.
(iv) Draw a semi-circle with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> as diameter.
(v) Draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>⟂</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, which intersects the semi-circle at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>.
(vi) With <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> as centre and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> as radius draw arcs to intersect the given circle at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(vii) Join <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><msup><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> are the required tangents.
To construct the direct common tangents to the circles of radii 3.5 cm and 1.5 cm whose centres are 6.5 cm apart.
Step 1: Draw line segment, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>6.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Step 2: Draw circles with radii 3.5 cm and 1.5 cm respectively with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> as centres.
Step 3: Bisect <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> at P and draw a circle taking P as centre and radius equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
Step 4: Draw another circle with radius equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, taking the centre of larger circle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> intersecting the circle drawn in step 3 at A and B .
Step 5: Join <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and produce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></math> to meet the outer circle at S and T respectively.
Step 6: Draw line segments <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>, such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>U</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mi>V</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> arc points on the circle with centre <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
Step 7: Join SU and TV. These are the required direct common tangents.
## Learn More
Locute the centre of a circular disk.
Hint: Perpendicular bisectors of two non parallel chords of circle passes through the centre of the circle.
## Steps of construction:
(i) Draw two non parallel chords of any length AB and PQ .
(ii) Draw perpendicular bisectors XY and LM of AB and PQ respectively, which intersect at point O .
So, O is the required centre of circle.
## MISCELLANEOUS SOLVED EXAMPLES
1. Draw a triangle ABC with side <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>75</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Construct a triangle whose sides are (4/3) times the corresponding side of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Sol. Steps of construction :
(i) Draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(ii) Draw a ray BX and CY such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Y</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>75</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Suppose BX and CY intersect at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>.</mo><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, so obtained is the given triangle.
(iii) Draw a ray BZ making an acute angle with BC on opposite side of vertex A with respect to BC .
(iv) Draw four (greater of 4 and 3 in 4/3) arcs intersecting the rays BZ at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
(v) Join <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to C and draw a line through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> parallel to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>, intersecting the extended line segment BC at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(vi) Draw a line through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> parallel to CA intersecting the extended line segment BA at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
Triangle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> so obtained is the required triangle.
2. Construct a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> in which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>7.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Now construct a triangle similar to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> such that each of its sides is third-fourth
of the corresponding sides of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Also prove your assertion.
Sol. Steps of construction :
(i) Draw a line segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(ii) With B as centre and radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, draw an arc.
(iii) With C as centre and radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>7.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, draw another arc, intersecting the arc drawn in step (ii) at the point A .
(iv) Join A to B and C to obtain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(v) Below BC draw ray BX , making an acute angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(vi) Draw four arcs intersecting the ray BX at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(vii) Join <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
(viii) Since we have to construct a triangle each of whose sides is third-fourth of the corresponding sides of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. Hence draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
(ix) From <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, intersecting BA at point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is the required triangle.
3. Construct a triangle similar to a given equilateral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow></math> with side 5 cm such that each
of its sides is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> th of the corresponding side of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Sol. Steps of construction :
(i) Draw a line segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) With Q as centre and radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, draw an arc.
(iii) With R as centre and radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, draw another arc intersecting the arc drawn in step (ii) at the point P .
(iv) Join PQ and PR to obtain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(v) Below QR , draw ray QX making an acute angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
(vi) Draw seven arcs intersecting the ray QX at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>; such that
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
(vii) Join <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>.
(viii) Draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msub><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>, intersecting QR at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(ix) From <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> draw <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, intersecting the QP at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
We get required <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> similar to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>.
4. Construct a triangle similar to a given triangle ABC with its sides equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">5</mn></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> th of the corresponding sides of triangle ABC .
Sol. Steps of construction :

rows.question: A square park has each side of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. At each corner of the park, there is a flower bed in the form of a quadrant of radius 14 m as shown in Fig. Find the area of the remaining part of the park (Use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">π</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ).
rows.answer:
Let A be the area of each quadrant of a circle of radius 14 m . Then,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>154</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
∴ Area of 4 quadrants <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>154</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>616</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Area of square park having side 100 m long <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Hence, Area of the remaining part of the park <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>616</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>9384</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

Circumference of planets helps us to compare their relative sizes \& artificial satellite that are launched in space to travel in orbits of certain circumference.
## CONGRUENT CIRCLES AND ARCS
Two circles or arcs are said to be congruent if we can superpose (place) one over the other such that they cover each other completely.
## PERIMETER AND AREA OF SECTOR OF A CIRCLE
Two radii OA and OB enclose a portion of the circular region which makes a central angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math>. The region is called a sector of the circle. In fig., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the sector with central angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math>. Area of major segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Area of the circle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo></mrow></math> Area of minor segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>360</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 4
rows.question: A chord <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> of a circle of radius 10 cm makes a right angle at the centre of the circle. Find the area of the major and minor segments (Take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">π</mi></mrow><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold">=</mo></mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mo mathvariant="bold">.</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow></math> )
rows.answer:
We know that the area of a minor segment of angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math> (in degrees) in a circle of radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is given by
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>360</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mi>sin</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>cos</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>90</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo>∴</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3.14</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>90</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>360</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mi>sin</mi><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>cos</mi><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3.14</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>3.14</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>50</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>78.5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>50</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>28.5</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>
Area of the major segment <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Area of the circle - Area of the minor segment
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mn>3.14</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>28.5</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>314</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>28.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>285.5</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
## AREA OF COMBINATIONS OF PLANE FIGURES
Whenever a plane figure is made by combination of two or more plane figures, then the area of combination of plane figures is always equal to the sum of the areas of the constituent figures.
## IMPORTANT POINTS TO BE REMEMBER
(i) Distance moved by a wheel in 1 revolution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Circumference of a wheel
(ii) Number of revolutions in one minute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Distance covered in1minute </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Circumference </mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(iii) Angle described by minute hand in 60 minute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(iv) Angle described by hour hand in 12 hour <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(v) The sum of the arcs of major and minor sectors of a circle is equal to the circumference of the circle.
(vi) The sum of the areas of major and minor sectors of a circle is equal to the area of the circle.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 1
rows.question: A square park has each side of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. At each corner of the park, there is a flower bed in the form of a quadrant of radius 14 m as shown in Fig. Find the area of the remaining part of the park (Use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">π</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ).
rows.answer:
Let A be the area of each quadrant of a circle of radius 14 m . Then,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>154</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
∴ Area of 4 quadrants <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>154</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>616</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Area of square park having side 100 m long <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Hence, Area of the remaining part of the park <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>616</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>9384</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 2
rows.question: A race track is in the form of a ring whose inner circumference is 352 m and the outer circumference is 396 m . Find the width of the track.
rows.answer:
Let the outer and inner radii of ring be R meter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>&</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> meter respectively.
According to question,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>396</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>352</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>396</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>352</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>63</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>56</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Hence, width of the track <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>63</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>56</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> metres
Circumference of planets helps us to compare their relative sizes \& artificial satellite that are launched in space to travel in orbits of certain circumference.
## CONGRUENT CIRCLES AND ARCS
Two circles or arcs are said to be congruent if we can superpose (place) one over the other such that they cover each other completely.
## PERIMETER AND AREA OF SECTOR OF A CIRCLE
Two radii OA and OB enclose a portion of the circular region which makes a central angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math>. The region is called a sector of the circle. In fig., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the sector with central angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math>. Let ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> ' be the length of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>arc</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo>⏜</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mtext> circumference </mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> [Corresponding arcs subtend proportional central angles] or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>180</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, where r is the radius of the circle
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Perimeter of the sector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mover><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mo>⏜</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>180</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Also, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Area of sector </mtext><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext> Area of the circle </mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>⇒</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Area of sector </mtext><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> or Area of sector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 3
rows.question: Find the area of the sector of a circle with radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mtext mathvariant="bold"> </mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and of angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold">∘</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Also, find the area of the corresponding major sector. (Take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">π</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">3</mn><mo mathvariant="bold">.</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">4</mn></mrow></mrow></math> )
rows.answer:
Here, radius of circle (r) is 10 cm . and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
In figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the minor sector corresponding to angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>60</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>Q</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the major sector.
The area of the sector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>P</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>360</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>3.14</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>314</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>157</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>360</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mi>sin</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>cos</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo>∴</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3.14</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>90</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>360</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mi>sin</mi><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mi>cos</mi><msup><mn>45</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3.14</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>3.14</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>50</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>78.5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>50</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>28.5</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>

## AREA OF COMBINATIONS OF PLANE FIGURES
Whenever a plane figure is made by combination of two or more plane figures, then the area of combination of plane figures is always equal to the sum of the areas of the constituent figures.
## IMPORTANT POINTS TO BE REMEMBER
(i) Distance moved by a wheel in 1 revolution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Circumference of a wheel
(ii) Number of revolutions in one minute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Distance covered in1minute </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Circumference </mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(iii) Angle described by minute hand in 60 minute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(iv) Angle described by hour hand in 12 hour <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>360</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
(v) The sum of the arcs of major and minor sectors of a circle is equal to the circumference of the circle.
(vi) The sum of the areas of major and minor sectors of a circle is equal to the area of the circle.

## SPHERE
Sphere is a set of points in the space which are equidistant from a fixed point. The fixed point is called the centre of the sphere and the distance is called the radius of the sphere.
A football, a cricket ball, the earth are some examples of sphere.

- Volume <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
(b) Hemisphere
If a solid sphere is cut into two halves by a plane passing through the centre of sphere, then each of the two halves is called a hemisphere.
For a hemisphere of radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>, we have
- Curved surface area <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
- Total surface area <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
- Volume <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
## (c) Hollow Sphere/Spherical Shell
From a sphere, a smaller sphere having the same centre of the sphere, is cut off, then hollow sphere is obtained.
- External surface area <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
- Internal surface area <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
- Volume <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
## (d) Hemispherical Shell
If a spherical shell is cut into two halves by a plane passing through the centre of spherical shell, then each of the two halves is called a hemispherical shell.
- Internal curved surface area <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> sq. units
- External curved surface area <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> sq. units
- Total surface area <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Internal surface area + Ext. surface area + Area of ring
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mtext> units </mtext></mrow></math>
- Volume of the material used to form hemispherical shell
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mtext> cubic units </mtext></mrow></math>
## Learn
## তি⿴囗大
## More
Let us consider a cone exactly fitted in a cylinder．
Volume of the cylinder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
Volume of a cone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
In this case，volume of cone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>（Volume of cylinder）
Again，consider a sphere exactly fitted in a cylinder
Volume of a sphere <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>（Volume of cylinder）
In this case，volume of a sphere <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>（Volume of cylinder）
So，volume of a cone and a sphere together makes a cylinder，if radius and height of solids are same，having height is 2 r ．

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 3
rows.question: Three cubes each of side 5 cm are joined end to end. Find the surface area of the resulting cuboid.
rows.answer:
The dimensions of the cuboid so formed are as under :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Breadth <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>,
and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Height <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
∴ Surface area of the cuboid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
⇒ Surface area of the cuboid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>75</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>75</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>350</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
## VOLUME OF A COMBINATION OF SOLIDS
Whenever a solid is formed by combining two or more solids, then the amount of matter present in the combination of solids is equal to the sum of amounts of matter in the constituting solids.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> Volume of new solid <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Sum of the volumes of the individual solids.
Did You
Know!
If the volume is same for different solids then sphere is shape that has smallest surface area. That is why it appears in nature in the form of water drops, bubbles and planets.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 4
rows.question: A solid wooden toy is in the shape of a right circular cone mounted on a hemisphere. If the radius of the hemisphere is 4.2 cm and the total height of the toy is 10.2 cm , find the volume of the wooden toy.
rows.answer:
We have, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>V</mi><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>10.2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4.2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> be the radius of the hemisphere and h be the height of the conical part of the toy.
Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4.2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>V</mi><mi>O</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>V</mi><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>O</mi><msup><mi>O</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10.2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4.2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Also, radius of the base of the cone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>O</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4.2</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
∴ Volume of the wooden toy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Volume of the conical part
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo>+</mo><mtext> Volume of the hemispherical part </mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>4.2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4.2</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4.2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>22</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>4.2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4.2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>14.4</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>266.11</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>
## CONVERSION OF SOLID FROM ONE SHAPE TO ANOTHER
- When a solid is converted from one shape to other, then its volume remains same only its shape and size changes
- If a solid is converted into a number of small identical solids of same or a different shape then
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Number of small items </mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext> Volume of larger object </mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext> Volume of smaller object </mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

rows.question: A metallic sphere of radius 4.2 cm is melted and recast into the shape of a cylinder of radius 6 cm . Find the height of the cylinder. Take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">π</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">7</mn></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> unless stated otherwise.
rows.answer:
Let the height of the cylinder made <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Its radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Volume of the cylinder made = Volume of the given metallic sphere of radius 4.2 cm
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4.2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>⇒</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4.2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4.2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4.2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2.774</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
rows.question: A container shaped like a right circular cylinder having diameter 12 cm and height 15 cm is full of ice-cream. The ice-cream is to be filled into cones of height 12 cm and diameter 6 cm , having a hemispherical shape on the top. Find the number of such cones which can be filled with ice-cream.
rows.answer:
Volume of one ice-cream cone as shown in figure
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Volume of conical part + Volume of hemispherical part
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Volume of the ice-cream in the cylindrical container (of height 15 cm and diameter 12 cm )
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math>
Let the number of cones made be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.
Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>×</mo><mn>45</mn><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>×</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mn>45</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>36</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math>
∴ Required number of ice-cream cone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math>

rows.question: How many silver coins, 1.75 cm in diameter and of thickness 2 mm , must be melted to form a cuboid of dimensions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>×</mo><mn>10</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>×</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> ?
rows.answer:
Let the required number of coins be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. ## FRUSTUM OF A CONE
If a cone is cut by a plane parallel to the base of the cone, then the portion between the plane and base is called the frustum of the cone.
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> be the height, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi></mrow></math> the slant height and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> the radii of the ends ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>></mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> ) of the frustum of a cone. Then we can directly find the volume, the curved surface area and the total surface area of frustum by using the formulae given below :
(i) Volume of the frustum of cone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(ii) Curved surface area of the frustum of cone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>ℓ</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>
(iii) Total surface area of the frustum of the cone <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mi>ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>π</mi><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>π</mi><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>
(iv) Total surface area of a bucket <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mi>ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>

Clearly, bucket forms a frustum of a cone such that the radii of its circular ends are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>28</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and height <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. ⇒ Capacity of the bucket <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>28</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⇒</mo></mrow></math> Capacity of the bucket <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>330</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>147</mn><msup><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> be the radii of the ends of the frustum. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>≠</mo></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>≠</mo></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
