(iii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is an even prime number greater than 2<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is the empty set, because 2 is the only even prime number.
(iv) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> is odd <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is the empty set, because the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> is not satisfied by any odd value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
## Singleton Set
A set, consisting of a single element is called a singleton set. For example: The sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> are singleton sets. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is a singleton set, because this set contains only one integer -6 .
## Finite and Infinite Sets
A set which is empty or consists of a definite number of elements is called finite otherwise, the set is called infinite.
## Consider some examples :
(i) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> be the set of the days of the week. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> is finite.
(ii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> be the set of solutions of the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> is finite.
(iii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> be the set of points on a line. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> is infinite.
We represent the infinite set in the roster form by writing a few elements which clearly indicate the structure of the set followed (or preceded) by multiple of three dots. For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is the set of natural numbers, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is the set of odd natural numbers,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mi>…</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is the set of integers. All these sets are infinite.
Note : All infinite sets can not be described in the roster form.
The three dots ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>…</mi></mrow></math> ) are called an ellipsis and it means "Continue on".
## Equal Sets
Two sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are said to be equal if they have exactly the same elements. Two equal set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are represented as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. Otherwise, the sets are said to be unequal and we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
For example : Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
## ILLUSTRATIOM : 3
Which of the following pairs of sets are equal? Justify your answer.
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>, the set of letters in "ALLOY" and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, the set of letters in "LOYAL".
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>≤</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix" /></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix" /><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
(i) We have, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are equal sets as different order of elements in a set do not change a set. Thus, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Since some elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> do not belong to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, therefore <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> are not equal sets.
## DISJOINT SETS
Two sets A and B are said to be disjoint, if they have no elements in common.
For example: Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>&</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are disjoint sets.
## Subsets
A set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is said to be a subset of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> if every element of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is also an element of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. Here, set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is called superset of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.
Symbolically, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> if whenever <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Here ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ' is read as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is the subset of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Note : It is often convenient to use the symbol "⇒" which means implies. Using this symbol, we can write the definition of subset as follows: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
We read the above statement as " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is an element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> implies that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is also an element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ". If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is not a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⊄</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. For example :
(i) The set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> of rational numbers is a subset of the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> of real numbers, so we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>.
(ii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is the set of all divisors of 56 and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> the set of all prime divisors of 56 , then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>. So we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.
(iii) Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is not a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, also <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is not a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.
## IMPORTANT POINTS ABOUT SUBSETS
(i) Every set is a subset of itself.
(ii) The empty set is a subset of every set.
(iii) Number of subsets of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is number of elements in the given set.
## INTERVALS AS SUBSETS OF SET OF REAL NUMBERS (R)
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>. Then, the set of real numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>y</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>y</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is called an open interval and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as interval. All the points between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> belong to the open interval <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> themselves do not belong to this interval.
The interval which contains the end points also, is called closed interval and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>. Thus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>a</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
We can also have intervals closed at one end and open at the other, i.e.,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>a</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is a semi-open interval from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, including <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> but excluding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is a semi-open interval from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> including <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> but excluding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>.
These sets can be shown by the dark portion of the number line and use dark circle for included number and hollow circle for not included point.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 4
rows.question:
Write the following intervals in set builder form:
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
rows.answer:
The following intervals are written in set builder form as :
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is an open interval which does not include both -3 and 0 . So, it can be shown in the set builder form of a set as : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>.
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math> is a closed interval which includes both 6 and 12 . So, it can be shown in the set builder form as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>.
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math> is an interval closed at the second end only i.e., it excludes 6 but includes 12 . So, it is shown in the set builder form as : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>.
(iv) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is an interval closed at the first end point but open at the second end point. It means that the interval includes -23 but excludes 5 . It is written in the set builder form as : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>.
## POWER SET OF A SET
The set of all subsets of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is called the power set of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>. It is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Note that in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, every element is a set.
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> elements, then its power set has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> elements.
Ex. : Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
Here, number of elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>
## UNIVERSAL SET
If there are some sets under consideration, and out of these sets, there is a set which is the superset of each one of the given sets. That is all other sets under consideration are subsets of this set. Such a set is known as the universal set, denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math>. For example :
(i) In the context of human population studies, the universal set consists of all the people in the world.
(ii) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> are sets under consideration, then set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> can be considered as universal set because all other three sets are the subset of this set.
## ILLUSTRATIOM : 5
What universal set would you propose for each of the following :
(i) The set of right triangles.
(ii) The set of isosceles triangles.
(i) The universal set for the set of right triangles is the set of triangles.
(ii) The universal set for the set of isosceles triangle is the set of equilateral triangles or set of triangles.
## VENN DIAGRAMS
In order to illustrate universal sets, subsets and certain operations on sets in a clear and simple way, we make use of geometric figures. These figures are called Venn-Diagrams. In Venn Diagrams, a universal set is represented by a rectangle and any other set is represented by a circle in it.
In the Venn-diagrams, the elements of the sets are written in their respective circles.
In the Venn-diagram, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is the universal set of which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> are subsets.
## OPERATION ON SETS
## Union of Sets
The union of two sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the set which consists of all those elements which are either in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> or in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> (including those which are in both). In symbols, we write
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
The union of two sets can be represented by a Venn diagram as shown in Figure.
The shaded portion in Figure represents <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">6</mn></mrow></mrow></math>
rows.question:
Find the union of each of the following pairs of sets :
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a natural number and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a natural number and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></math>
rows.answer:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a natural number and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a natural number and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>⇒</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>∪</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) We have, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>∪</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
## Intersection of Sets
The intersection of two sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the set of all those elements which belong to both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. Symbolically, we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
The shaded portion in Figure indicates the intersection of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
## ILLUSTRATIOM : 7
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>, then find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a multiple of 3 and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a multiple of 4 .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a multiple of 3 and 4 both
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is a multiple of 12
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math>
Hence, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
## Difference of Two Sets
The difference of the sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is the set of elements which belong to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> but not to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. Symbolically, we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and read as " <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> minus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> ".
Using the setbuilder notation, we can rewrite the definition of difference as
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∉</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
The difference of two sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> can be represented by Venn diagram as shown in the figure. The shaded portion represents the difference of sets A and B i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
## Complement of a Set
Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> be the universal set and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> be a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math>. Then, the complement of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is the set of all elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> which are not the elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>. Symbolically, we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> to denote the complement of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> with respect to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math>. Thus, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∉</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>.
Obviously, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>
The complement <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> of a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> can be represented by a Venn diagram as shown in the figure. The shaded portion represents the complement of the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>.
## Some Properties of Complement of a Set
1. Complement laws: (i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> (ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>′</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></math>
2. ## RELATION
## Ordered Pair
Two elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> listed in a specific order form an ordered pair denoted by ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> ).
In general, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≠</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
Two ordered pairs are equal, if and only if the corresponding first elements are equal and the second elements are also equal.
## Cartesian Product of Sets
If A and B are two non-empty sets, then the set of all ordered pairs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is called the Cartesian product of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Thus, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>:</mi><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>, then we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></math>.
## Relation
A relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> from a non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> to a non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is a subset of the cartesian product <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. The subset is derived by describing a relationship between the first element and the second element of the ordered pairs in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
A relation from a non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> to non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is symbolically represented by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Eg : Consider two non-empty sets:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and a rule "less than" which relate the elements of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> to the elements of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. Then, the relation from set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
Here order pairs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are the element of relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>.

## Image

## Domain of a Relation

So, range of the relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
## Co-domain of a Relation
The set B is known as the codomain of a relation from a non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> to non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.
Consider the relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> from set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
Then, codomain of the relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
Note: 1. Rang <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>≤</mo></mrow></math> Co-domain.
2. If there is a relation from a non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> to the same non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>, then it said that 'relation in set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> '.
For example, a relation 'less than' in set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
## FUNCTION
A relation ' <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> ' from a non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> to a non-empty set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is symbolically written as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, is said to be function if every element of set A has a unique image in set
B. Since function is a special type of relation. So, it has also domain, codomain and range as of relation.
Like a relation, for the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is called the domain and set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> is called the codomain of the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math>.
For example : Let us consider a relation from set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, where
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and the
relation is defined by the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.
Hence, the relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
This relation can be also shown diagramatically in the figure.
Here, we see that each element of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> is related with unique (only one) element of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>. Hence, the above relation is a function.
Domain of the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
Range of the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
Co-domain of the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
Example : Let consider another relation from set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>25</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and the relation defined by the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>.
Hence, the relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
This relation can also be shown in the figure.
Here, we see that an element 9 of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is related with two elements -3 and 3 of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>.
Hence, each element of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is not related with the unique (only one) element of set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>.
Therefore, the given relation is not a function.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 11
rows.question:
Which of the following relations are functions? Give reasons. If it is a function, determine its domain and range.
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
rows.answer:
(i) We have, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
No two ordered pairs have the same first component, i.e. each element of the domain is uniquely related to the element of codomain, therefore this relation is a function.
Domain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>17</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>, Range <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
(ii) We have, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
We observe that no two ordered pairs have the same first component, so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> is a function.
Domain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>14</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>; Range <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
(iii) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>
We observe that 1 has appeared more than once as first component of the ordered pairs in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> i.e. each element of the domain is not uniquely related to the element of codomain,
Therefore, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> is not a function.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 12.
rows.question: Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> be a function from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math> defined by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, for some integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>. Determine <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.
rows.answer:
We have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>
for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>
Subtracting eq. (ii) from (i), we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.

rows.title: ILLUSTRATION : 13
